title: `GetOldObject` not implemented by `admission.VersionedAttributes`
body:
### What happened?

While implementing and testing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633; I realized that `admission.VersionedAttributes` does not override the `GetOldObject` method, which is used for admission webhooks. This means that the embedded `admission.Attributes`' `GetOldObject()` method actually becomes used, and returns the internal object (if core type) or previously stored (if CRD).

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/90b175c8760fcdfea7b9757fb3c366bbe1d4a1fa/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/conversion.go#L55-L60

/sig api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected `GetOldObject` to be implemented for `VersionedAttributed`, so that the versioned old object is returned, not the unversioned one. It should work similarly to `GetObject`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Example integration test, that was failing before overriding `GetOldObject` correctly: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141959/changes/3e9a132e3f7b8cfbb12189a4671289ab7aec5488

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

Latest master, 90b175c8760fcdfea7b9757fb3c366bbe1d4a1fa

title: Kubelet emits spurious Pod status updates due to nondeterministic allocated resource health ordering
body:
### What happened?

With `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled, kubelet can change the order of entries in `status.containerStatuses[*].allocatedResourcesStatus` even when device and claim health have not changed.

There are two nondeterministic paths in kubelet v1.36.3:

1. The device manager constructs each `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice by iterating a map of device IDs. The same resource IDs can therefore be emitted in a different order on later syncs.
2. The DRA manager rebuilds `AllocatedResourcesStatus` by iterating `resourceStatusMap`. This can reorder device-plugin and claim statuses, for example:

```text
[nvidia.com/gpu, claim:channel]
[claim:channel, nvidia.com/gpu]
```

The resulting Pod status is semantically unchanged but serialized differently. Kubelet treats it as a status change and sends a Pod status update. The API server then stores a new resource version and broadcasts a full `MODIFIED` watch event. This can create continuous status and watch churn for otherwise unchanged Pods.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should produce a stable `AllocatedResourcesStatus` representation when resource health is unchanged. Both the outer `[]ResourceStatus` and each inner `[]ResourceHealth` should have deterministic ordering, so repeated syncs do not cause unnecessary Pod status updates.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run kubelet v1.36.3 with `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled.
2. Start a Pod whose container has at least two device-plugin devices and a DRA resource claim with health reporting. Generic test device-plugin and DRA drivers are sufficient.
3. Keep all reported health values unchanged.
4. Trigger or wait for repeated Pod status syncs and watch:

```console
kubectl get pod <pod> -w -o json
```

5. Observe that either:
   - entries in a `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice change order, or
   - entries in `AllocatedResourcesStatus` change order.

The Pod `resourceVersion` advances and a `MODIFIED` watch event is emitted despite no health change.

This can also be reproduced in unit tests by calling the two `UpdateAllocatedResourcesStatus` implementations repeatedly with multiple map entries and asserting that their output is canonical.

### Anything else we need to know?

The relevant v1.36.3 code paths are:

- Device ID map iteration while constructing `ResourceStatus.Resources`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L1162-L1177
- DRA map iteration while rebuilding `AllocatedResourcesStatus`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L936-L943
- The device-manager-then-DRA call order: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L1135-L1145

A minimal fix is to canonicalize the final status by `ResourceStatus.Name` and each resource list by `ResourceHealth.ResourceID`, with regression tests covering stable output across repeated calls.

/sig node

```console
$ kubelet --version

```

author: soltysh

comments.body: /assign

Root cause is deterministic rather than a flake in the log path itself: `OpenWebSocketForURL` rewrites the scheme of the caller's `*url.URL` in place (`https` -> `wss`, then on the next call `wss` -> `ws`). The test builds the URL once and retries with `Eventually`, so whenever the first attempt returns before the container has flushed its output, every retry dials plaintext `ws://` against the TLS port and gets Go's `400 Bad Request`, which the client reports as `bad status`. That matches the failing runs: one hijacked `CONNECT .../log` in the apiserver log, nothing after it, and Gomega noting the function "did return successfully" once with an empty string. Fix in #142285.

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

title: [Feature][scheduler] Asynchronously or concurrently update (Composite)PodGroup status conditions to avoid scheduling cycle head-of-line blocking
body:
/sig scheduling
/area scheduler
/kind feature
### Description
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140670, status condition updates for `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` were integrated into the scheduler pipeline.
Currently, in `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go`), status updates for every group within a hierarchy are performed sequentially and synchronously on the main scheduling goroutine:
```go
for _, podGroupResult := range podGroupResults {
    pgi := podGroupResult.podGroupInfo
    if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil {
        sched.submitCompositePodGroupResult(ctx, podGroupResult)
        continue
    }
    queuedPodInfos := rootPodGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos[pgi.GetKey()]
    sched.submitPodGroupResult(ctx, schedFwk, podGroupState, queuedPodInfos, podGroupResult)
}
```
Each call to `submitCompositePodGroupResult` / `submitPodGroupResult` issues an individual, synchronous status patch request to the API server (`util.PatchPodGroupStatus` / `util.PatchCompositePodGroupStatus`).
### Why this is a problem
For larger or deeper hierarchies containing multiple intermediate composite groups and leaf pod groups, issuing sequential synchronous HTTP patch calls directly on the scheduling thread:
- Multiplies scheduling cycle latency linearly by the number of groups in the subtree.
- Contributes to head-of-line (HoL) blocking in the active scheduling queue, as the scheduler cannot pick up the next queued workload until all status updates complete.
### Potential Mitigations to Discuss
- **Asynchronous dispatch**: Offload status patching to background goroutines (similar to `sched.runBindingCycle`) or a dedicated worker queue so the main scheduling goroutine can immediately proceed to the next cycle.
- **Concurrent patching**: If status updates must be bounded or completed within the cycle, patch group statuses concurrently (e.g., using an `errgroup` or bounded worker pool) rather than strictly sequentially.
author: jdzikowski

title: [Flaking Test] [sig-testing] ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master kubetest.Timeout [gce-cos-alphafeatures-master, gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37]
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master`)
sig-release-1.37-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37 (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta`, the fork of the same job)

Triage: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?job=%5Eci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master%24&test=%5ETimeout%24

Status 2026-09-23: tracked as FLAKY on the CI Signal board per the Release Signal lead. Triage accepted by SIG Node (harche); priority/critical-urgent as set at triage. I hold the Release Signal follow-up. Next step per upodroid is a test-side improvement by SIG Node; no test owner confirmed yet. The blocking or non-blocking call for v1.38.0-alpha.1 (2026-09-23) is with SIG Node and pending; no mitigation is agreed. Master count from the 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC run through the 2026-09-23 18:44 UTC run is 23 of 93 completed runs timed out (25%), 2 of the last 13; 1.37 is 1 of its last 4. The three recent failures are the same pattern: suite passed, teardown interrupted by the timer. The numbers below are the 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC snapshot.

### Which tests are flaking?

`kubetest.Timeout`. The e2e suite passes in all but one of the timed-out runs; in that one the timeout interrupted the suite.

### Since when has it been flaking?

Snapshot 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC. On master, 15 of the 61 runs since 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC hit the timeout: the first at 2026-09-17 13:04 UTC, the last two at 2026-09-21 00:16 UTC and 02:19 UTC, with passing runs in between. On the 1.37 fork, 7 of the 21 runs since 2026-09-16 01:00 UTC, the latest at 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC.

Examples:
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101858636748820480 (2026-09-21 02:19 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101736329489420288 (2026-09-20 18:13 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008 (2026-09-19 12:07 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta/2101658314709405696 (1.37, 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC)

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The job runs out of its kubetest budget, not out of tests. It passes `--timeout=120m` to kubetest, which covers cluster up, the tests and teardown. Up and teardown are steady at about 15 minutes together, which leaves roughly 105 minutes for the suite. In 14 of the 15 timed-out master runs the suite finished with `91 Passed | 0 Failed` after 105 to 112 minutes and the budget ran out in the teardown steps; in the other run ginkgo was interrupted at 113 minutes with one spec still running (`90 Passed | 1 Failed`).

The suite's runtime is not fixed. The same 91 specs took 76 minutes in a passing run on 2026-09-19 at 14:08 UTC (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101312282582585344) and 106 minutes in the timed-out run two hours earlier (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008), on the same Kubernetes commit (`v1.38.0-alpha.0.948+96b5e4e3ae3f8d`) and the same COS image. So a code or image change alone does not explain the timeouts; whether something makes the resize path slower under some conditions is open. Across the 59 runs since 2026-09-16 the test phase ranged from 76 to 113 minutes; the 45 passing runs took 76 to 103 minutes with a median of 87, and passing and timed-out runs occur on the same commits.

Almost all of that variance sits in one feature. `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` is 63 of the 91 specs and took 57 minutes in the fast run and 86 in the slow one; the other 28 specs took 19 minutes in both. 62 of the 63 resize specs are slower in the slow run, by 20 seconds at the median and up to 83 seconds, with no single spec standing out, so the extra time is inside the resize specs themselves. What inside them is slower I have not established; the kubelet logs of both runs show no deferred or infeasible resizes.

This is the same shape as #141186 on `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-alpha-features`, which runs almost the same focus. That was resolved by kubernetes/test-infra#37724: kubetest to `--timeout=180m`, the prow timeout to 3h20m, and the job moved to release-informing, on the basis that alpha-feature lanes do not fit the two-hour release-blocking budget. The note on that issue that the 1.37 blocking board shows the same thing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141186#issuecomment-5316283473) was not followed up for the sig-release jobs, which still have `--timeout=120m` and a 2h20m prow timeout in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-release/gce-cos-e2e-master.yaml` and `release-branch-jobs/1.37.yaml`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Update after upodroid's comment (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142262#issuecomment-5759352510): the next step is on the test side. SIG Node is asked to look at reducing the resize specs' execution time or their run-to-run variance while keeping the coverage. Skipping the resize tests is not on the table, and a timeout increase or dashboard change is not agreed; it would come after that attempt, if at all. A test-side owner is not confirmed yet.

Background for whoever picks it up: InPlacePodVerticalScaling is Stable since 1.35, and this lane is the only blocking coverage the 63 resize specs have. The sig-node node-e2e lanes skip `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` explicitly or do not focus on it; the node alpha-features lane (`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`) ran 3 memory-backed-volume resize specs in its latest build, none of the 63. The job runs ginkgo with `--nodes=1`, and the presubmit alpha-features job sets `--ginkgo-parallel=1` explicitly, so I have not assumed parallelism is safe for these specs. The sibling job's uncensored timing distribution is in the comments.

SIG Node's call on whether this blocks v1.38.0-alpha.1 on 2026-09-23 is still needed, with the reason and any conditions; I will relay it to the Release Signal lead and the release-cut representative. FLAKY on the CI Signal board is a tracking category and says nothing about the cut.

This is not #142205. That one is a single spec (the allocated pods endpoint test) failing on the kind alpha-beta lane. Here the specs pass, apart from the one interrupted run, and the job runs out of its time budget.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig testing
/sig node
/sig release

/kind flake
/priority critical-urgent
/cc @kubernetes/release-team-release-signal
author: thc1006

comments.body:
/assign

Taking the Release Signal follow-up. @kubernetes/sig-node-test-failures, SIG Testing: can one of you take the technical side and say whether this blocks the alpha.1 cut on Wednesday? The evidence and the open options are in the description; nothing is agreed yet. I can open the test-infra change once there is agreement.

/triage accepted
/priority critical-urgent

Update: two more timeouts since the snapshot in the description, 2026-09-21 00:16 UTC and 02:19 UTC, both 91 Passed | 0 Failed with a 107-minute test phase on v1.38.0-alpha.0.950. That is 15 of 61 master runs since 09-16, and the last two finished runs both timed out. The 1.37 fork passed at 01:03 UTC.

Edited 2026-09-21: the paragraph below replaces one that used only this job's own runs, which are cut off at the timeout. The sibling job ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-alpha-features runs the same 91 specs (checked spec by spec), serially, with the same feature gates, region and node image, and has had a 180m kubetest budget since kubernetes/test-infra#37724, so its runs show the tail this job cannot. Since 2026-08-21: 394 runs, 0 timeouts; test phase p50 97, p75 108, p90 113, p95 115, p99 119, max 140 minutes; 23 runs over 115 minutes (5.8%), 4 over 120 (1.0%), 3 over 130, all on 09-05 and 09-07. Since 09-10: 135 runs, max 116. Its wall time p75 is 125 minutes, over the 120-minute p75 target in release-blocking-jobs.md. With about 15 minutes of non-test steps, a 130m kubetest budget would have left roughly 2 to 6% of those runs timing out and 135m roughly 0 to 1%; 135m leaves only the 15-minute interrupt grace between kubetest and the 2h30m prow cap that the blocking policy test enforces. None of this is agreed; it is here so the owners can choose.

> * Trimming InPlacePodVerticalScaling out of the focus would cut about three-quarters of the runtime

We can't skip testing features. SIG Node needs to modify that test so it runs faster.

Can SIG Node reengineer this test to reduce execution time or reduce variance in test duration? I would like to see this attempted first before we discuss increasing the test timeout.

btw, this situation will only get worse as we add more features

I pulled `artifacts/ginkgo/report.json` for the two runs in the description (same commit, 63 resize specs, 57 vs 86 minutes) and split each spec by its `By` steps and the klog lines it captured.

Most of the time is exec. Each run does 1104 execs into the test pod to read cgroup files (547 `head -n 1 cpu.weight`, 243 `memory.max`, 243 `cpu.max`, 70 `cat /proc/1/oom_score_adj`, 1 `mount -t cgroup2`), 3 to 30 per spec, and 61 of the 63 specs issue the exact same sequence in both runs. Those execs add up to 50 minutes in the fast run and 77 in the slow one. Everything else (namespace, pod creation, the resize wait, deletion) is 7 to 10 minutes in both.

What an exec costs depends on the pod's CPU limit. Pods without one (the BestEffort cases and the invalid-patch cases that set only requests; one of them has a memory limit and no CPU limit) take 0.1 to 0.3 s per exec in both runs. Burstable pods with limits take 1.8 s in the fast run and 2.9 s in the slow one, Guaranteed pods 2.9 s and 4.5 s, and that is the same at creation, after the resize and after the rollback. The fixtures use 25m to 35m limits, so the shell that exec starts gets 2.5 to 3.5 ms per 100 ms. That fits the numbers. How badly it throttles would depend on the host, which would explain the day-to-day swing. I cannot tell from the logs why Guaranteed pods come out slower than Burstable pods with the same limits. The 1.37 fork has the older helper but the same exec checks.

So in these two runs the resize wait did not get slower; the exec-based cgroup checks did. Throttling fits the timings. The timings alone do not prove it. Reading the values without an exec in the throttled container, or at least doing one exec for the three files instead of three, should remove most of that time while keeping the same checks. If SIG Node wants the batching tried I can send a PR.

> > * Trimming InPlacePodVerticalScaling out of the focus would cut about three-quarters of the runtime
> 
> We can't skip testing features. SIG Node needs to modify that test so it runs faster.
> 
> Can SIG Node reengineer this test to reduce execution time or reduce variance in test duration? I would like to see this attempted first before we discuss increasing the test timeout.
> 
> btw, this situation will only get worse as we add more features

For sig-node we have been moving some of these tests to a slow lane

Reproduced the exec cost outside CI with podman (runc 1.4.0) on a desktop i5-14500: a `busybox:1.36` container idling in `sh -c 'trap exit TERM; while true; do sleep 1; done'`, then timing `podman exec ctr /bin/sh -c 'head -n 1 /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max'`, 6 to 8 runs per point, medians.

No CPU limit 0.20 s; `--cpus 0.025`: 2.6 to 2.8 s; 0.03: 2.3 to 3.0 s; 0.035: 1.7 to 2.0 s; 0.05: 1.7 s; 0.1: 0.6 s; 0.2: 0.3 s; 0.3 and 1.0: 0.2 s. The ranges are two sessions; within a session the order is monotonic.

So a container limited to 25m to 35m costs about 2 to 3 s per exec even on a fast CPU; the e2e nodes are e2-standard-2. Most of that is the exec setup inside the throttled cgroup, not the shell. In the same 30m container, interleaved: `sh -c head` 2.5 s, `head` with no shell 2.5 s, `cat` 2.2 s, and one `sh -c head` reading all three files 2.2 s. On the test side that leaves, smallest change first: raise the fixture limits (an exec is 0.6 s at 100m and 0.3 s at 200m), read the three files in one exec per check, or read them without exec.

`TearDown` follow-up for the two runs Jubitta reported in the Release Signal Slack thread:

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2102165921954009088
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2102318176564940800

Both are the tracked pattern: the suite passes, then the kubetest timer interrupts `e2e-down.sh`.

| Build | Run start, UTC | Suite | `Test` | `TearDown` | `Deferred TearDown` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2102165921954009088 | 2026-09-21 22:40 | 91 Passed, 0 Failed | 106.1 min | Started at minute 115 of the 120 min budget. Interrupted 4m52s later, after the subnet was already deleted. | Completed in 55s |
| 2102318176564940800 | 2026-09-22 08:45 | 91 Passed, 0 Failed | 107.4 min | Started at minute 117. Interrupted 2m35s later, while `kube-down` was still working on the instance group and the master. | Completed in 2m31s |

I found no cleanup error before the interrupt in either build log. In five other reviewed runs the `TearDown` step completed in 5.2 to 5.5 minutes, so these two were cut short, not slow.

The `Error: 58 leaked resources` line in 2102318176564940800 comes from the resource listing that runs between the interrupted `TearDown` and the deferred one. It lists what was still there at that moment. There is no listing after the deferred run, so I cannot say what remained.

I am keeping these two here. No separate issue.

Master count, same window as the description (2026-09-16 00:57 UTC through the 2026-09-22 16:49 UTC run, which also timed out): 21 of 80 completed runs hit `kubetest.Timeout`, about 26%. 20 of the 21 finished the suite; one was interrupted mid-suite. The two runs above are in that count.

That covers the tracking question. The test-time problem and the alpha.1 call are still open.

title: Kubelet OOM score calculation collapses to 999 for small/medium containers on large-memory nodes and ignores per-container memory guarantees
body:
/sig node
/kind bug

This bug description was assisted by AI.

### What happened / What would you like to be added?

Update `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` in `pkg/kubelet/qos/policy.go` for `Burstable` QoS containers (guarded behind a new Kubelet feature gate) to fix precision collapse on large-memory nodes and recognize per-container memory guarantees:

1. **Replace linear node-capacity division with logarithmic scaling (`log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C)`)** so container memory requests (`R`) across multiple orders of magnitude maintain distinct `oom_score_adj` values on large nodes (1 TiB to 4 TiB+).
2. **Incorporate per-container memory guarantee ratio (`R / L`)** so "memory-guaranteed" containers (`memory.requests == memory.limits`, such as orchestrators or control agents) receive lower OOM score adjustments than containers configured to overcommit/burst far above their requests (`R << L` or unlimited).
3. **Reserve a safety gap between maximum `Burstable` baseline (`800`) and `BestEffort` (`1000`)** so mild bursts do not immediately invert kill priority against `BestEffort` workloads.
4. **Gate behind a Feature Gate** so operators can roll out or revert to the legacy calculation without risk.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` computes `oom_score_adj` for `Burstable` containers as:

```text
oom_score_adj = 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequest) / memoryCapacity
```

clamped to `[3, 999]`, while the Linux kernel calculates process badness points as:

```text
points = oom_score_adj + (usage_bytes * 1000) / memoryCapacity
```

When this heuristic was written in 2015, nodes typically had 4 GiB–64 GiB of RAM. On modern 1 TiB–4 TiB nodes running microservices, this formula breaks down in three ways:

#### 1. Integer Quantization Collapse ("Everything is 999")
Because the formula divides by `memoryCapacity` in integer arithmetic across 1000 buckets, any container requesting less than `memoryCapacity / 1000` evaluates to:

```text
(1000 * memoryRequest) / memoryCapacity == 0  =>  oom_score_adj = 999
```

* On a **1 TiB (1024 GiB)** node, every container requesting **< 1.024 GiB** gets `oom_score_adj = 999`. A container requesting 50 MiB, 256 MiB, or 1 GiB receives the exact same score (`999`).
* On a **4 TiB** node, every container requesting **< 4.096 GiB** gets `oom_score_adj = 999`.
* Note: While #111356 observed this symptom and PR #128029 mitigated native sidecars by copying the minimum score of regular containers, regular containers themselves still collapse to `999` on large nodes (making the sidecar adjustment a no-op as well).

#### 2. Loss of Per-Container Memory Guarantee (`R / L`)
Because Kubernetes QoS is evaluated at the Pod level across both CPU and memory, a container that explicitly sets `memory.requests == memory.limits` (zero memory overcommit) is forced into `Burstable` QoS whenever:
* The Pod has another container that is burstable (e.g., an **Orchestrator + Executor** Pod), or
* CPU limits are unset or differ from CPU requests (previously noted in #78848).

Consider a `Burstable` Pod on a 1 TiB node with two containers:
* **Orchestrator (`O`):** `request = 500 MiB`, `limit = 500 MiB` (`R / L = 1.0`, memory-guaranteed). Steady usage = `200 MiB`.
* **Executor (`E`):** `request = 500 MiB`, `limit = 32 GiB` (`R / L = 0.015`, burst-heavy). Spikes to `1.5 GiB` (3x request).

Under the current formula:
* `oom_score_adj(O) = 999` => `points(O) = 999 + (0.2 / 1024) * 1000 = 999.2`
* `oom_score_adj(E) = 999` => `points(E) = 999 + (1.5 / 1024) * 1000 = 1000.5`

The kernel badness score between a memory-guaranteed orchestrator using 40% of its request and an executor bursting 300% over its request differs by **only 1 point**. If the executor spawns multiple worker processes, each worker process has fewer kernel points than the orchestrator, causing the kernel OOM killer to kill the orchestrator first.

#### 3. 1-Point Margin Between `Burstable` and `BestEffort`
Because small `Burstable` containers get `oom_score_adj = 999` and `BestEffort` containers get `1000`, the baseline margin is only **1 point** (0.1% of host RAM). On a 1 TiB node, a `Burstable` container exceeding its request by 1.1 GiB reaches score `1000.1`, making it more likely to be killed than an unreserved `BestEffort` container.

---

### Proposed Formula

Replace the linear formula for `Burstable` containers with a two-factor formula combining **per-container memory guarantee ratio (`R / L`)** and **logarithmic request sizing (`log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C)`)**, anchored at a baseline of `800`:

```text
oom_score_adj = 800 - 400 * (R / L) - 350 * (log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C))
```

Where:
* `R` = effective container memory request (including pod-level / DRA share if enabled)
* `C` = node memory capacity
* `L` = effective container memory limit (if unset or `> C`, `L = C`)
* Result is clamped to `[3, 999]` (with sidecar clamping preserved).

In Go, integer `floor(log2(x)) + 1` can be computed in a single instruction via `math/bits.Len64(uint64(x))` without floating-point arithmetic.

---

### Concrete Comparison Across Node Sizes

#### Scenario 1: Large Node (`C = 1 TiB = 1024 GiB`, `bits = 40`)

| Workload Spec (`Request / Limit`) | Current `oom_score_adj` | Proposed `oom_score_adj` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| `50 MiB / 50 MiB` (Small Orchestrator) | `999` | **`176`** |
| `500 MiB / 500 MiB` (Std Orchestrator) | `999` | **`147`** |
| `500 MiB / 32 GiB` (Spiky Executor) | `999` | **`541`** |
| `500 MiB / unset` (Unbounded Worker) | `999` | **`547`** |
| `4 GiB / 8 GiB` (Medium Service) | `996` | **`320`** |
| `64 GiB / 64 GiB` (Large Database) | `938` | **`85`** |
| `500 GiB / 500 GiB` (Huge Database) | `512` | **`59`** |
| BestEffort (`0 / 0`) | `1000` | **`1000`** |

#### Scenario 2: Small Node (`C = 16 GiB`, `bits = 34`)

| Workload Spec (`Request / Limit`) | Current `oom_score_adj` | Proposed `oom_score_adj` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| `50 MiB / 50 MiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `997` | **`137`** |
| `500 MiB / 500 MiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `970` | **`103`** |
| `500 MiB / 4 GiB` (Bursty) | `970` | **`454`** |
| `2 GiB / 2 GiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `875` | **`81`** |
| `12 GiB / 12 GiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `250` | **`54`** |
| BestEffort (`0 / 0`) | `1000` | **`1000`** |

---

### Rollout & Why a KEP Is Not Required

* **Feature Gate Protection:** The updated calculation in `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` will be guarded behind a Kubelet feature gate, allowing safe rollout and immediate fallback to the legacy formula if needed.
* **No Semantic or API Changes:** This change does not alter any Kubernetes API, CRI protocol, or documented QoS contract:
  * The strict ordering `Guaranteed` (`-997`) < `Burstable` (`[3, 999]`) < `BestEffort` (`1000`) is preserved.
  * Within `Burstable`, the documented intent—that containers reserving more memory and staying within their bounds are protected over containers consuming memory beyond their requests—is unchanged and preserved on small nodes, while fixing the integer truncation bug where containers collapse to `999` on large nodes.
  * Prior refinements to `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` (such as PR #128029 for sidecars) followed the same path without requiring a standalone KEP.

title: Kubelet omits volume stats after all pod container cgroups are removed
body:
### What happened?

The kubelet's cAdvisor stats provider can omit a Running pod's mounted volume stats after cAdvisor has removed every pod-managed container record.

PR #142249 preserves volume stats when all container samples are filtered as terminated, but `ListPodStats` still builds its pod map from cAdvisor records carrying pod labels. If every container cgroup has already been garbage-collected and cAdvisor reports only the unlabeled pod-level cgroup, the provider cannot build a `PodReference`. The pod and its cached volume stats are therefore absent from the Summary API and from `kubelet_volume_stats_*`.

### What did you expect to happen?

A Running pod should retain cached stats for its mounted volumes while the kubelet still knows the pod and the resource analyzer still has volume data, even when no pod-managed container cgroup remains.

### How can we reproduce it?

At the unit-test level:

1. Have the pod manager return a Running pod with a valid start time.
2. Have the resource analyzer return cached persistent volume stats for that pod.
3. Have cAdvisor return the root cgroup and the pod-level cgroup, with no labeled container records.
4. Call the cAdvisor provider's `ListPodStats`.

The current provider returns an empty pod list. A focused regression test fails with:

```
"[]" should have 1 item(s), but has 0
```

### Proposed fix

Use the kubelet pod manager as the fallback source of pod identity when cAdvisor has no labeled container record. Only seed a missing pod when cached volume stats exist, then apply the existing start-time and Running-phase validation before returning it.

This is a follow-up to #141350 and #142249.

/kind bug
/sig node
author: harshitgupta31415

comments.body:
Hi @harshitgupta31415, thanks for the detailed write-up and the unit-level repro.

Are you planning to send a PR for this one? I'd like to pick it up if you're not already on it. Falling back to the pod manager for pod identity when cAdvisor has no labeled container record, and seeding only when cached volume stats exist, makes sense to me. I'd keep the existing start-time and Running-phase validation on that path and add the regression test from your repo.

Since this builds on #142249, I'll rebase on it, or wait for it to merge if you'd prefer that.

﻿## Update: regression actually started ~2026-08-16, not 09-16 — and it's specific to this job

Dug through `finished.json`/`junit_*.xml` in the public GCS bucket back to June for this job and the sibling `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd` (#140094), no auth needed. Summary — happy to share the script/data.

### Regression started ~5 weeks before it was noticed
Weekly failure rate: Jul 5–Aug 9 sat at 8–19%. Week of **Aug 16 it jumps to 43.4%**, stays there (45%, 46%), and hits 76% by early Sep (partial week) / 47.1% over the most recent 6 days (Sep 13–18, 70 builds). A binomial changepoint scan independently pins the split at **2026-08-16 14:04 UTC** (before 14.3%, after 47.9%).

### Broad, not one flaky spec
Pre-Aug-14 vs post-Aug-17 fail counts: MirrorPod-restart 10→20, MirrorPod-volume-unmount 3→12, ImageGarbageCollect 1→8, container-lifecycle-reboot 5→8, plus new failures in GarbageCollect/Swap/PodResources/image-pull specs that barely failed before.

### Mostly timeout, not logic
78% of post-regression failed builds (59/76) have ≥1 `[TIMEDOUT]`. Failing builds average 77–79 min wall-clock vs 64–74 min for passing ones — right at ginkgo's default 70-min suite timeout (confirmed via build-log: "ginkgo flags are missing explicit --timeout... updated ginkgo flags: --timeout=70m").

### Ruled out
No k/k commit touching `pkg/kubelet`/`test/e2e_node`, no test-infra job-config or `image-config.yaml` change, and no containerd/kernel version drift (COS: containerd 2.2.6, kernel 6.12.94+ constant across 4 image respins; Ubuntu: containerd 2.1.9 constant, kernel only bumps after Aug 18 — too late) in the changepoint window.

### Sibling job (same runtime, not Serial-only) shows no spike
`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd` stays in single digits to ~20% the whole period — actually *lowest* (2.4%) the exact week this job hits 43.4%. Rules out a fleet-wide/image-wide cause; points at this job specifically, likely its all-`[Serial]` test set having far less timing margin than a parallel-eligible suite.

### Concrete mechanism, top offender
"MirrorPod when kubelet restarts should not change container status": kubelet.log shows the post-restart kubelet racing to recreate the mirror pod while the pre-restart one still exists (`already exists`), and `Ready` flaps False→True over ~254ms while it reconciles. If the node's running marginally slower, that window widens enough to trip the test's watcher more often.

### Suggested next steps
Root cause is still open (not code/config/version) — possible small general slowdown that only this job's tight timeout margin exposes. Worth: (1) bumping `--timeout` explicitly above 70m as a mitigation, (2) looping in sig-testing-infra to check GCE/Boskos latency around 2026-08-16.

/cc @harche

@harche proposed next steps, splitting this into two tracks:

1. Mitigation (this job's timeout margin)
This job runs an all-[Serial] suite with no parallel headroom, and it's now landing within a few minutes of ginkgo's 70-min default suite timeout on a regular basis. Sibling job ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd (not Serial-only) shows no spike over the same period, which is consistent with this being a margin problem specific to the Serial job rather than a fleet-wide slowdown.

Proposing to open a PR against kubernetes/test-infra adding an explicit --timeout to the ginkgo flags for ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial (e.g. 90–100m), matching the prow job's own 90-min budget. This won't fix an underlying slowdown if there is one, but it should stop the rotating-spec noise that's currently defeating the 3-consecutive alert.

2. Root cause (why the margin got worse ~2026-08-16)
Ruled out: k/k commits touching kubelet/e2e_node, test-infra job/image-config changes, and containerd/kernel drift across the changepoint window (all constant). That points outside the repos this issue can see — GCE machine/zone behavior or Boskos project latency around us-central1-b in that window.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-testing-infra or whoever owns node-e2e Boskos capacity — did anything change around 2026-08-16 14:00 UTC in the k8s-infra-e2e-boskos-* pool or us-central1-b? Happy to share the per-build timing data if useful.

3. Separately: the MirrorPod restart race is a real, independent flake
"MirrorPod when kubelet restarts should not change container status" was already failing before Aug 16 (10 times pre-regression) and got worse after. The kubelet log shows the post-restart kubelet's first mirror-pod status write landing before its own readiness probe completes, so Ready genuinely goes False→True for a short window during every restart — not just under timeout pressure. This looks like a test assertion that's too strict for how kubelet actually reports status post-restart, independent of the timeout issue above. I'll file this as its own issue/PR once I've nailed down the exact timing, so it doesn't get lost inside this one.
@ayanasarkar If you have found the fix, please send the PR, and the review can take place there.
Filed the two follow-ups discussed above: #142417 (ImageGCPeriod configurability) and #142422 (MirrorPod restart race). Root cause on the Boskos/GCE side is still open — will update here.

title: kubelet: containers that fail before ever running don't get exponential CrashLoopBackOff treatment
body:
### What happened?

When `startContainer` fails before the container ever reaches a running state — e.g. `CreateContainer` is rejected by the CRI because a resource limit (such as memory) is below the runtime's floor, or a pre-create/pre-start hook fails , no container status is ever recorded for that attempt.

`kubeGenericRuntimeManager.doBackOff` decides whether to apply `CrashLoopBackOff` by looking for an *exited* container status in `podStatus.ContainerStatuses`. Since these pre-run failures never produce a container status, `doBackOff` never finds one to back off against.

The pod is still retried (the pod-worker's flat ~10s backoff on `SyncPod` errors still applies , see `backOffPeriod` in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go`), but these container-start failures never get the *exponential* backoff or the `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event that other persistently-failing containers get once they've run and exited at least once. This is inconsistent: two containers that both fail forever are treated differently depending on whether the failure happened before or after the container briefly started.



### What did you expect to happen?

Containers that repeatedly fail to start , even before ever reaching a running state — should get the same exponential backoff escalation (up to the standard cap) and `CrashLoopBackOff` status/event reporting as containers that repeatedly exit after starting.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Pod with a container whose resource request/limit is set below what the container runtime enforces as a floor (e.g. a memory limit below the runtime's minimum).
2. Observe that `CreateContainer` is rejected on every retry.
3. Observe that kubelet retries at a flat ~10s cadence indefinitely, without back-off escalating over time, and without a `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event ever appearing ,unlike a container that starts and then repeatedly exits

title: kubelet: cut PLEG relist memory with CRI field projection + delta listing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Two additive, opt-in changes to the CRI container/pod list calls so the kubelet's PLEG can stop decoding data it doesn't use:

1. **Field projection** Let the client request only the fields it needs (container id, state, and the `io.kubernetes.*` identity labels). The runtime omits everything else; older runtimes ignore the request field and behave as today.
2. **Delta listing** Let the client receive only the containers that changed since the last relist, instead of the full set every cycle.

### Why is this needed?
This came out of a hallway conversation at gRPCConf after my talk on CRI list streaming: a few gRPC maintainers and I got into why server-streaming a big response doesn't actually cut memory and the receiver still decodes the whole object graph. That pointed back at the kubelet's own CRI list path, so I went and measured it.

PLEG relists every container on the node about once a second and the kubelet decodes the entire
result each time. On dense or high-churn nodes this is large, mostly-redundant memory and CPU:

- Measured on master: ~18k containers with realistic annotations ≈ **1.57M allocations / ~79 MB
  held per relist**, re-paid every second.
- A full "fat" response can cross the 16 MiB CRI client cap (`maxMsgSize`), so `ListContainers`
  fails → PLEG stalls → node NotReady → and container GC can't run because it needs the same list
  (the "PLEG is not healthy" failure on high-churn nodes).
- The list is dominated by accumulated terminated containers that never change, re-decoded every
  second for nothing.

Existing work doesn't cover this axis: KEP-5825 (CRIListStreaming) fixes the per-message size cap but, in its own words, "does not reduce kubelet memory usage"; KEP-3386 / PLEGOnDemandRelist change relist *frequency*, not per-object payload.

I have a small benchmark harness (happy to push it) that measures decode + hold cost for full vs projected vs changed-only responses on representative payloads:

- **Projection** (measured): −45% memory, −65% wire, −34% allocations.
- **Changed-only** reduces it much further, since the list is mostly static terminated containers, the mechanism is measured and linear, and the exact factor depends on per-relist churn, which isn't instrumented upstream today (I model it at ≤1% for the accumulated-dead-container case, giving ≥99%; grounding that number would be step one of an alpha).
- **Correctness:** projection is client-declared per call, so it can't remove a field a consumer is reading and safe by construction. For the PLEG path specifically, the needed set is small and verified in code (event generation uses only id + state; container→pod mapping uses only `pod.uid`; the restart hash comes from `ContainerStatus`, not the list).

I'd like to bring this to sig-node as a KEP; opening this to track the problem and gather input.

/sig node
/kind feature

cc @haircommander @SergeyKanzhelev

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

title: DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate overlong rolling-update service socket paths
body:
### What happened?

On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name.

With normal defaults:

```text
plugin directory:
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name>

rolling service socket:
dra-<Pod UID>.sock
```

With a normal 36-byte Pod UID:

```text
full endpoint length = 71 + len(driverName)
```

A valid 37-byte driver name:

```text
abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io
```

produces exactly a 108-byte endpoint under the affected implementation. Kubernetes requires AF_UNIX pathname-based endpoints to remain shorter than 108 bytes. A valid 63-byte driver name produces a 134-byte old-style endpoint.

### What did you expect to happen?

Valid DRA drivers using `RollingUpdate` with the normal automatic/default directory and socket naming should receive an AF_UNIX-compatible endpoint. Rolling instances must remain distinguishable.

This expectation does not extend to arbitrary custom `PluginDataDirectoryPath` values.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use:

```go
DriverName("abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io")
RollingUpdate("11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555")
// no PluginDataDirectoryPath override
// no PluginSocket override
```

An injected `PluginListener` can observe the real automatically generated endpoint without relying on the local macOS Unix-socket behavior.

The affected implementation produces:

```text
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io/dra-11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555.sock
```

and its length is exactly 108 bytes. The valid 36-byte control driver produces 107 bytes.

### Anything else we need to know?

### Root cause

Rolling-update service socket naming includes the complete Pod UID. The default containing directory independently contains the complete driver name. The service socket did not check the combined full-path budget or fall back to a shorter basename.

### Relationship to existing work

- #139166 / #139623 addressed the rolling **registration socket** under `plugins_registry`.
- #139623 explicitly left `dra-<uid>.sock` service sockets unchanged.
- #141815 corrected the registration fallback's exact-108 boundary.
- #140837 added kubelet-side endpoint and driver validation but does not prevent this helper from generating an invalid automatic service endpoint.

### Affected scope

Reproduced on Kubernetes master at `3af569e862d19a046cdfd63cda837f9bb29da6fa`. Older releases were not verified.

No production incident was observed.

title: Memory Manager accepts an incomplete pod-level checkpoint as a restored allocation after kubelet restart
body:
### What happened?

With the static Memory Manager, pod-scope Topology Manager, and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, pod-level allocation is persisted through independent checkpoint updates: `PodMemoryAssignments` first, then per-container assignments, then `MachineState`. If kubelet stops after the real `SetPodMemoryBlocks` write completes but before the first `SetMemoryBlocks`, the resulting checkpoint is structurally valid but contains a PodEntry for UID `podUID`, no container assignments for that pod, and the pre-allocation machine state.

On restart, `validateState` reconstructs expected accounting by iterating `ContainerMemoryAssignments`. Because this pod has no container entries, the orphan pod assignment is not inspected and startup succeeds. `GetPodTopologyHints` then regenerates a hint from the PodEntry, and pod-scope admission calls `AllocatePod`. `AllocatePod` sees `GetPodMemoryBlocks(podUID) != nil` and returns success as though allocation were complete. The container `MemoryBlocks` and machine reservation remain absent.

This is an ordinary functional-correctness issue. No security impact is being claimed.

### What did you expect to happen?

An incomplete pod-level allocation must not be treated as a completely restored allocation. Restart handling should reject the inconsistent checkpoint, repair it, or safely reconstruct/reallocate the missing state before successful admission is reported.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit reproducer, `TestMemoryManagerRestorePartialPodCheckpoint`, uses pod name `pod1` and UID `podUID`. It:

1. enables `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`;
2. creates the real static Memory Manager with the real checkpoint backend and a real best-effort, pod-scope Topology Manager;
3. wraps the state so `SetPodMemoryBlocks` first invokes the real setter and only then simulates process interruption;
4. verifies that the PodEntry is durable, container assignments are empty, and `MachineState` is unchanged;
5. creates new managers against the same checkpoint directory; and
6. performs normal pod-scope Topology Manager admission.

With the proposed validation guard removed on current master, the restored manager starts and admission succeeds, followed by these invariant failures:

```text
successful restored pod allocation left container "container1" without memory blocks
successful restored pod allocation left machine state without the pod reservation
```

This constructs the precise checkpoint through production state APIs; it does not claim that a live production node was intentionally crashed.

### Anything else we need to know?

Related but distinct work:

- #140906 / #141077 preserve a fully completed restored pod allocation; this issue concerns a PodEntry-only partial checkpoint.
- #141070 restores pod topology hints from the pod-level allocation, which is why the orphan PodEntry can supply the post-restart hint.
- #141261 addresses a sibling CPU Manager partial-state cleanup problem.
- kubernetes/enhancements#5526 is the Pod Level Resource Managers design context.

A deterministic regression test and minimal startup-validation fix are prepared, and I intend to open a PR shortly.

### Kubernetes version

Current upstream `master` at `654c2de7b8cabdb8353ec891122ee433deeb4457` (fetched and verified on 2026-09-10).

### Cloud provider

Not provider-specific.

### OS version

The deterministic unit reproducer ran on macOS 26.6.2 (Build 25G83), arm64, against the platform-independent Memory Manager and Topology Manager code. The affected production static Memory Manager policy is Linux-specific. I did not intentionally crash a live production node.

### Install tools

body:
### What happened?

Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870, which replaced `user.Lookup("kubelet")` with a `getent passwd` shell-out.

[`getentUserExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L188-L191) returns early when `LookPath` fails:

```go
getent, err := exec.LookPath("getent")
if err != nil {
	return false, nil // no getent: same as "not configured"
}
```

[The caller](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L151-L158) reads that as "no kubelet account", skips `getsubids` and returns the built-in default range. The account itself is never examined, so a local `/etc/passwd` entry is affected the same way, which is wider than the directory-service case the PR body describes.

Same node, with `getent` on PATH and then off it:

```
getent on PATH   firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608
getent off PATH  firstID=65536   rangeLen=4294901760
```

Before 6bb4235 the cgo `user.Lookup` resolved a local account without `getent`, so a node in this state used to get its configured range. I ran the two versions of that branch side by side against a real local account with `getent` off PATH: `user.Lookup` reports the account, `getentUserExists` reports it missing.

### What did you expect to happen?

The configured subordinate IDs to still be used when the account is in `/etc/passwd`, or something in the log saying they were skipped. Today it is a `V(5)` line and no error.

@kginonredhat suggested a fallback during review: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870#discussion_r3966541751

That shape looks right to me with one adjustment. I would gate it on `exec.ErrNotFound` only, since `LookPath` also returns `ErrDot` alongside a usable path, and swallowing that turns a resolvable `getent` into a missing account.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run from anywhere inside a checkout of master. No root, cleans up after itself.

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
W=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$W" pkg/kubelet/zz_getent_repro_test.go' EXIT
mkdir -p "$W/with" "$W/without"

# stand-ins for a node whose /etc/passwd has a kubelet account and whose
# /etc/subuid delegates 1048576/8388608 to it
cat > "$W/with/getent" <<'G'
#!/bin/sh
[ "$1" = passwd ] && [ "$2" = kubelet ] && { echo "kubelet:x:999:999::/var/lib/kubelet:/sbin/nologin"; exit 0; }
exit 2
G
cat > "$W/with/getsubids" <<'G'
#!/bin/sh
[ "$1" = -g ] && shift
[ "$1" = kubelet ] && { echo "0: kubelet 1048576 8388608"; exit 0; }
exit 1
G
chmod +x "$W/with/getent" "$W/with/getsubids"
cp "$W/with/getsubids" "$W/without/"   # same node, only getent is off PATH

cat > pkg/kubelet/zz_getent_repro_test.go <<'T'
package kubelet

import (
	"os"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/klog/v2/ktesting"
)

func TestGetentRepro(t *testing.T) {
	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
	t.Setenv("PATH", os.Getenv("REPRO_PATH"))
	first, length, err := (&Kubelet{}).getKubeletMappings(logger, 65536)
	t.Logf("firstID=%d rangeLen=%d err=%v", first, length, err)
}
T

for d in with without; do
	printf -- '--- getent %s PATH ---\n' "$([ "$d" = with ] && echo on || echo off)"
	REPRO_PATH="$W/$d" go test ./pkg/kubelet/ -run '^TestGetentRepro$' -count=1 -v 2>&1 | grep firstID
done
```

</details>

```
--- getent on PATH ---
    zz_getent_repro_test.go:14: firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608 err=<nil>
--- getent off PATH ---
    zz_getent_repro_test.go:14: firstID=65536 rangeLen=4294901760 err=<nil>
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Two things a fix would have to deal with.

[`TestGetentUserExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go#L8595-L8598) has a `"getent not installed"` case expecting `wantFound: false`, so that case has to change with the behavior. It also only asserts `found`, never the range `getKubeletMappings` ends up with, which is the part that matters here.

The second one is smaller. [The comment above the lookup](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L145-L150) says the account is checked first so a getsubids backend that is unreachable can be told apart from one that simply has no entry. glibc's `getent` sets exit 2 whenever `getpwnam()` returns NULL without consulting errno, while the cgo `os/user` gave `UnknownUserError` for a genuine miss and a plain error otherwise. So an account-backend error that used to stop kubelet can now arrive as exit 2 and select the default range instead. I have not reproduced a real directory-service outage, so I would treat that as a question about the contract, not a second bug.

I am happy to send the PR if the fallback is the direction people want.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# N/A, reproduced by building master at 6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e with go1.27.1.
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

N/A

</details>

### OS version

<details>

```console
$ cat /etc/os-release
# Debian GNU/Linux 13. The repro above does not depend on the distribution.
```

</details>

### Install tools

_No response_

_No response_

_No response_

/kind bug

comments.body:
Correcting the repro in this issue, since it cannot be used to check a fix.

The script never creates a real local `kubelet` account. The fake `getent` stands in for one, so once `getent` is off PATH there is nothing left for `os/user` to find, and on a host with no `kubelet` account it prints the same two lines before and after #141971. It shows the early return and nothing more.

Redid it with a real account: uid 999 in `/etc/passwd`, `kubelet:1048576:8388608` in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`, and the real shadow-utils `getsubids`.

```
PATH                  master (6bb4235)     with #141971
getent + getsubids    1048576/8388608      1048576/8388608
getsubids only        65536/4294901760     1048576/8388608
neither               65536/4294901760     0,0 exec: "getsubids": executable file not found in $PATH
```

The middle row is what this issue is about. The last one is new: restoring the lookup makes the missing-`getsubids` branch reachable, where `os.IsNotExist` does not match `exec.ErrNotFound` and kubelet stops. #141971 carries @halaney's one-line fix from #141345 for that, so the last row stays on the default range.

One correction to what I wrote above as well. Gating the fallback on `exec.ErrNotFound` only is not what #141971 does. With the fallback in place `ErrDot` lands in `os/user` instead of in "account absent", which is the safe answer for it too, so every `LookPath` error falls back.

/cc @dims @BenTheElder 
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

Thanks. The fix is up at #141971 and CI is green on it.

One detail that is not in this issue and may matter for sizing. That PR also carries @halaney's one-line change from #141345, `os.IsNotExist` to `errors.Is(err, exec.ErrNotFound)` around the `getsubids` lookup. It had to come along: restoring the account lookup makes that branch reachable again.

`os.IsNotExist` does not match what `LookPath` returns there. A node with a `kubelet` account but no `getsubids` on PATH then stops during startup, and the same code is in v1.36.0 and v1.37.0. I read that from their sources, not from running them. That half is a fix to released behavior and has its own release note in the PR.

Edit, 2026-09-14: #141971 does not carry that change any more. It belongs to #141345, and #141971 is held until #141345 merges. Until then, #141971 on its own would stop the kubelet on a node that has neither getent nor getsubids, the last row of the table above. Master uses the default range there.

title: kubelet can fail to start when the user namespace ID pool changes while pods with user namespaces exist on the node
body:
### What happened?

If the subordinate ID pool kubelet uses for user namespaces changes between restarts, and a pod on disk holds a mapping that falls outside the new pool, the kubelet does not start:

```
create user namespace manager: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
```

[`record()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L252-L255) rejects a persisted mapping outside the current pool, and [the replay loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L185-L189) returns on the first such pod, so `MakeUserNsManager()` fails and `NewMainKubelet()` with it. As far as I can tell the only ways out are to restore the previous pool or to delete the pod directory by hand, and the message points at neither.

Several ordinary things change the pool. Editing `/etc/subuid` to move kubelet's range does it. So does installing `getsubids` on a node that did not have it, or creating the `kubelet` account on a node where it did not exist, since both move the node from the built-in default range to whatever `getsubids` then reports. None of these involve cgo or #135870; that PR just adds one more way to get here, which is where I ran into it.

Whether a given node survives is luck. Blocks come from `allocator.NewAllocationMap`, which picks at random, so it depends on where the running pod happens to sit relative to the new pool. Going from the default pool to a delegated one is close to a certainty: the default holds 65535 blocks against a typical delegated pool of ~128.

`UserNamespacesSupport` has been GA with `LockToDefault` since 1.36, so the path is active on every Linux kubelet, but only nodes running pods with `hostUsers: false` are affected, since pods without a user namespace write no mapping file and are skipped on replay.

### What did you expect to happen?

Something recoverable. Failing the whole kubelet over one pod whose persisted mapping no longer fits seems heavy next to, say, refusing that pod and saying why, and either way the error could name the pod directory an operator would have to clear.

I do not know which is right, and it overlaps with #140190, which is looking at persisted-mapping replay from the terminal-ID angle and deliberately kept its guard on the allocation side so that older on-disk mappings stay replayable.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Drop this in `pkg/kubelet/userns/` and run `go test ./pkg/kubelet/userns/ -run TestPoolChangeReplay -v`. No cgo, no NSS, no changes to the host.

```go
package userns

import (
	"testing"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/types"
	utilfeature "k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/feature"
	featuregatetesting "k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/testing"
	pkgfeatures "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/features"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2/ktesting"
)

func TestPoolChangeReplay(t *testing.T) {
	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
	featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, pkgfeatures.UserNamespacesSupport, true)

	hostUsers := false
	try := func(label string, fromFirst, fromLen, toFirst, toLen uint32) {
		dir, uid := t.TempDir(), types.UID("p")
		m, err := MakeUserNsManager(logger, &testUserNsPodsManager{podDir: dir, userns: true,
			maxPods: 110, mappingFirstID: fromFirst, mappingLen: fromLen}, nil)
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("%s: %v", label, err)
		}
		pod := &v1.Pod{Spec: v1.PodSpec{HostUsers: &hostUsers}}
		pod.UID = uid
		uns, err := m.GetOrCreateUserNamespaceMappings(logger, pod, "")
		if err != nil {
			t.Fatalf("%s alloc: %v", label, err)
		}
		_, err = MakeUserNsManager(logger, &testUserNsPodsManager{podDir: dir, userns: true,
			maxPods: 110, mappingFirstID: toFirst, mappingLen: toLen,
			podList: []types.UID{uid}}, nil)
		res := "restarts OK"
		if err != nil {
			res = "FAILS: " + err.Error()
		}
		t.Logf("%-42s block %-6d %s", label, uns.GetUids()[0].GetHostId()/65536, res)
	}

	try("subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608", 1048576, 8388608, 8388608, 8388608)
	try("subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks", 1048576, 8388608, 1048576, 7208960)
	try("default pool -> delegated pool", 65536, 4294901760, 1048576, 8388608)
}
```

One run:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608      block 112    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks      block 131    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 8585216 is out of range
default pool -> delegated pool             block 15363  FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 1006829568 is out of range
```

All three depend on where the pod happened to land, so one run understates it. Over 20 runs:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608   19 fail,  1 restarts OK   [16..143] -> [128..255], survives on 16 of 128 blocks
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks    2 fail, 18 restart OK    [16..143] -> [16..125],  survives on 110 of 128
default pool -> delegated pool          20 fail,  0 restart OK    [1..65535] -> [16..143], survives on 128 of 65535
```

which matches the geometry in each case. The third row is the one that matters in practice: a node coming from the default pool has roughly a 0.2% chance per userns pod of sitting somewhere a delegated pool can still replay.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a unit-level reproduction in a checkout rather than something I have watched a real node do. It came out of #135870, where I raised it before @dims suggested splitting it into separate issues, but the PR is a trigger rather than the cause, so it stands on its own.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# N/A - reproduced against master at 79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841
# with go1.27.1, not observed on a running cluster.
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

N/A

</details>

### OS version

<details>

N/A, reproduced from source.

</details>

Thanks for the offer.

Same caveat as on #141940: this is waiting on a decision more than on code. The open question is what kubelet should do instead of refusing to start, and it overlaps with #140190, which is looking at persisted-mapping replay from the terminal-ID angle. Those two probably want to settle on one contract rather than be solved separately, so until sig-node picks a direction a patch here would be guessing at the shape.

Assignment is not mine to give since I only filed this, so a maintainer would need to do that.

/cc @dims @BenTheElder

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

One thing worth settling before anyone picks this up. #137930 already states the baseline: two pods must never get overlapping mappings, and a kubelet that would have to break that to start is right to refuse. So ignoring the mapping and carrying on is not an option, and I should have said so in the description rather than leaving it open.

What is still open is narrower. Whether the failure can name the pod UID, the mapping file and the two pools, so the operator knows what to remove. Whether a pod whose mapping no longer fits can be refused on its own rather than stopping the node, provided its range is never handed out again. And whether a persisted mapping that is disjoint from the new pool can be kept without becoming allocatable. Those are recovery and diagnostics questions, and I think they can be settled without touching the invariant.

I'd like to pick up the diagnostics part only, which per the comment above can be settled without touching the invariant. The kubelet still refuses to start; the error just says enough to recover.

Reproduced on a v1.36 kubelet in a kind node: allocate a `hostUsers: false` pod under the default range, move the kubelet to a delegated range via `/etc/subuid`, restart. The kubelet crash-loops with only `id 1153695744 is out of range`.

With the change, the error names the file and both ranges:

```
record pod mappings for existing pod "<uid>" from /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/userns:
user namespace IDs [1815871488, 1815937024) are out of range [65536, 7274496)
available to the kubelet; if the kubelet ID range changed, restore the previous one
```

It only suggests restoring the previous range, not removing the pod directory, since that is still open here. Refusing a single pod instead of the whole kubelet is left for SIG Node to decide. PR incoming.

title: [1.36] Kubelet retries DRA health streams for plugins that do not advertise health support
body:
### What happened?

On Kubernetes 1.36, kubelet starts a `NodeWatchResources` health stream for every registered DRA plugin whenever `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled. It does this even when the plugin does not advertise the optional `DRAResourceHealth` service in its registration response.

When the service is not implemented, kubelet receives `codes.Unimplemented`, logs it as an error, and retries every five seconds:

```text
E0902 21:16:20.306285 manager.go:1045] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = device health reporting is not supported by this driver" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="compute-domain.nvidia.com"
```

`ResourceHealthStatus` is Beta and enabled by default in 1.36, so this occurs on the default feature-gate configuration when a DRA plugin does not implement health reporting.

This does not appear to affect DRA workload correctness, but it continuously emits error-level kubelet logs. At one retry every five seconds, each unsupported plugin produces 17,280 error records per day per node. This creates unnecessary log storage and ingestion costs and makes genuine kubelet errors harder to identify.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should only start the health stream when the plugin advertises a supported `DRAResourceHealth` service.

If a plugin advertises the service but returns `codes.Unimplemented`, kubelet should treat that as a terminal indication that health reporting is unsupported and stop retrying until the plugin re-registers.

This is the behavior in Kubernetes 1.37.

### How can we reproduce it?

This was reproduced with a kind v1.36.1 cluster using the head of:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/pull/1243

The GPU plugin streams health normally when its health reporting feature is enabled. Kubelet nevertheless continues attempting `NodeWatchResources` every five seconds for `compute-domain.nvidia.com`, which does not advertise the health service.

The same driver configuration is quiet on kubelet 1.37.

Full reproduction findings and logs:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/issues/1423#issuecomment-5532233065

Although the report uses the NVIDIA DRA driver, the behavior is generic to any DRA plugin that registers without the optional health service.

### Anything else we need to know?

In release-1.36, `RegisterPlugin` receives the plugin's `supportedServices`, but the health stream is started without checking that list:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L324-L334

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L387-L407

Kubernetes 1.37 fixed this as part of #139477 by:

- selecting an advertised health service during registration;
- starting the stream only when such a service was advertised;
- stopping retries when the stream returns `codes.Unimplemented`.

This issue is intended to track a targeted backport of that behavior to release-1.36, not the larger v1 health API and kubeletplugin helper changes from #139477.

The proposed 1.36 fix would:

1. Start `NodeWatchResources` only if the plugin advertises `v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth`.
2. Treat `codes.Unimplemented` as non-error and stop retrying.
3. Add regression tests for an absent health service and an `Unimplemented` stream.

A backport to 1.35 or earlier is not requested because `ResourceHealthStatus` was Alpha and disabled by default there.

cc @shivamerla @guptaNswati @pohly

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.36.1
```

The current release-1.36 source remains affected. Kubernetes 1.37 is not affected.

### Cloud provider

kind

### Related plugins

NVIDIA DRA driver, although the kubelet behavior is driver-independent:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/issues/1423

/kind bug
/kind regression

/area kubelet
/wg device-management
/priority important-soon
/assign @harche

title: DRA: AllocationMode All errors for incomplete or invalid pools are not per-node failures
body:
### What happened?

An `AllocationMode: All` request returns a plain error when a pool gathered for the candidate node is incomplete or invalid. In `validateDeviceRequest`, same code in the stable, incubating and experimental variants:

```go
if pool.IsIncomplete {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
if pool.IsInvalid {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently invalid", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
```

Neither wraps `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`. `DynamicResources.Filter` maps only that sentinel to an `Unschedulable` result for the node; anything else becomes a framework `Error`, and `checkNode` in `findNodesThatPassFilters` cancels the remaining node checks when one shows up.

The other failing cases in the same suite do wrap it. Probe on master `a818af18fe2`, logging `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` for every case that errors:

```
all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool                                                false | claim claim-0, request req-0: asks for all devices, but resource pool driver-a/pool-1 is currently being updated
invalid-pool-is-error-if-no-other-device-can-be-allocated                          true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
duplicate-slice                                                                   true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-validation-error-on-non-targeting-slice                     true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-device-counter-consumption-references-unknown-counter-set    true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-same-counter-set-name-in-different-resource-slices           true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
```

Same in all three variants.

`IsIncomplete` does not need a malformed object. `GatherPools` sets it when the generation resolved for the node holds fewer slices than its declared `resourceSliceCount`, which is what a pool looks like while a driver is publishing a new generation.

### What did you expect to happen?

The check itself looks right and I would leave it alone: a slice that has not arrived may hold another device matching the request, so the allocator cannot know the full set yet.

The classification is the part that looks wrong. Wrapping the sentinel keeps the visible message, since it has no text of its own, and keeps the failure on one node:

```go
return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated%w",
	klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)
```

Other nodes then keep being evaluated, and if all of them fail the Pod is `Unschedulable`. `EventsToRegister` already lists `ResourceSlice` `Add` and `Update`, so the slice update that finishes the rollout requeues it. The invalid branch wants the same treatment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool` in `allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` already reaches the incomplete branch. Adding this next to the existing `expectError` assertion produces the output above:

```go
if err != nil {
	t.Logf("PROBE %s errors.Is=%v", name, errors.Is(err, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode))
}
```

No case covers the invalid branch today.

### Anything else we need to know?

Same classification shape as #141214 and #141338, different trigger. Those need a malformed stored per-device `nodeSelector`; this one fires during an ordinary generation rollout. Filing separately so the accepted scope of #141214 stays as it is.

@trungminhdo4-glitch offered on #141214 to fold this into #141338 if the maintainers would rather keep the per-node classification changes together. I am not opening a competing PR either way.

### Kubernetes version

Read and probed on master `a818af18fe2`. The code path is unchanged on current master.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

---

This issue was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. I verified the code references and ran the probe above myself.
