[UPDATED 2026-09-14] This is the runner before kubernetes/test-infra#37733 (merged 08-21, in the job image since 09-07) copied the pod's `cpu.max` into the `init` leaf. A real quota visibility problem, but not what fails this job. The throttling cliff reading and the explicit GOMAXPROCS idea are struck through.

I need to walk back the GOMAXPROCS part before anyone wires up that env and finds it doesn't help.

I'd assumed e2e.test runs directly in the pod's 2-CPU cgroup, and going by the runner it doesn't. The kubekins runner (`images/bootstrap/runner.sh`, from kubernetes/test-infra#37440) moves the job's processes into an `init` leaf under our own cgroup so it can enable controllers on the `dind` sibling, and a fresh cgroup v2 leaf comes up with `cpu.max=max`. Go's GOMAXPROCS reads only the process's own leaf, not the ancestor that carries the quota, so it sees `max` and sizes to the node's core count. That's the exact shape I'd already tested (2-CPU outer with subtree_control, unlimited leaf, process in the leaf) and watched come out at the host count, so apologies for sending you toward the GODEBUG idea, I just didn't connect the two.

So the 20-vs-2 story doesn't hold on Prow. Both 1.34 and 1.35 e2e.test land in that unlimited leaf and size to the node count, which means godebug doesn't separate them, and `GODEBUG=containermaxprocs=1` reads the same leaf so it won't move anything here.

What does still hold: the kernel enforces the 2 CPUs across the whole subtree, the processes just can't see it, so e2e.test and the kind control plane both oversubscribe. The three release jobs are set up identically (2 CPU, `--nodes=8`), and 1.34 is flaky rather than always red, ~~so this looks more like everything sitting close to the throttling cliff with 1.34 going over most often than a clean 1.34-only cause~~.

~~That points at an explicit `GOMAXPROCS` as the dependable knob rather than the cgroup-detection one. `GOMAXPROCS=2` (or 1) on the e2e.test env at 2 CPU would be worth a run next to kubernetes/test-infra#37717's 2->4, which still helps by lifting the enforced ceiling even though nothing can see it.~~ It would help to have the first canary print `/proc/PID/cgroup`, the leaf and ancestor `cpu.max`, and `cpu.stat`, so the next round is on real numbers rather than my inference. And a small factual fix: the change that made the limit actually bite was kubernetes/test-infra#37440, not kubernetes/test-infra#37421 as I said earlier.

@BenTheElder, you know this runner layer far better than I do, so please tell me if I've read the cgroup layout wrong.

> And a small factual fix: the change that made the limit actually bite was https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/37440, not https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/37421 as I said earlier.

Neither of these seem related? Different repo perhaps?

Sorry, those are kubernetes/test-infra PRs and the bare numbers linked to the wrong repo: kubernetes/test-infra#37440 (the nested cgroup delegation) and kubernetes/test-infra#37421 (the earlier dind change). The code is `images/bootstrap/runner.sh`, and it shows up near the top of a failing job's log as the `cgroup: delegating ...` and `subtree_control=[...]` lines.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] Both links are only about the runner's CPU quota visibility (`cpu.max` of the `init` leaf was `max`). Not the cause of the DRA failures, which is memory. kubernetes/test-infra#37733 fixed the leaf later.

~~Root-cause writeup~~ Runner CPU-quota writeup plus a diagnostic PR, for the record here:

- kubernetes/test-infra#37727: after kubernetes/test-infra#37440 the runner put the job in an `init` cgroup leaf that has no `cpu.max`, so Go sizes GOMAXPROCS to the whole node instead of the 2-CPU pod quota (leaf-vs-parent repro included; the container-aware default reads the leaf, not the parent).
- kubernetes/test-infra#37728: adds a best-effort cgroup snapshot to `ci-kind-dra-1-34` (failing) and `ci-kind-dra-1-35` (green control), before the suite and at cleanup, so we can confirm this from the actual job instead of only my local repro.

Still trying to understand. So https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37440 caused a regression in the sense that the auto-GOMAXPROCS detection no longer works. But then why does that only break the 1.34 job where that Go feature is not active yet? I'm confused.

/cc @stmcginnis

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] 20 is my local box's CPU count, the jobs were not measured; the probe in #141492 got 8 on a master presubmit node. "Explicit GOMAXPROCS=2 is the real fix" was wrong: in a replica of the 1.34 job the cap did not keep the pod under 6Gi (one run each way, both pinned at the limit, neither finished clean). The problem is memory.

Good question, i dig into it. The Go feature being on does not actually save 1.35.

I test a containermaxprocs=1 binary two ways. Run directly in a 2 CPU cgroup, it get GOMAXPROCS=2, so the feature work. But in an unbounded leaf under a 2 CPU parent, same shape as the runner init leaf, it get GOMAXPROCS=20, not 2. It read its own leaf, not walk up to the parent. I also read the runner (kubernetes/test-infra#37440): it never set cpu.max on the init leaf, so the leaf is really unbounded.

~~So 1.35 e2e.test also get 20, same as 1.34, and both job cpu limit is 2. So both oversubscribe, and 1.34 is just where the timeout show up first (maybe heavier suite or more flaky).~~ containermaxprocs=1 alone will not fix 1.34 because it read the unbounded leaf. ~~Explicit GOMAXPROCS=2 like you say is the real fix.~~

I open a draft #141492 to print the real GOMAXPROCS from a presubmit, so we can confirm 1.35 also get 20 on real Prow, not only my local test.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] Historical. The runner fix went in as kubernetes/test-infra#37733; kubernetes/test-infra#37731 was never merged, and in a local replica of the job the cap did not keep the pod under 6Gi. See the top of the issue.

The presubmit experiment #141492 confirm one part of the hypothesis on a real Prow worker. The ginkgo binary print `GOMAXPROCS=8 NumCPU=8`, with the process in `.../cri-containerd-<hash>.scope/init` (`cpu.max=max`) under a `.../scope` with `cpu.max=200000 100000` (2 CPU).

So the outer Go process does not see the effective 2 CPU ancestor quota for its automatic GOMAXPROCS in this runner topology. The runner and the leaf are the same for the other DRA jobs, so they likely behave the same, but this probe ran in the master presubmit, not a direct per-job measurement, and it did not measure the Go processes inside the nested kind control plane.

So the next single-variable canary is command-local `GOMAXPROCS=2` in kubernetes/test-infra#37731, keeping CPU, memory, `--nodes=8` and the test selection unchanged. I will wait for repeated periodic results before calling it the root cause or a sufficient fix; if the control plane still fall behind, more CPU is the next lever.

> So both oversubscribe, and 1.34 is just where the timeout show up first (maybe heavier suite or more flaky).

Not just "first", we "only" (!) see it there. I still find this suspicious because I cannot think of a good explanation why 1.34 should have a more demanding set of tests than 1.35.

Let's merge https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37731, but I am not convinced yet that this is the only and/or right fix.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] "Both get 8" was one master presubmit, not each release job, and a green run after a change would not have proven the cause anyway, so the last paragraph is struck. What makes 1.34 worse is at the top of the issue.

You are right to be suspicious. The GOMAXPROCS part is the same on both branches: 1.34 and 1.35 e2e.test both land in the init leaf and both get 8, so that alone does not explain why only 1.34 time out. `GOMAXPROCS=2` is a demand-side cap that help either way, but it is not a 1.34-only cause.

Two things could put 1.34 over the cliff and not 1.35: the e2e.test is built from release-1.34, so the actual suite and its timing differ from 1.35 (the test code, not the label-filter), or 1.34 just runs closer to the 90m limit and tips over more often. I have no proof for either yet.

~~So the periodic is the real test. If 1.34 go green and stay green with the cap, parallelism was the trigger. If it still time out, the cap is not enough and the kind control plane (also unbounded, also oversubscribing) is the next suspect. I can also diff the 1.34 vs 1.35 DRA suite for a slow test that 1.35 dropped, if that help narrow it.~~

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] Points 2 to 4 below were overtaken the next morning: the recent failures are memory (the pod's 6Gi), not the runner's GOMAXPROCS. I struck through those sentences and kept them because my next comment refers to them. The measurements are in my comment of 09-12 (09:33 UTC) below.

Update after the 09-07 image bump, which put kubernetes/test-infra#37733 into every `kubekins-e2e:v20260907-*` image.

1. The runner fix is live and 1.34 still fails. The bump landed 09-07 20:06 UTC, so the first `ci-kind-dra-1-34` run on the new image is 09-08: FAILURE 09-08, FAILURE 09-09, SUCCESS 09-10, FAILURE 09-11 (podinfo shows `v20260907-7013e6a654-1.34` on all four). `ci-kind-dra-1-35` on the same image: SUCCESS 09-08, 09-09 and 09-10, FAILURE 09-11.

2. Why 1.34 and not 1.35. `release-1.34/go.mod` has `godebug default=go1.24`, `release-1.35` has `default=go1.25`. The container-aware GOMAXPROCS from Go 1.25 sits behind the `containermaxprocs` GODEBUG, and the `default=go1.24` line switches it off for every main package built in that module. The periodic takes `ginkgo` and `e2e.test` from the CI test tarball at `dl.k8s.io/ci/$revision`, and the presubmits build the same two targets with `make WHAT=...`; either way they are built inside the k/k module. In the tarball the 09-11 run extracted (`v1.34.11-5+27b30ec9411c5a`) both binaries carry `DefaultGODEBUG=containermaxprocs=0,...,updatemaxprocs=0` in `go version -m`; the 1.35 tarball (`v1.35.8-8+e3f8d085115f38`) has neither setting. Under a 2 CPU cgroup quota on a 20 core machine (`systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=200%`) a `default=go1.24` binary reports `GOMAXPROCS=20`, a `default=go1.25` binary reports `2`, and `GOMAXPROCS=2` in the environment gives `2` for both. So on release-1.34, ginkgo and e2e.test still ignore the `cpu.max` that kubernetes/test-infra#37733 copies into the init leaf. ~~1.34 is the one branch where the runner stays oversubscribed, which fits the per-branch numbers, though it does not prove it is the whole story.~~ [UPDATED] Real, but not what fails the runs. With `GOMAXPROCS=2` in the runner env my replica of the job still ran into the 6Gi limit and did not finish clean either (one run each way, random seeds: 12 failed specs and 39 OOM kills with the cap, 8 and none without).

3. ~~That makes kubernetes/test-infra#37731 (explicit `GOMAXPROCS=2` on `ci-kind-dra-1-34`) the right runner-side fix for that branch after all, since the environment variable wins over the GODEBUG default. I rebased it and dropped the hold. The 1.34 presubmit forks in `release-branch-jobs/1.34.yaml` build the same way and can get the same line if this helps.~~ [UPDATED] kubernetes/test-infra#37731 does not address the memory limit and does not reach the kind control plane.

4. 1.35 and master are not clean either, with the runner sized right. `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all` on #141924 (release-1.35) failed 3 of 3 with the kind apiserver unreachable (`TLS handshake timeout` and `connection refused` in the framework `BeforeEach`). In the last run the control-plane journal has 154 etcd `apply request took too long` and 13 apiserver liveness probe failures within 5 minutes, no restart and nothing about OOM. #142023 on the same release-1.35 base passed the job, and so did the same cherry-pick on 1.34, 1.36 and 1.37. On master the presubmit failed 6 of 13 completed runs on 09-11, at least two of them on unrelated PRs (#142026, #142015) with the same signature, while the `ci-kind-dra-all` periodic was 8 of 8 green, ~~so it also depends on what else the build node is running~~ [UPDATED: a guess, never tested]. ~~The processes inside the kind node containers are the part kubernetes/test-infra#37733 leaves out (docker starts them without a CPU limit, so apiserver, etcd and kubelet size themselves to the host). That is my next suspect for these branches. I have not tried anything for it yet; a `docker update --cpus` on the node containers after `kind create cluster` would be the smallest experiment, if you think it is worth one.~~ [UPDATED] Measured since then: in my replica of the job (8 CPUs visible, 2 CPU quota) the kind control plane runs at GOMAXPROCS=8 on both branches (kube-apiserver `go_sched_gomaxprocs_threads` is 8 on 1.34 and 1.35; the node containers have their own cgroup namespace, so the pod's cpu.max is invisible to them). Same on both branches, so not the difference. Prow labeled 3 of the 4 #141924 runs as OOM killed, two of the three above plus the one that started a minute after this comment; the 09-11 20:45 run whose journal I quoted was not OOM labeled, it failed at 27 minutes with the same apiserver errors. Why `-all` is the one that fails on 1.35 is at the top of the issue.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] This correction is now also inline in the comment above. Last paragraph fixed below.

Correction to my last comment. I had only looked inside the kind node journal for OOM, and that cannot see the pod cgroup. The prow status for the runs says otherwise: `ci-kind-dra-1-34` ended with `Job pod was OOM killed by the cluster.` on 09-04, 09-05, 09-08, 09-09 and 09-11 (5 of the last 10 runs), `ci-kind-dra-1-35` on 09-11, and 3 of the 4 `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all` runs on #141924 (release-1.35) as well.

So the recent 1.34 failures are memory, not the runner's GOMAXPROCS, and the per-branch fit I described in point 2 does not hold. The GODEBUG difference is real, but it is not what killed these runs.

~~The forks run these jobs at 6Gi while master moved them to 12Gi in kubernetes/test-infra#36376; the 1.36 and 1.37 forks have 12Gi.~~ [UPDATED] Not quite. The 1.34 and 1.35 forks run all of these jobs at 6Gi. Master raised only `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all`, `-all-slow` and `ci-kind-dra-all` to 12Gi (kubernetes/test-infra#36376, together with race detection), and the 1.36 and 1.37 forks carry that 12Gi for their `-all` presubmits; their periodics and plain presubmit stay at 6Gi, with the 10 slice test. kubernetes/test-infra#37865 raises the 1.34 and 1.35 jobs to 12Gi. The 2 CPU contention on master presubmits (12Gi there, no OOM kills) is a separate question.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] Two paragraphs here were wrong, see the strike-through and the notes next to them, and I added one paragraph at the end with what I measured since. Also, the numbers in the second paragraph are 1 to 3 runs per branch with random ginkgo seeds, "not reclaimable" there is node anon plus the whole ginkgo cgroup, a rough figure, and the 1.34 row is one run.

Measured it instead of guessing. I replayed `ci-kind-dra-1-3x` locally (same CI tarballs `v1.34.11-5` / `v1.35.8-8` / `v1.36.4-15`, same kind.yaml, same `ginkgo run --nodes=8` command and filter, current kind, 20 cores, no memory limit) and sampled the cgroups of the four kind nodes and of ginkgo/e2e.test every 5 seconds. The 1.34 and 1.35 runs passed; the 1.36 runs had one failing spec each (DeviceTaintRule eviction).

Peak memory, nodes + ginkgo (not reclaimable part in brackets): release-1.34 9360 MiB (6626), release-1.35 6958 / 7384 / 7391 MiB over three runs (5360 / 5723 / 5502), release-1.36 5228 / 5600 MiB (3474 / 3736). The difference is the control plane: kube-apiserver peaks at 1880 MiB on 1.34 and 1846 MiB on 1.35 against 732 MiB on 1.36, and on 1.34 kube-scheduler reaches 1267 MiB as well.

~~The apiserver number is not load. On 1.34 and 1.35 it jumps from about 420 MiB to about 1.8 GiB within a few seconds during the run and never comes down; at the end of the run, with zero ResourceSlices and zero ResourceClaims left, `/debug/pprof/heap` still shows about 680 MiB in `resource/v1.(*Device).Unmarshal` and `(*DeviceAttribute).Unmarshal`, all allocated under `etcd3.(*watchChan).transform`, so the watch cache is holding decoded ResourceSlice objects that no longer exist. On 1.36 the same profile holds under 100 MiB of those. I am collecting the watch cache metrics for both and will file it against kube-apiserver separately.~~ [UPDATED] Not a leak, I withdraw this. The 1.8 GiB is the watch history of the 100 max-size ResourceSlices that `ResourceSlice Controller creates slices` publishes on these branches; the apiserver keeps that for any resource. Master cut the test to 10 slices in #136156 (1847d5b1a, "created too much load for an E2E test"). See also the next comment.

~~For the jobs this means 6Gi cannot work on 1.34 and 1.35 as they are, whatever the CPU quota does: the pod also holds dockerd, containerd and the runner, and 1.34 alone peaks at 9.4 GiB on an idle host. That is kubernetes/test-infra#37865.~~ [UPDATED] Too strong. The 1.34 number is 9360 MiB (about 9.14 GiB, not 9.4), nodes plus ginkgo, one run, no memory limit. It is not a minimum requirement. Together with prow's OOM reports it is a reason to try 12Gi (kubernetes/test-infra#37865), not proof that 12Gi fixes every run. The limit only started to reach the kind nodes with the 07-13 image (kubernetes/test-infra#37440 put dind under the pod cgroup); the first OOM labeled run is 07-14.

[UPDATED] What I measured since, first on the same branch with only the slice count changed (two e2e.test binaries from one base commit), then with the real kubekins image, docker-in-docker, 2 CPU, 6Gi or 12Gi. The numbers are summarized in the PRs linked from the top of the issue; I have the raw samples if anyone wants them. With 100 slices the ginkgo seed decides whether some pod gets scheduled while the slices exist. On release-1.34 the default gates pick the scheduler's experimental structured allocator, and its V(5) `Gathering pools` line prints the whole slice list once per node it evaluates, per scheduling attempt, about 74 MB per line while the 100 slices are there; the jobs run kube-scheduler at `--v=5`. That is why the same 1.34 binaries peaked at 6609 to 7036 MiB with one seed and at 8210, 8996 and 11373 MiB with three others (kube-scheduler at 1434 to 1720 MiB, up to 5.9 GB of scheduler log in one run). release-1.35 with default gates uses another allocator without that line: both 1.35 periodic replicas completed at 6Gi, at 87 to 94% of the limit non-reclaimable, while none of the five 1.34 replicas at 6Gi finished clean (three of the periodic, one with the `-all` gates, one presubmit built from source). Going from 100 to 10 slices takes about 2 GiB of non-reclaimable memory off the suite on both branches (3.0 to 3.4 GiB in the 1.34 random seed runs that hit the log mode). Deleting the log line (master does not have it since #136588) let the 100 slice presubmit replicas finish at 6Gi on both branches, still at 93 to 95% of the limit non-reclaimable. All of this is 1 to 3 runs per condition.

[UPDATED 2026-09-14] This correction is now also in the comment above (its apiserver paragraph is struck through there). Keeping this one because the reply below refers to it.

One correction to the apiserver part above, after digging further: it is load after all, not an apiserver bug, and I am not going to file one.

The 1.8 GiB is the watch cache holding the history of one test. `ResourceSlice Controller creates slices` on release-1.34 and release-1.35 publishes 100 ResourceSlices of the maximum size (128 devices with 32 maximum-length attributes each), the apiserver keeps that watch history for the rest of the run as it would for any resource, and the heap shows exactly those decoded slices. On release-1.36 the same test was rewritten to publish 10 slices (1847d5b1a, "DRA e2e+integration: test ResourceSlice controller"), so its apiserver stays under 1 GiB. The 6Gi conclusion for the 1.34 and 1.35 jobs does not change; the reason is that their suite is heavier, not that the apiserver leaks.

> One correction to the apiserver part above

Instead of adding more comments, can you edit existing comments? As it stands now, someone reading from top-to-bottom first finds incorrect comments, then corrections and has to assemble the full picture in their head.

There are now strict rules how comments are edited. It depends a bit on whether it is important that readers recognize that something was changed. From less to more obvious:
- Just edit. Suitable if the expectation is that readers will start anew from the top.
- Edit and add an [EDIT] or [UPDATED] tag near the place that you changed. This tells readers that they may have to re-read and that this reflects a revised understanding of the problem.
- Keep the old text in strike-through markup next to new text. This explicitly tells readers what is no longer valid, which can be relevant in longer discussions.

Such markers are also useful for a third party in discussions where someone has already replied, because the reply might relate to something that isn't in the original comment anymore.

Done, thanks for the pointer. The wrong conclusions in my comments above are now corrected in place (strike-through and [UPDATED] notes) and the current picture is at the top of the description. The two release-1.35 changes are #142082 and #142083.

With the root cause of the higher memory requirement identified I am okay with raising the limits in the job definitions. Let's not touch the production code, they don't meet the cherry-pick guidelines.

title: A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in CreateContainerError after its node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.
body:
### What happened?

A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in `CreateContainerError` after its
node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.

Setup: a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim, already `Running` with its device allocated and
prepared. I rebooted the node (a full reboot — kubelet and the container runtime both restart, along with
every workload container on that node, including the DRA driver's own pod).

After the node came back:
- The driver re-registered and kubelet re-prepared the same already-allocated claim (confirmed via the
  driver's own logs — it logged a fresh "prepare" call for the exact same claim UID and returned success).
- Despite that, the pod's container repeatedly failed to start:
  ```
  Warning  Failed  Error: failed to create containerd container: CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices k8s.gpu.example.com/gpu=<uid>-gpu-0
  ```
- This did not resolve on its own. I watched it for 5+ minutes: kubelet kept retrying the identical
  container creation with the identical (still-unresolvable) device reference, backing off further each
  time. It never attempted to re-prepare the claim again.
- The only way I found to recover was deleting and recreating the pod, which allocates a fresh claim and
  works immediately.


Note: a plain `systemctl restart kubelet` alone (container runtime left untouched, containers kept running)
does **not** reproduce this — I tried that first and saw no re-prepare attempt at all over several minutes.
The container runtime itself needs to also restart (i.e. an actual node reboot, or restarting kubelet and
the container runtime together) for this to trigger.


### What did you expect to happen?

Either the pod should recover cleanly after the node comes back, or if the replayed prepare produces a
result that doesn't actually work, there should be some way to detect that and retry — an Event, a condition,
or another re-prepare attempt — rather than an indefinite retry loop with a generic container-runtime error
that gives no indication anything DRA-related happened.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up a DRA driver and create a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim (used
   [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0 for
   this repro). Confirm it reaches `Running` with the claim allocated.
2. Fully reboot the node the pod is running on (in a `kind` cluster: `docker restart <node-container>`; on a
   real cluster: an actual node reboot, or restarting the container runtime and kubelet together).
3. Wait for the node to report `Ready` again and the driver's pod to come back up and re-register.
4. Observe: `kubectl describe pod` shows repeated `CreateContainerError` / `CDI device injection failed:
   unresolvable CDI devices ...` events, with a growing `BackOff`. This does not resolve on its own.
5. Delete and recreate the pod — it comes up fine immediately with a fresh claim.


### Anything else we need to know?

I reproduced this the same way on a second, real (non-kind) cluster — same sequence of events, same
`CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices` error, same lack of self-recovery. A comparison pod
on a node that wasn't rebooted kept running the whole time, so this is specifically tied to the reboot, not
something intermittent.

Two things worth separating here, since I've only tested with one driver:

- Kubelet does not appear to remember, across a restart, that a claim was already successfully prepared —
  every claim gets treated as unprepared again after a reboot, and gets a fresh `NodePrepareResources` call
  regardless of which driver is behind it. This part reproduced identically on both clusters.
- Once that replayed call happens, kubelet accepts whatever the driver responds with and never re-checks or
  retries even after the resulting container creation keeps failing — it just repeats the identical failing
  attempt indefinitely. This also isn't specific to any one driver's behavior; it's what kubelet does with
  the response once it gets it, and I did not see it change over the retries.
- What I can't say for certain is whether every DRA driver would produce an unusable result the way this one
  did on replay. I tested only [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver).
  A driver with more robust logic may not have any visible symptom. But it seems that kubelet
  gives a driver no way to tell "this is a replay of something you already told me was ready" versus a fresh
  request, and never verifies or retries regardless. So any driver whose restart-recovery isn't airtight may hit
 this type of problem. This happened on the very first attempt, with the reference driver
  meant to demonstrate best practices, using nothing more unusual than a node reboot.


### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
kind v0.32.0, node image kindest/node:v1.36.1
```

</details>



### Cloud provider

<details>

Local `kind` cluster, not cloud-hosted.

</details>


### OS version

<details>

N/A — reproduced on a local `kind` cluster.

</details>


### Install tools

<details>

`kind create cluster`, DRA driver installed via its own Helm chart
([kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0).

</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>

</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

comments.body:
/sig scheduling
/sig node

Hi @yogeshbendre , thanks for the detailed reproduction. I'd like to work on this.

I'll trace the kubelet DRA prepare/re-prepare lifecycle across a full node/runtime restart, including how the prepared device/CDI state is reconstructed and how container creation failures are handled after NodePrepareResources succeeds. I'll also verify whether the recovery gap is in kubelet or in the driver's replay behavior before implementing the fix, and add regression coverage for the identified failure path.

/assign

Hi @yogeshbendre, I traced the restart path further and I believe the observed failure is in dra-example-driver v0.4.0 rather than kubelet.

On kubelet restart, DRA preparation is intentionally replayed. The DRA prepare contract is idempotent, and kubelet calls NodePrepareResources again as expected.

In the example driver, DeviceState.Prepare() first restores the claim from its checkpoint. When restoreClaimFromCheckpoint() returns prepared devices, the function returns those devices immediately. The call to CreateClaimSpecFile() only happens on the fresh preparation path.

This creates a failure mode after a full node/runtime reboot: the driver's checkpoint may still say the claim is prepared while the claim-specific CDI spec is no longer present. The replayed prepare then returns success with the previous CDI IDs without recreating the corresponding CDI spec, after which containerd cannot resolve those IDs.

Based on that, I don't currently see a safe Kubernetes-side fix. Retrying DRA preparation for a generic CreateContainerError would conflate unrelated runtime failures with DRA failures. The more direct fix appears to be making the driver's restored-claim prepare path re-establish the CDI artifacts before returning success.

If SIG Node / WG Device Management agrees with that diagnosis, I'm happy to send the fix and regression test to kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver.

both dra driver and kubelet didn't handle very well. 
- dra-drvier side: it didn't check the cdi artifact existence before returning device id
- kubelet side: for cdi resolution issue, it's better offer another chance to trigger dra-driver to reprepare.
I have a working implementation (kubelet + in-tree test driver) with unit tests if SIG Node would like me to send a PR.

/kind bug

Thanks @yong-jie-gong, that makes sense. I also confirmed the driver-side gap and have a tested fix locally that recreates the claim CDI spec on checkpoint-restored Prepare().

For the kubelet side, my concern was that the current CRI failure path appears generic, so I avoided triggering DRA re-prepare on arbitrary CreateContainerError. If your implementation can identify the CDI-resolution case narrowly without relying on brittle error-string matching, that sounds worth evaluating.

I'll hold off on opening either change until SIG Node / WG Device Management confirms whether they want:
1. the driver fix only,
2. kubelet recovery as well,
3. or both.
/cc

Hi @yogeshbendre @ffromani @yong-jie-gong,

Following up after the investigation above.

I have a tested driver-side fix in kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver that recreates the claim-specific CDI spec when Prepare() restores a prepared claim from checkpoint. I also added regression coverage for the restart/spec-loss case and the CDI recreation failure path.

The current dra-example-driver main branch still has the restored-claim path returning the checkpointed devices without recreating the claim CDI spec.

I also reviewed the kubelet-side recovery concern raised by @yong-jie-gong. I'm happy to work on the kubelet recovery as well if SIG Node / WG Device Management wants both sides addressed.

Could you confirm whether the preferred direction is:
1. driver-side fix only,
2. kubelet recovery as well, or
3. both?

Once the direction is confirmed, I'll open the appropriate PR(s).

Thank you @Gaurav598 and @yong-jie-gong 
Looking forward to the decision :)

> Hi [@yogeshbendre](https://github.com/yogeshbendre) [@ffromani](https://github.com/ffromani) [@yong-jie-gong](https://github.com/yong-jie-gong),

@Gaurav598 
Due to kubelet checkpoint machanism, "prepared" state will be written on the disk.  even if kubelet/node restart, kubelet will not retrigger node re-prepare.  in other words, once cdi device lost after restart, kubelet will never retrigger it unless remove kubelet checkpoint data or pod.    that is why  both side  need changes. kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver has the same issue — it restores from its own checkpoint without verifying CDI spec files

Thanks @yong-jie-gong. This makes the split clear.

I'll proceed with the driver-side fix in kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver: recreate the claim-specific CDI spec when a prepared claim is restored from checkpoint, with regression coverage for both CDI spec loss and idempotent restored Prepare().

I'll open the driver PR separately and link it back to #141433 / #141619 so the two fixes can be reviewed independently.

Definitely a bug in the example driver.

Whether kubelet should retry is open for debate. If the driver behaved incorrectly in the first call, why should it behave better in the second? This doesn't seem to help and probably makes kubelet more complex, so I'm not convinced.

> Whether kubelet should retry is open for debate. If the driver behaved incorrectly in the first call, why should it behave better in the second? This doesn't seem to help and probably makes kubelet more complex, so I'm not convinced.

It didn't behave incorrectly in the first call. Kubelet doesn't call `PrepareResources` after reboot because it gets 'prepared' `ClaimInfo` flag from its checkpoint and [skips claim preparation if the flag is set](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L387-L390).

> It didn't behave incorrectly in the first call. Kubelet doesn't call PrepareResources after reboot 

Hmm, we never formally specified this, did we? I was expecting that kubelet would call it, because a) doing so is safe (= consistent with our gRPC API contract) and b) it might fix whatever is not right after a reboot (= practical benefit).

It also doesn't match what @Gaurav598 said in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141433#issuecomment-5332122381 ("On kubelet restart, DRA preparation is intentionally replayed").

> because it gets 'prepared' ClaimInfo flag from its checkpoint and [skips claim preparation if the flag is set](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L387-L390).

This checkpoint file has given us so much trouble - do we really want and/or need it? What's the benefit?

/reopen

> > It didn't behave incorrectly in the first call. Kubelet doesn't call PrepareResources after reboot
> 
> Hmm, we never formally specified this, did we? I was expecting that kubelet would call it, because a) doing so is safe (= consistent with our gRPC API contract) and b) it might fix whatever is not right after a reboot (= practical benefit).
>
> It also doesn't match what [@Gaurav598](https://github.com/Gaurav598) said in [#141433 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141433#issuecomment-5332122381) ("On kubelet restart, DRA preparation is intentionally replayed").

My bad, I was wrong with this. `prepared` attribute is not checkpointed. It's part of the ClaimInfo structure, but not all of its attributes are checkpointed. [Only ClaimInfo.ClaimInfoState field is checkponted](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/claiminfo.go#L353). 

Now I agree, we can close this issue and the implementation PR.

> > because it gets 'prepared' ClaimInfo flag from its checkpoint and [skips claim preparation if the flag is set](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L387-L390).
> 
> This checkpoint file has given us so much trouble - do we really want and/or need it? What's the benefit?
> 
As far as I remember it keeps claim -> pods map that allows to correctly call UnprepareResources even after reboots and Kubelet restarts.

> Now I agree, we can close this issue and the implementation PR.

Ack. Let's keep this issue open for a short while longer while I document this behavior.

> As far as I remember it keeps claim -> pods map that allows to correctly call UnprepareResources even after reboots and Kubelet restarts.

That makes sense.

/triage accepted
/kind documentation
/priority important-longterm

comments.body: I'll take this. The write side is podActions.String() (pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go) dumping VolumesToUpsize/VolumesToDownsize with %v, which calls the generated EmptyDirVolumeSource.String() and mutates the shared Quantity string cache while the allocation manager reads it. I don't like that fix. It seems very fragile. A better solution would be to call `String` after the code which sets the value because that code is more likely to be understood as something that must not run concurrently - depends a bit on how many places set the value, of course.

title: DRA structured allocator overflows the native-int device-count sum in the per-claim limit check
body:
### What happened

The structured allocator adds device counts in native `int` before comparing to `resourceapi.AllocationResultsMaxSize`. `allocateOne` forms `len(results) + requestData.numDevices - r.deviceIndex`, and the pre-flight `Allocate` loop accumulates `minDevicesPerClaim += numDevices`. `DeviceRequest.Count` is validated only as `> 0`, never against the result limit, so several large-but-valid counts sum past the limit and wrap. Two counts of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` wrap to a negative total, so `total > MaxSize` is false and the check is skipped; four wrap back near zero. A `FirstAvailable` request whose first alternative carries a huge count, sitting behind a device already allocated for the claim, drives the overflowing subtraction and misdirects the backtracking rather than pruning the oversized alternative.

### What you expected to happen

Each request is refused against the remaining capacity before the sum is formed, so no addition overflows and an oversized count is rejected with `number of requested devices exceeds the claim limit`.

### How to reproduce it

A single claim with two `ExactCount` requests of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` each: the total overflows negative and is admitted today. A `FirstAvailable` request with a first subrequest of `math.MaxInt` behind one already-allocated device: the oversized alternative should be pruned and the small one taken. Both are covered by the tests in #141307, and the fix is applied identically across the stable, incubating, and experimental tiers.

### Anything else we need to know

`math.MaxInt` makes the counts overflow on 32-bit builds as well. This is worth a backport decision for the release branches that already carry the per-claim result-limit check.

### Related

This is the concrete in-tree instance behind #140424, which asks for an upper bound or overflow-safety contract on `DeviceRequest.Count`. #140424 observes that the structured allocator guards the single-count path; the gap here is the multi-count sum on that same path, one large count plus the devices already allocated for the claim, which was not guarded until #141307.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

_This issue was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. I checked the allocator paths and the overflow cases against the code and the tests myself._

title: [Bug] Device taint NoExecute eviction does not evict pods using DRA-backed extended-resource claims (pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus)
body:
### What happened?

**TL;DR:** the device-taint eviction controller (`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction`) only discovers which
claims a pod is using by reading `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. A pod that got its device through the newer
Extended Resource Backed by DRA path (KEP-5004, `DRAExtendedResource`) has its claim reference in
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus` instead — a field this controller never looks at. Both
`DRADeviceTaints` and `DRAExtendedResource` are Beta and **default-on since v1.36**, so this affects any
cluster running a stock 1.36+ apiserver/controller-manager with a DRA driver installed — no unusual
configuration required.

Live-reproduced on a `kind` cluster (full steps and output below): two pods, each holding one device from the
same driver, then a single `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` applied against that driver:

| Pod | Requests its device via | Claim reference lives in | Result after `NoExecute` taint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pod-to-be-evicted` | `ResourceClaimTemplate` | `pod.spec.resourceClaims` | Evicted within ~10s (correct) |
| `pod0` | plain `resources.limits` extended-resource request | `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus` | **Still `Running`, untouched** — the bug |

The `DeviceTaintRule`'s own status confirms only one pod was ever considered:
`"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace"` → `"1 pod evicted since starting the controller"`.

**Scope note, to save a maintainer the round-trip:** this is specifically about the *post-allocation eviction*
path. Allocation-time taint enforcement (a **new** pod being blocked from a `NoSchedule`/`NoExecute`-tainted
device it doesn't tolerate) is unaffected and works correctly for both request styles. The bug is
narrowly in the separate, already-allocated-pod eviction controller.

**Couple of affected use cases**
- GPU health-triggered auto-remediation. A node-health/GPU-health controller (e.g. something reacting to Xid/ECC errors, similar in spirit to NVIDIA GPU Operator's health checks) detects a failing GPU and applies a NoExecute DeviceTaintRule to force workloads off it before quarantining or repairing the device. Any pod still using the classic nvidia.com/gpu: 1-style request — which is the majority of existing GPU workloads, since KEP-5004's entire purpose is letting them keep working unmodified under DRA — is never evicted, and keeps running on a known-bad GPU instead of being cleanly rescheduled. Worst case: silently corrupted training/inference output rather than a clean failure.
- Targeted single-device maintenance on a multi-GPU node. An admin wants to service or replace one GPU on a node without draining the whole node (disruptive to the node's other GPUs/workloads), so they taint just that device NoExecute instead of cordoning the node. Any pod holding that device via an extended-resource request keeps running through the "drain," so the device can't actually be safely pulled for maintenance without an admin separately hunting down and manually killing those pods — defeating the point of device-level (vs. node-level) maintenance tooling.
- Clusters mid-migration from device plugins to DRA. KEP-5004 exists specifically so clusters can adopt DRA drivers without immediately rewriting every pod spec — meaning a long transitional period where legacy extended-resource-requesting Deployments/Jobs and newer ResourceClaim-based workloads coexist on the same devices. During that period, any device-taint-based enforcement (decommissioning a device, isolating a suspect one) only works for the already-migrated minority of workloads, silently failing for everyone else — undermining the mechanism cluster-wide for as long as the migration takes, which for large fleets could be months.

### What did you expect to happen?

A `NoExecute` device taint should evict every pod actually consuming the tainted device, independent of which
API surface the pod used to request it. An admin tainting a failing/draining GPU for maintenance has no way to
know (and shouldn't need to know) whether a given consumer pod requested it via a `ResourceClaim` or via a
classic `resources.limits` extended-resource request — both end up running on the same physical device via
the same DRA driver and the same underlying `ResourceClaim` object. Today only one of the two is actually
evicted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducible deterministically on a `kind` cluster with no real GPU hardware, using
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) (a maintained,
public example DRA driver that simulates GPUs). All manifests below are the driver's own unmodified example
manifests (`demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/` and
`demo/examples/extended-resource-request/`), just applied side by side.

**Prerequisites:** Docker, `kind` v0.20+, `helm` v3.7+, `kubectl`.

```bash
# 1. Create a kind cluster with the required feature gates and API version.
#    (DynamicResourceAllocation and DRAAdminAccess are already GA/locked-on by v1.36 and are
#    omitted; DRADeviceTaints/DRAExtendedResource are Beta+default-on in 1.36 but included
#    explicitly for clarity; DRADeviceTaintRules is Beta+default-OFF in 1.36 and must be set.)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  DRADeviceTaints: true
  DRAExtendedResource: true
  DRADeviceTaintRules: true
runtimeConfig:
  resource.k8s.io/v1beta2: "true"
containerdConfigPatches:
- |-
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    enable_cdi = true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name dra-repro --image kindest/node:v1.36.1 --config kind-config.yaml --wait 3m

# 2. Install the example DRA driver (8 simulated GPUs, no real hardware, default values).
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.4.0 https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver.git
helm upgrade -i --create-namespace --namespace dra-example-driver dra-example-driver \
  dra-example-driver/deployments/helm/dra-example-driver
kubectl -n dra-example-driver wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=kubeletplugin --timeout=90s

# 3. Control pod: requests a GPU via a ResourceClaimTemplate (pod.spec.resourceClaims).
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/1-basic-resourceclaimtemplate.yaml
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/2-pod-to-be-evicted.yaml
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod-to-be-evicted --timeout=60s

# 4. Treatment pod: requests a GPU via the classic extended-resource field. The scheduler
#    satisfies it via DRA and records the claim in pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus instead
#    of pod.spec.resourceClaims (confirmed with the jsonpath check below).
kubectl create namespace extended-resource-request
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: extended-resource-request
  name: pod0
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ctr0
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["export; trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
    resources:
      limits:
        deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com: 1
EOF
kubectl -n extended-resource-request wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod0 --timeout=60s
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}{"\n"}'

# 5. Taint the whole driver's devices NoExecute — both pods' devices are in scope.
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    driver: gpu.example.com
  taint:
    key: gpu.example.com/unhealthy
    value: "true"
    effect: NoExecute
EOF

# 6. Observe.
sleep 15
kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted   # expect: NotFound (evicted+deleted)
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide           # expect: still Running
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}'
{"requestMappings":[{"containerName":"ctr0","requestName":"container-0-request-0",
"resourceName":"deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com"}],
"resourceClaimName":"pod0-extended-resources-v77pc"}

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}'
spec.resourceClaims=

$ kubectl apply -f device-taint-rule.yaml
devicetaintrule.resource.k8s.io/example created

$ kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
# immediately after creation:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:42Z","message":"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"PodsPendingEviction","status":"True","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

# ~10s later:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:52Z","message":"1 pod evicted since starting the controller.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"Completed","status":"False","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted
Error from server (NotFound): pods "pod-to-be-evicted" not found

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -3
28s   Normal   DeviceTaintManagerEviction   pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Marking for deletion
28s   Normal   Killing                      pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Stopping container ctr0

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
pod0   1/1     Running   0          69s   dra-repro-worker

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
# Scheduled / Pulled / Created / Started only — zero eviction-related events, ever.

$ kubectl get resourceclaim -A
NAMESPACE                   NAME                            STATE
extended-resource-request   pod0-extended-resources-v77pc   allocated,reserved
# (pod-to-be-evicted's generated claim is gone — cleaned up along with the deleted pod)
```

Only one of the two pods using tainted devices from the same driver was ever evicted. This reproduces every
time; there is no timing dependency.


### Anything else we need to know?

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`;
live-reproduced above on `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (closest publicly available `kind` node image to `v1.36.3` at
time of testing — same code, confirmed by reading).

**1. The eviction controller enumerates claims from exactly one field.**

`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go`, `podEvictionTime`
([current source](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go)),
is the *only* place this controller determines which claims a pod uses:

```go
func (tc *Controller) podEvictionTime(pod *v1.Pod) *evictionAndReason {
    if pod.Spec.NodeName == "" {
        return nil
    }
    var eviction *evictionAndReason
    for i := range pod.Spec.ResourceClaims {
        claimName, mustCheckOwner, err := resourceclaim.Name(pod, &pod.Spec.ResourceClaims[i])
        ...
    }
    return eviction
}
```

Grepping the full 1691-line file for `ExtendedResource` returns zero matches, on both the tag and master.

**2. The sibling `resourceclaim` controller already had to solve this exact problem.**

`pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go`, `enqueuePod`:

```go
// Check if pod has any resource claims to process.
// Extended resource claims are stored in pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus,
// not in pod.Spec.ResourceClaims, so we need to check both locations.
hasResourceClaims := len(pod.Spec.ResourceClaims) > 0
hasExtendedResourceClaims := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus != nil
...
// Without this, extended resource claims would never be cleaned up when
// pods complete, causing device resources to remain allocated indefinitely.
if hasExtendedResourceClaims {
    claimName := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName
    ...
}
```

The device-taint eviction controller never received the equivalent treatment.

**3. Both contributing feature gates are Beta and default-on as of this release**
(`pkg/features/kube_features.go`):

```go
DRADeviceTaints: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.33"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
DRAExtendedResource: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
```

So this isn't an edge-case opt-in combination — it's the default state of a stock 1.36+ cluster with any DRA
driver and `DeviceTaintRule` usage.

**4. No test coverage exercises this interaction.** `test/integration/dra/device_taints.go` and
`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction_test.go` (2926 lines) both have zero hits for
`ExtendedResource`.

**5. Allocation-time taint enforcement is unaffected (see "Scope note" above)** —
`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`,
`taintPreventsAllocation`, is reached identically for extended-resource and explicit-claim requests, since
`extendeddynamicresources.go` builds an in-memory claim for the extended-resource path before `Filter` runs.
Included here to preempt the natural "does this mean extended-resource claims ignore taints entirely?"
question — they don't; only post-allocation `NoExecute` eviction is blind.

### Suggested fix direction

Mirror the `resourceclaim` controller's dual-location check into `podEvictionTime` — i.e. also resolve
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName` when present, using the same claim lookup/ownership
logic already used for `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. This looks like a contained, well-scoped fix; happy to
attempt a PR once a maintainer confirms this is the intended approach (rather than, say, deprecating the
implicit extended-resource path's exemption from eviction on purpose — which seems unlikely given point 2
above, but worth confirming).



### Kubernetes version

<details>
Live reproduction (above): `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream via `kind`. Code paths involved confirmed
identical at tag `v1.36.3` (latest stable at time of this report) and master HEAD
`94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f` by direct source comparison.
</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
None — plain `kind` (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster.
</details>


### OS version

<details>
Whatever the `kind` node image ships (containerized, not relevant to this bug).
</details>


### Install tools

<details>
`kind` v0.32.0, Helm v3.7+ (for the example driver chart).
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd (as shipped in the `kind` node image), with `enable_cdi = true` (required by the example DRA
driver to advertise its simulated devices via CDI).
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0 — a
maintained, public example/reference DRA driver used purely to simulate GPU devices with no real hardware
dependency. Not specific to this driver: the bug is entirely in core `kube-controller-manager` code and would
reproduce identically with any DRA driver.
</details>

Not a regression. This has basically never worked in this combination. Do we need to cherry pick anyway?

/cc @yliaog @johnbelamaric

From https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141297#discussion_r3976208124 (PR closed because it didn't get fixed):

> This copy-and-pastes the entire code from above. Let's instead change how the for loop above iterates over claims for the pod:
> 
> - introduce a iterator in the "resourceclaim" package which provides claimName, mustCheckOwner
> - use that instead of iterating over pod.Spec.ResourceClaims and calling resourceclaim.Name
@yliaog: can you fix this or do we need a different owner?

@troychiu would you be open to taking this one?

I also think it should be cherry picked at least to 1.37

One more caller with the same gap, in case it matters for the iterator's shape. `podResourceClaimIndexFunc` in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go` also walks only `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. That index is what `preQueueingHint` reads to find which pods use a claim when a ResourceClaim event arrives, so a pod holding an extended-resource claim is not in the result and misses the targeted requeue. Much smaller than the eviction case, since such a pod still gets retried on other events, but it is the same omission.

I went looking for the same shape elsewhere. The resourceclaim controller and the node authorizer both handle the extended claim next to their `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims` loop, and the kubelet DRA manager folds it into the same list by synthesizing a `PodResourceClaim` for it, which is fairly close to the iterator you described. That index function was the one that stood out.

One thing about the backport: adding an exported helper to the resourceclaim staging package is awkward in a patch release, so the iterator and whatever goes to 1.37 may need to be different shapes.

@yogeshbendre offered at the end of the report to attempt the PR once the approach was settled, in case that got lost in the thread.
@johnbelamaric let me take a look!
/assign

thanks @troychiu 

+1 to cherrypick to 1.37

> One thing about the backport: adding an exported helper to the resourceclaim staging package is awkward in a patch release, so the iterator and whatever goes to 1.37 may need to be different shapes.

I wouldn't worry about modifying the staging package because adding the iterator is not going to break any consumers of the 1.37 packages.

> That index is what preQueueingHint reads to find which pods use a claim when a ResourceClaim event arrives, so a pod holding an extended-resource claim is not in the result and misses the targeted requeue. Much smaller than the eviction case, since such a pod still gets retried on other events, but it is the same omission.

This should be okay: the missed ResourceClaim is one which gets generated by the scheduler, so there should never be a situation where the scheduler waits for its creation. Worth adding a comment in the source code.

title: compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test always fails since the 1.37 cut: validator ignores MinCompatibilityVersion
body:
**What happened**:

The periodic job [`ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test`](https://prow.k8s.io/?job=ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test) has failed on every run since 2026-08-06 12:48 UTC. The failure rate is 100 percent.

The validator reports one failure:

```
Validating features for emulated_version=1.37, current_version=1.38...
FAIL: feature 'DRAFractionalCapacityRange' expected value 1, got 0
```

The trigger is the release-1.37 branch cut, not a code change. The `v1.37.0-rc.0` tag moved master from `v1.37.0-beta.0` to `v1.38.0-alpha.0`. That shifted the version pair the job validates:

| | Build | Time (UTC) | k/k SHA | Validated pair |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Last green | [2085330939616956416](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416) | 2026-08-06 11:45 | `4f5591ab57b` | emulated 1.36, current 1.37 |
| First red | [2085346290606018560](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560) | 2026-08-06 12:48 | `b882c60b402` | emulated 1.37, current 1.38 |

The commit window holds one commit, `b882c60b402 CHANGELOG: Update directory for v1.37.0-rc.0 release`. It changes only CHANGELOG files, so it is not the cause.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is absent from the `release-1.36` reference list. The job therefore never checked the gate before the cut.

**Root cause**

The kubelet and the control plane report the correct value. The validator expects the wrong one.

`pkg/features/kube_features.go` declares two specs at the same version:

```go
DRAFractionalCapacityRange: {
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta, MinCompatibilityVersion: version.MustParse("1.37")},
},
```

`SetEmulationVersion` sets the minimum compatibility version to `emulated - 1`. See `staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go`. The job passes only `--emulated-version=1.37`, so the minimum compatibility version is 1.36. The second spec needs 1.37 or higher. The runtime therefore selects the first spec and reports `0`. This matches the documented behavior of `MinCompatibilityVersion` and the plan in kubernetes/kubernetes#140594, which schedules the on-by-default promotion for 1.38.

Two problems in the tooling make the validator disagree:

1. The generator `test/compatibility_lifecycle/cmd/feature_gates.go` in kubernetes/kubernetes does not write `minCompatibilityVersion` into `versioned_feature_list.yaml`. In that file the two specs differ only in `default`, so no consumer can tell them apart.

   ```yaml
   - name: DRAFractionalCapacityRange
     versionedSpecs:
     - default: false
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
     - default: true
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
   ```

2. `get_target_spec` in `experiment/compatibility-versions/versioned_specs_util.sh` takes `last` of the matching specs. It selects the `default: true` spec and expects `1`.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is the only feature in kubernetes/kubernetes that uses `MinCompatibilityVersion`. That is why the problem appears now.

**What you expected to happen**:

The job passes. The validator selects the spec that applies at the minimum compatibility version the job actually runs with.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

```bash
SPECS='[{"default":false,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"},
        {"default":true,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}]'

# current get_target_spec behavior
echo "$SPECS" | jq -r --arg ver 1.37 \
  '[ .[] | select((.version|tonumber) <= ($ver|tonumber)) ] | last | .default'
# => true   (validator expects 1)

# what the control plane reports at --emulated-version=1.37
# kubernetes_feature_enabled{name="DRAFractionalCapacityRange",stage="BETA"} 0
```

**Please provide links to example occurrences, if any**:

- First red build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560
- Last green build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416
- TestGrid tab: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-api-machinery-emulated-version#compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test

Of the 229 builds still in GCS, 150 passed and 79 failed. Every pass is before the boundary. Every failure is after it. No build interleaves, so this is not a flake.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Control that isolates the cause.** The job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test-n-2` runs the same validator against the same master build, but it validates emulated 1.36 against current 1.38. It stays green. The break is specific to the 1.37 spec pair.

**Suggested fix, in two parts.**

Part 1 clears CI. Change `get_target_spec` to take the first spec at the highest matching version instead of the last. That selects the spec that applies at the default minimum compatibility version.

```jq
[ .[] | select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) <= ($ver|sub("^v";"")|tonumber)) ] as $c
| ($c | map(.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) | max) as $m
| ($c | map(select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) == $m)) | first)
```

I checked this against normal features at 1.31, 1.33 and 1.35. The result does not change. The result changes only when two specs share a version.

This part is necessary, not only convenient. The `release-1.37` reference list is frozen. It will never carry `minCompatibilityVersion`. The validator must therefore fall back to first-wins for the 1.37 pair whatever else changes.

Part 2 prevents the next occurrence. Write `minCompatibilityVersion` from the kubernetes/kubernetes generator, then compare against it in the validator for 1.38 and later.

**Related.** This validator has missed a feature gate lifecycle pattern twice before. See kubernetes/test-infra#34396 and kubernetes/test-infra#35179. Expect the problem to return at the 1.38 cut if the gate is promoted per kubernetes/kubernetes#140594 without matching validator work.

Owner is SIG API Machinery. The alert address on the job is `compatibility-version-test@google.com`. Feature owners are @sunya-ch and @pohly.

title: CPU manager exclusive allocation metrics drifts
body:
### What happened?

The static policy in CPU Manager maintains the `CPUManagerExclusiveCPUsAllocationCount` and `CPUManagerSharedPoolSizeMilliCores` gauges by applying per-event deltas, and updates `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` only for the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation. This drifts away from the actual allocation state in several scenarios:

1. Init container CPU reuse is double counted (container scope). When an app container reuses the CPUs of a non-restartable init container, `allocateCPUs` returns the full allocation including the reused CPUs, which stay assigned to the init container too. The allocation path adds the full size of both allocations, counting the reused CPUs twice. The release path correctly subtracts the sibling-adjusted sets, so after the pod is removed the gauge keeps a permanent positive residue equal to the number of reused CPUs. The shared pool gauge has the mirrored problem: the allocation delta subtracts CPUs which have never been taken out of the default CPU set.

2. Fresh allocations and restarts disagree. During a kubelet run the exclusive allocation gauge accumulates deltas with the duplicates described above, while after a restart `initializeMetrics` recomputes it as the union of the checkpointed assignments (no duplicates). The same node state can therefore report two different values before and after a kubelet restart.

3. Pod-level (pod scope) allocations can leak on partial failure. `allocatePodForAdd` updates the metrics and stores the pod-level CPU set, but a failure while partitioning the bubble among the containers (takeByTopology) returns an error without releasing anything: the bubble stays out of the default CPU set, the gauge stays inflated, and nothing can ever clean it up, because `RemoveContainer` returns early for a pod with no container assignments and `removeStaleState` only iterates over container assignments.

4. Pod-level releases can drift the gauge below the real value. `RemoveContainer` subtracts the whole pod-level CPU set when the last container assignment is removed, but after a kubelet restart `initializeMetrics` only accounts the union of the remaining container assignments, which is smaller than the bubble if some containers have already been removed before the restart. Releasing a pod which died while the kubelet was down then over-subtracts the difference.

5. `initializeMetrics` ignores the pod-level CPU sets. After a restart the gauge is seeded only from the container assignments, so the part of a pod-level bubble not covered by any container assignment is not counted, even though it is excluded from the default CPU set.

6. `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` never drops back to zero. The update loop only writes the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation, so once the last exclusively allocated CPU of a node is released, the node keeps reporting its last non-zero value forever. The metric is also fed only with the container assignments, making a pod-level bubble invisible at allocation time, because the container assignments are stored later than the pod-level CPU set.

### What did you expect to happen?

Metrics always present valid current state of exclusive CPUs allocations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The scenarios are described in issue.
They are also fully covered by unit tests.
Running unit tests without changes to the code will reveal the problems.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: LimitRange maximum can be exceeded by declaring hugepages at the pod level
body:
### What happened?

A `LimitRange` of type `Pod` with a `max` for `hugepages-*` does not constrain a Pod that
declares its hugepages through pod-level resources (`spec.resources`). Such a Pod is admitted
even when its effective hugepages consumption exceeds the configured maximum.

The LimitRanger admission plugin keeps a private copy of the "is this a pod-level resource?"
predicate that lists only cpu and memory:

```go
// plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger/admission.go
var supportedPodLevelResources = sets.New(api.ResourceCPU, api.ResourceMemory)

func isSupportedPodLevelResource(name api.ResourceName) bool {
	return supportedPodLevelResources.Has(name)
}
```

The canonical predicate in component-helpers also matches the `hugepages-` prefix. Because of the
drift, `podRequests`/`podLimits` skip the pod-level override for hugepages and evaluate the
aggregated **container** values instead.

API validation explicitly permits the pod-level value to exceed the container aggregate (it only
rejects the reverse: "pod level limit for %s is insufficient to cover the aggregated container
and node-allocatable DRA limits"), so the two numbers can legitimately differ.

### What did you expect to happen?

The Pod-scoped `LimitRange` maximum should be enforced against the effective pod-level hugepages
value, the same way it is enforced when the value is written at container level.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Requires the `PodLevelResources` feature gate (Beta, on by default since 1.34).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: hugepages-max
  namespace: demo
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Pod
      max:
        hugepages-2Mi: 4Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: over-the-limit
  namespace: demo
spec:
  resources:                 # pod-level: 8Gi, twice the LimitRange max
    requests:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
    limits:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
      resources:             # container aggregate stays within the max
        requests:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
        limits:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
```

Observed: the Pod is admitted.
Expected: rejected, as with `maximum hugepages-2Mi usage per Pod is 4Gi, but limit is 8Gi` -
which is exactly what happens if the same `8Gi` is written on the container instead.

Equivalent unit-level reproduction in `plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger`:

```go
err := PodValidateLimitFunc(&limitRange, &pod)  // returns nil; expected an error
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The duplicated helper carries a `TODO(ndixita): Find alternatives to avoid duplicating the code`
and a comment saying it exists "to avoid conversion of v1.Pod to api.Pod". That rationale does not
apply to this function - it takes only a resource name - so it can simply delegate to
`resourcehelper.IsSupportedPodLevelResource`.

The neighbouring duplicated helpers (`podRequests`, `podLimits`, `addResourceList`,
`maxResourceList`) carry the same TODO and are worth auditing for similar drift.

Found by source inspection plus a unit test at commit `b882c60b402` (v1.37.0-rc.0).

```console
# Not applicable - reproduced from source at v1.37.0-rc.0 (commit b882c60b402).
# Affects any release where PodLevelResources is enabled (Beta / default-on since 1.34).
```

</details>

Thanks for the report and for the clear analysis of where the drift came from. I verified this end to end; summary below in case it is useful for others landing here.

**Setup**
- kind cluster with the released `kindest/node:v1.37.0` image (PodLevelResources Beta, enabled by default)
- `kube-apiserver` rebuilt from #141248, and once more from the same tree with only `plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger/admission.go` reverted, so the only variable is that file
- LimitRange of type `Pod` with `max: hugepages-2Mi: 4Gi`

**Results**

| Pod | v1.37.0 release | #141248 with fix reverted | #141248 |
|---|---|---|---|
| pod-level `8Gi`, containers `2Gi` | admitted | admitted | rejected: `maximum hugepages-2Mi usage per Pod is 4Gi, but limit is 8Gi` |
| container-level `8Gi` (control) | rejected | rejected | rejected |
| pod-level `4Gi` (control) | admitted | admitted | admitted |

With hugepages actually allocated on the node, the admitted over-limit pod goes Running, its pod cgroup `hugetlb.2MB.max` is set to the pod-level value, and it takes the node's full `hugepages-2Mi` allocation. A second pod that stays within the LimitRange cap then fails scheduling with `Insufficient hugepages-2Mi`. So the impact is real, not just a bookkeeping difference.

**One correction to the reproducer**

The YAML in the description does not reach LimitRanger. Both the pod-level and container-level resource blocks declare hugepages without `cpu` or `memory`, and API validation rejects that first:

```
spec.containers[0].resources: Forbidden: HugePages require cpu or memory
spec.resources: Forbidden: HugePages require cpu or memory
```

Adding `cpu` (or `memory`) to both blocks makes it reproduce exactly as described. Could you update the description so the next person does not hit the validation error and conclude the issue does not reproduce? The unit test pod in #141248 has the same shape, so it would be good to add `cpu` there too so it mirrors a pod that can actually exist.

title: DRA converting watch does not stop on Stop(): `break` inside `select` never leaves the loop
body:
### What happened?

In `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/client/generic.go`, `watchSomething.run` uses a
naked `break` in the `<-w.stopChan` case of a `select`:

```go
for {
	e, ok := <-resultChan
	if !ok {
		break
	}
	... convert e ...
	// This must not get blocked when the consumer stops reading,
	// hence the stopChan.
	select {
	case w.resultChan <- e:
	case <-w.stopChan:
		break        // exits the select, NOT the for loop
	}
}
```

In Go a naked `break` inside a `select` terminates the `select`, not the enclosing `for`. The
surrounding comment makes the intent clear, but after `Stop()` the goroutine loops back, keeps
pulling from the upstream watch, converts each event via `scheme.Convert` and discards it, and
never reaches the deferred `close(w.resultChan)`.

`watch.Interface` consumers expect `ResultChan()` to be closed after `Stop()`; here that only
happens if the upstream happens to close its own channel.

### What did you expect to happen?

`run` should return when `stopChan` is closed, running both deferred calls
(`utilruntime.HandleCrash` and `close(w.resultChan)`), and should stop consuming upstream events.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Needs an upstream whose channel stays open after `Stop()`. Add to the `client` package:

```go
type stalledWatch struct{ ch chan watch.Event }

func (s *stalledWatch) Stop()                          {}
func (s *stalledWatch) ResultChan() <-chan watch.Event { return s.ch }

func TestRepro(t *testing.T) {
	up := &stalledWatch{ch: make(chan watch.Event, 8)}
	for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
		up.ch <- watch.Event{Type: watch.Added, Object: &resourcev1.ResourceSlice{}}
	}
	w := &watchSomething[*resourcev1.ResourceSlice, resourcev1.ResourceSlice, *resourcev1beta1.ResourceSlice]{
		upstream: up, resultChan: make(chan watch.Event), stopChan: make(chan struct{}),
	}
	done := make(chan struct{})
	go func() { defer close(done); w.run() }()

	time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
	w.Stop()

	select {
	case <-done:
	case <-time.After(5 * time.Second):
		t.Fatal("run did not return after Stop")   // this fires
	}
}
```

Observed: `run` never returns; the wrapper also drains the queued upstream events
(`upstream queue before Stop()=4, after Stop()=0`).
Expected: `run` returns promptly and the queued events are left untouched.

### Anything else we need to know?

**This is usually masked in production.** `Stop()` calls `w.upstream.Stop()` first, and a
well-behaved `watch.Interface` closes its result channel in response, which ends the loop via the
`!ok` branch instead. I was not able to demonstrate a hang with a real client-go watch. It shows
up when the upstream is slow to close or does not close, and the wrapper should not depend on
upstream behaviour for its own termination in any case.

Grading this as a latent defect rather than an active outage. A repo-wide scan for `break` inside
a `select` inside a `for` found this as the only occurrence in `pkg/`, `cmd/`, `plugin/` and
`staging/`.

Found at commit `b882c60b402` (v1.37.0-rc.0).

```console
# Not applicable - reproduced from source at v1.37.0-rc.0 (commit b882c60b402)
# with the unit test above.
```

</details>

title: CPU Manager incorrectly spans sockets with distribute-cpus-across-cores and align-by-socket enabled
body:
### What happened?

When using CPU Manager with `static` policy and both of the following options enabled:
- `distribute-cpus-across-cores=true` (distributes CPUs evenly across NUMA nodes)
- `align-by-socket=true` (prefers NUMA nodes within the same socket)

CPUs may be allocated across multiple sockets instead of staying within a single socket. This violates the socket affinity guarantee that `align-by-socket=true` is supposed to provide.

For example:
- Socket 0: NUMA 0-3 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 0: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 1: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 2: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 3: (30 CPUs available)

- Socket 1: NUMA 4-7 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 4: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 5: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 6: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 7: (30 CPUs available)

Result: CPUs are allocated from NUMA 0,1,3,6 across both sockets.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `align-by-socket=true`, the 120 CPUs should be allocated entirely from Socket 0 (NUMA 0,1,2,3) (which has 126 available CPUs).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure kubelet with:
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--cpu-manager-policy-options="distribute-cpus-across-cores=true,align-by-socket=true"

Set the available CPUs as above example, and create a pod with 120 CPUs.
