title: Kubernetes ships etcd 3.6.6-0 with 61 CVEs (2 Critical) across all supported versions — upstream 3.7.1 available
body:
/sig cluster-lifecycle
/sig etcd
/kind bug
/priority critical-urgent

## Summary

All currently supported Kubernetes versions (v1.34.x, v1.35.x, v1.36.x)
ship `registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0`, which contains **61 known
vulnerabilities** in the etcd binary alone including **2 Critical**.
The upstream etcd project has released v3.7.1.

etcd 3.6.6-0 has the **oldest dependencies of any Kubernetes control
plane component**, compiled with Go 1.24.10 and gRPC 1.71.1.

## Confirmed Across All Supported K8s Versions
```
$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.1
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.35.7
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

$ kubeadm config images list --kubernetes-version v1.36.3
registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0
```

## Scan Results
```
$ trivy image registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

etcd binary: 61 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 32, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3)
etcdctl: 42 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 20, MEDIUM: 17, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 2)
etcdutl: 59 CVEs (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 30, MEDIUM: 23, LOW: 1, UNKNOWN: 3)
```

## CRITICAL Vulnerabilities

| CVE | Library | Installed | Fixed | Title |
|-----|---------|-----------|-------|-------|
| CVE-2026-33186 | google.golang.org/grpc | **v1.71.1** | 1.79.3 | **gRPC-Go: Authorization bypass due to improper HTTP/2 path validation** |
| CVE-2025-68121 | Go stdlib | **v1.24.10** | 1.24.13 | **Incorrect certificate validation during TLS session resumption** |

**Both are directly exploitable in etcd:**
- etcd IS a gRPC server — gRPC is its primary communication protocol
- etcd uses mTLS for peer-to-peer and client communication

## etcd-Specific CVEs 

etcd 3.6.6 has additional CVEs due to its older Go stdlib (1.24.10):

| CVE | Severity | Title |
|-----|----------|-------|
| CVE-2025-61726 | HIGH | Memory exhaustion in net/url query parameter parsing |
| CVE-2025-61729 | HIGH | DoS via excessive resource consumption in crypto/x509 |
| CVE-2025-61727 | MEDIUM | x509 subdomain constraint doesn't restrict wildcard SANs |
| CVE-2025-61728 | MEDIUM | Excessive CPU in archive/zip |
| CVE-2025-61730 | MEDIUM | TLS handshake messages at incorrect encryption level |
| CVE-2025-47913 | HIGH | SSH client panic (x/crypto 0.36.0 specific) |
| CVE-2025-47914 | MEDIUM | SSH Agent DoS via malformed messages |
| CVE-2025-58181 | MEDIUM | DoS via unbounded GSSAPI memory consumption |
| CVE-2025-47911 | MEDIUM | Quadratic HTML parsing complexity |
| CVE-2025-58190 | MEDIUM | Infinite HTML parsing loop |

## Impact

etcd stores **all Kubernetes cluster state** including secrets,
configmaps, RBAC policies, and service accounts. A compromise of
etcd means complete cluster compromise. The CRITICAL gRPC
authorization bypass (CVE-2026-33186) and TLS certificate
validation failure (CVE-2025-68121) in the component that guards
all cluster data is an urgent concern.

title: Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles CoreDNS v1.13.1 — 3 minor versions behind upstream v1.14.6, exposing clusters to 49+ known CVEs
body:
## Summary

Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles `registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1` as the
default DNS provider. The upstream CoreDNS project has since released v1.14.6,
which addresses the vast majority of known vulnerabilities present in v1.13.1.

Since Kubernetes controls which CoreDNS version ships with each release, and
cluster administrators rely on the officially bundled version, we are requesting
that the CoreDNS version be bumped in an upcoming Kubernetes patch release.

/sig network
/area dns
/kind bug
/priority important-soon

## Environment

- **Kubernetes Version:** v1.35.1
- **Bundled CoreDNS:** registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1
- **Latest Upstream CoreDNS:** v1.14.6
- **OS:** Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.0 (Coughlan)
- **Scanners:** Dependency-Track, Trivy

## Why This Matters

Cluster administrators installing Kubernetes v1.35.1 via kubeadm or other
official tooling receive CoreDNS v1.13.1 by default. Most organizations
rely on the officially bundled versions and do not independently upgrade
individual control plane components.

While it is technically possible to manually upgrade CoreDNS to v1.14.6,
this is:
- Not documented as a supported configuration for v1.35.1
- A burden on every individual cluster administrator rather than a fix at source

## Vulnerability Comparison: v1.13.1 vs v1.14.6

We scanned both versions to quantify the security impact.

### Dependency CVEs

| Dependency | v1.13.1 Version | v1.14.6 Version | CVEs in v1.13.1 | CVEs in v1.14.6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| golang.org/x/crypto | 0.42.0 | 0.53.0 | 32 (7 Critical) | 1 (Unknown) |
| golang.org/x/net | 0.45.0 | (newer) | 8 | 0 |
| google.golang.org/grpc | 1.75.1 | 1.82.0 | 2 (1 Critical) | 1 (High) |
| github.com/quic-go/quic-go | 0.55.0 | (newer) | 4 | 0 |
| github.com/expr-lang/expr | 1.17.6 | (newer) | 2 | 0 |
| golang.org/x/sys | 0.36.0 | (newer) | 1 | 0 |
| **Total** | | | **49** | **2** |

### CoreDNS-Specific CVEs Fixed Between v1.13.1 and v1.14.6

| CVE | Severity | Fixed In | Description |
|-----|----------|----------|-------------|
| CVE-2026-26017 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DNS access control bypass due to plugin execution order |
| CVE-2026-26018 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DoS via predictable PRNG |
| CVE-2026-32934 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS due to unbounded resource growth |
| CVE-2026-32936 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS via oversized DNS-over-HTTPS GET requests |
| CVE-2026-33190 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Auth bypass via flawed TSIG plugin verification |
| CVE-2026-33489 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Info disclosure via incorrect ACL stanza selection |
| CVE-2026-35579 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | Auth bypass for TSIG-protected functionalities |
| CVE-2025-68151 | MEDIUM | 1.14.0 | DoS via unbounded connections |
| CVE-2025-47950 | HIGH | 1.12.2 | DoQ Memory Exhaustion |
| CVE-2023-28452 | HIGH | 1.11.0 | TuDoor Attacks |
| CVE-2024-0874 | MEDIUM | 1.11.2 | CD bit response caching issue |

## Impact Summary

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total CVEs eliminated by bumping to v1.14.6 | ~47 dependency + 11 CoreDNS-specific |
| Critical CVEs eliminated | 8 |
| High CVEs eliminated | ~14 |
| Authentication bypass CVEs eliminated | 3 (CVE-2026-33190, CVE-2026-35579, CVE-2026-26017) |

## Remaining Vulnerabilities in v1.14.6

reporting these separately to the CoreDNS PST (security@coredns.io):

## Request

2. Is there a defined process or cadence for CoreDNS version updates

title: DRA: a negative device consumesCounters value is accepted and over-commits a shared counter set
body:
### What happened?

A device's `consumesCounters` value may be negative. ResourceSlice validation accepts it, and the
structured allocator subtracts it from the counter set, so a negative consumption inflates the set's
available capacity and admits an allocation that over-commits the set.

`validateDeviceCounter` (`pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`) returns nil for any parsed
quantity, with no sign check:

```go
func validateDeviceCounter(counter resource.Counter, fldPath *field.Path) field.ErrorList {
	// Any parsed quantity is valid.
	return nil
}
```

The allocator subtracts each allocated device's consumption from the set (`existingCounter.Value.Sub(c.Value)`
in `checkAvailableCounters`); a negative `c.Value` raises the available value instead of lowering it, so a
device consuming a large positive amount then fits against the inflated available.

The sibling consumable-capacity path already guards exactly this class. `CmpRequestOverCapacity`
(`.../structured/internal/experimental/consumable_capacity.go`) rejects a negative resolved capacity with
`errNegativeCapacity` (`if consumedCapacity.Sign() < 0`), and its comment notes a negative "can reach the
allocator from a stored ResourceSlice ... which admission does not re-check." The counter path has no such
guard — that asymmetry is the bug.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either ResourceSlice validation should reject a negative counter value (mirroring the capacity path's
stance that a negative is invalid input), or the allocator should fail closed on a negative consumption
rather than subtracting it into a larger available.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Publish a CounterSet of 8Gi, a phantom device consuming `-100Gi`, and a real device consuming `100Gi`:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-counters}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  sharedCounters:
  - name: mem
    counters: {memory: {value: 8Gi}}
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata: {name: nc-devices}
spec:
  driver: nc.example
  pool: {name: nc-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 2}
  allNodes: true
  devices:
  - name: phantom
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: -100Gi}}}]   # negative, accepted
  - name: real
    consumesCounters: [{counterSet: mem, counters: {memory: {value: 100Gi}}}]
```

The slice is accepted (`resourceslice ... created`; the `-100Gi` is stored). A ResourceClaim requesting
`count: 2` from `nc-pool` allocates **both** devices (Pod `Scheduled`), because the aggregate consumption is
`-100Gi + 100Gi = 0 ≤ 8Gi` — even though the `real` device alone consumes `100Gi` from an `8Gi` set. Without
the phantom device, a `count: 1` claim for the `100Gi` device is refused (`100Gi > 8Gi`). Observed on a real
v1.36.2 cluster.

### Anything else we need to know?

The straightforward fix is a sign check on counter values in `validateDeviceCounter` (fail closed on a
negative), matching `errNegativeCapacity` in the consumable-capacity path; an allocator-side guard on a
negative consumption is a defensive complement. Threat model: a negative reaches the allocator from a DRA
driver's ResourceSlice, or from a slice stored before stricter validation — the same model the capacity
path's guard already accepts.

`DRAPartitionableDevices` (shared counters) is Beta and enabled by default since v1.36.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management
author: thc1006

comments.body:
Cross-referencing the related capacity-side work: #140468 and #140563 add non-negative validation for `ConsumedCapacity` on the consumable-capacity path. This issue is the `consumesCounters` analogue on the partitionable-devices path, which `validateDeviceCounter` leaves unchecked.

One difference worth noting: the capacity path already has an allocator-side guard (`errNegativeCapacity`, rejecting a negative `Sign()`), while the counter path has neither validation nor that guard, so it over-commits instead of failing closed. If it is cleaner to fold the counter case into #140563's scope, I am happy to do that instead.

title: DRA: allocator should fail closed (per-node) on a malformed ResourceSlice nodeSelector term count
body:
### What happened?

Follow-up to #141212 and #141213. The validation fix in #141213 stops a new or modified ResourceSlice from carrying a per-device `nodeSelector` whose term count is not exactly one. It ratchets the new constraint, so a slice with a multi-term selector that was stored before the fix, or accepted by an older API server during a version-skewed rolling upgrade, is still admitted on an unchanged update.

Those already-stored multi-term slices can still reach the structured allocator. `createNodeSelector` handles the term count like this:

- `len == 0`: no-op. This is not reachable through a normal allocation. `ValidateNodeSelector` already rejects a zero-term selector ("must have at least one node selector term"), and even a stored one matches no node, because `nodeaffinity`'s `Match` returns false when there are no terms, so `isSelectable` filters the device through `NodeMatches` before `createNodeSelector` runs. Rejecting zero terms here would be defense in depth, not a fix for a demonstrated available-everywhere allocation.
- `len == 1`: merged.
- `len > 1`: returns `fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", ...)`.

The `> 1` error is not wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter plugin treats it as a framework error rather than an `Unschedulable` result for that node. A framework error from Filter cancels the remaining node search and aborts the scheduling cycle, and it recurs on retry while the malformed slice stays in place. #141212 has a v1.36.2 reproducer.

There is also an ordering edge. `createNodeSelector` returns as soon as it sees a result with a `nodeName`, so a multi-term selector on a device that appears after a `nodeName` device is never inspected, while the same selector before it returns the hard error. Whether a malformed slice aborts the cycle therefore depends on result order.

### What did you expect to happen?

Admission-time validation cannot retroactively fix a slice that was already stored, and version skew lets an older API server accept one during an upgrade, so the allocator should degrade gracefully instead of aborting the scheduling cycle for the whole Pod.

Proposed change, in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants (or their shared source):

- Treat a term count greater than one as a classified per-node failure: return an error wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so Filter reports `Unschedulable` for that node and keeps searching the rest.
- Check the term count for every selected result before the `nodeName` early return, so result order does not decide whether a malformed slice is caught.
- Optionally reject zero terms in the same place as defense in depth, even though the normal path filters it earlier.

Tests would assert that a more-than-one-term selector returns an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` with the malformed selector both before and after a `nodeName` device, and that a single term keeps its current behavior.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is intentionally kept out of #141213 to keep that admission fix small and reviewable during the v1.37 freeze. Linking here so the allocator gap is not lost when #141212 is closed by #141213.

/kind bug
/sig node
author: thc1006

title: CPU Manager strict reservation can leave an empty default CPUSet
body:
### What happened?

With the static CPU Manager policy and `strict-cpu-reservation`, exclusive allocations can consume every non-reserved CPU and leave `defaultCPUSet` empty.

KEP-4540 discusses shared workloads starving when the shared pool reaches zero. The current implementation has different side effects:

- reconcile skips shared containers when their resolved CPUSet is empty, so an existing container can keep its previous affinity and overlap newly exclusive CPUs;
- a new shared container gets no `CpusetCpus` value because `PreCreateContainer` treats the empty set as unset;
- after a kubelet restart, CPU Manager rejects a checkpoint that has assignments and an empty default CPUSet with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

The allocator removes assigned CPUs from the default set without checking whether the result is empty:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L727-L729

The empty-set handling is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go#L511-L519
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/internal_container_lifecycle_linux.go#L31-L36
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L215-L223

### What did you expect to happen?

An empty shared pool should have defined behavior that does not silently drop CPU affinity, overlap exclusive CPUs, or prevent kubelet from restarting.

The fix might reject the final exclusive allocation, reject configurations that can produce an empty shared pool, or use another policy. This issue does not assume which behavior is preferred.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a four-CPU Linux node, configure the static policy with CPU 0 reserved:

```yaml
cpuManagerPolicy: static
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  strict-cpu-reservation: "true"
reservedSystemCPUs: "0"
systemReserved:
  cpu: "1"
```

1. Remove the old CPU Manager state and start kubelet. The initial default CPUSet is `1-3`.
2. Start a BestEffort Pod so it uses the shared pool.
3. Start a Guaranteed Pod whose CPU and memory requests equal its limits and whose CPU request is `3`.
4. Check `/var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state`. The Guaranteed Pod owns CPUs `1-3` and `defaultCpuSet` is empty.
5. Wait for reconciliation. The BestEffort container cannot be updated to an empty CPUSet and may keep its previous `1-3` affinity.
6. Restart kubelet. CPU Manager state validation fails with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

A BestEffort Pod created after step 4 also receives no explicit `CpusetCpus` from CPU Manager.

### Anything else we need to know?

KEP-4540 intentionally archived minimum-shared-CPU proposals and added a shared-pool-size metric:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4540-strict-cpu-reservation

The KEP describes starvation as the zero-pool outcome. It does not describe dropping cpuset enforcement or rejecting the checkpoint after restart.

Related work:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127483
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127506
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134388

`master` at `ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674`

```
Ran 91 of 3206 Specs in 6347.496 seconds
SUCCESS! -- 91 Passed | 0 Failed | 0 Pending | 3115 Skipped
2026/08/05 05:01:35 process.go:199: Interrupt after 2h0m0s timeout during ./hack/e2e-internal/e2e-down.sh
2026/08/05 05:03:07 main.go:326: Something went wrong: ... error during ./hack/e2e-internal/e2e-down.sh (interrupted): signal: interrupt
```

The suite finished green, then the 120m wall hit *during `e2e-down.sh`*. The one "1 Failed" in build 2084688953629216768 is not a real assertion — it's `[INTERRUPTED] [sig-node] Pod InPlace Resize ... [Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]`, i.e. the timeout killing the run mid-spec. So `kubetest.Test → Timeout → TearDown → DumpClusterLogs → listResources` are all downstream symptoms of one root cause.

### Why the margin is this tight (the structural "onset")

There is no code-regression onset — reds are interspersed with greens across the whole retained history (e.g. reds on 08-02, 08-03, 08-04, 08-05 among mostly-green runs). What *did* change is the budget. Per `test-infra` `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-cloud-provider/gcp/gcp-gce.yaml`, the timeout was tightened on **2026-05-11** in commit [`eae4fa683d`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/commit/eae4fa683d) ("fix remaining release-blocking job timeouts"):

```
-    timeout: 3h20m0s        +    timeout: 2h20m0s     (Prow deadline)
-      - --timeout=180m      +      - --timeout=120m   (kubetest budget)
```

The old 180m budget absorbed a 113-min test phase easily; the new 120m budget leaves only ~7–14 min for up **and** down when the test phase runs long. Given the observed ~30-min run-to-run variance, any slow run now tips over.

### What eats the variable ~30 min

This is the `AllAlpha=true,AllBeta=true` + `--runtime-config=api/all=true` job (91 specs, focus `AdmissionWebhookMatchConditions|InPlacePodVerticalScaling|StorageVersionAPI|PodPreset|StatefulSetAutoDeletePVC|Networking`). The `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` resize specs are the slow/variable set (the interrupted spec was one of them), and slow Boskos project bring-up/`kube-up` on the front end (as the issue body notes) further compresses the remaining budget. Both push against the same 120m ceiling.

### Recommendation

This is **infra/config, not code** — nothing to bisect in kubernetes/kubernetes. Options, in order of preference:

1. **Raise `--timeout` back toward ~150m** (and the Prow `timeout:` accordingly) in `gcp-gce.yaml` to restore headroom, since a full green run already needs ~113 min of test time alone.
2. Or trim runtime — e.g. reduce the `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` focus footprint or parallelism — to bring the p95 test phase comfortably under budget.
3. Owner is **sig-cloud-provider** (job config) with **sig-k8s-infra** / release-signal; the fix PR lands in `kubernetes/test-infra`, not this repo.

Suggested label: keep `kind/flake` but treat as a **job-timeout tuning** item, not a failing-test regression. No revert or code fix is warranted.

*(New vs. the issue body: confirms the suite passes on the red runs with concrete per-build durations, identifies the exact `--timeout` 180m→120m tightening commit `eae4fa683d` from 2026-05-11 as the reason the margin disappeared, and shows the "1 Failed" is an `[INTERRUPTED]`, not a real assertion — pointing the fix at the kubetest/Prow timeout rather than Boskos alone.)*

title: Liveness probe failure container restart leads to container starting up with started=true and liveness probes starting before startup probes have run
body:
### What happened?

The full details of the repro can be seen in the Bash script below, but roughly:

1. Start a container with startup and liveness probe.
2. Wait for both to succeed. All normal so far.
3. Flip liveness probe to fail.
4. Container restarts.
5. New container sees liveness probe before startup probe.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the new container to first need to pass its startup probes before liveness probes begin, as per the docs here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/#startup-probe.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproduction bash script:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

CLUSTER="probe-repro-$$"
K3S_IMAGE="rancher/k3s:v1.36.2-k3s1"
KIND_IMAGE="kindest/node:v1.36.1@sha256:3489c7674813ba5d8b1a9977baea8a6e553784dab7b84759d1014dbd78f7ebd5"
MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION="v1.36.2"
POD="probe-repro"
ENVIRONMENT="k3s"
KIND_KUBECONFIG=""

usage() {
  echo "usage: $0 [--k3s | --minikube | --kind]" >&2
}

if (($# > 1)); then
  usage
  exit 2
fi

case "${1:---k3s}" in
  --k3s) ENVIRONMENT="k3s" ;;
  --minikube) ENVIRONMENT="minikube" ;;
  --kind) ENVIRONMENT="kind" ;;
  --help)
    usage
    exit
    ;;
  *)
    usage
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

if [[ "$ENVIRONMENT" == "kind" ]]; then
  KIND_KUBECONFIG=$(mktemp)
fi

cleanup() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker rm --force "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    minikube) minikube delete --profile "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    kind) kind delete cluster --name "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
  esac
  if [[ -n "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" ]]; then
    rm -f "$KIND_KUBECONFIG"
  fi
}
trap cleanup EXIT

k() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker exec --interactive "$CLUSTER" /bin/kubectl "$@" ;;
    minikube) minikube --profile "$CLUSTER" kubectl -- --context="$CLUSTER" "$@" ;;
    kind) kubectl --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" "$@" ;;
  esac
}

c() {
  k exec "$POD" -- "$@"
}

echo "Booting $ENVIRONMENT..."

case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
  k3s)
    command -v docker >/dev/null
    docker run --detach --privileged --name "$CLUSTER" "$K3S_IMAGE" \
      server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb >/dev/null
    ;;
  minikube)
    command -v minikube >/dev/null
    minikube start \
      --profile "$CLUSTER" \
      --driver=docker \
      --container-runtime=containerd \
      --kubernetes-version="$MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION" \
      --keep-context
    ;;
  kind)
    command -v kind >/dev/null
    command -v kubectl >/dev/null
    kind create cluster \
      --name "$CLUSTER" \
      --image "$KIND_IMAGE" \
      --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" \
      --wait 120s
    ;;
esac

until k get serviceaccount default >/dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 0.2
done

echo "Applying manifest..."

k apply -f - >/dev/null <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: probe-repro
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 2
  volumes:
    - name: state
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: [sh, -c]
      args:
        - |
          instance=initial
          if test -f /state/container-seen; then
            instance=replacement
          else
            touch /state/container-seen
          fi
          echo "$instance" > /state/instance
          printf '%s  %-11s  container started\n' \
            "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
          on_term() {
            printf '%s  %-11s  received SIGTERM\n' \
              "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
            exit 0
          }
          trap on_term TERM
          sleep 3600 &
          wait $!
      volumeMounts:
        - name: state
          mountPath: /state
      startupProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=failure
              test "$instance" = initial && result=success
              printf '%s  %-11s  startup probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 100
      livenessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=success
              if test "$instance" = initial && test -f /state/fail-liveness; then
                result=failure
              fi
              printf '%s  %-11s  liveness probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 1
EOF

k wait "pod/$POD" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'=true \
  --timeout=120s >/dev/null

FIRST_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')

echo "First container ID: $FIRST_ID"
echo "Waiting 2 seconds to allow some probe successes..."

sleep 2

echo "Failing liveness probe..."
c touch /state/fail-liveness

echo "Waiting for container to restart..."

SECOND_ID="$FIRST_ID"
for _ in {1..600}; do
  SECOND_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')
  [[ -n "$SECOND_ID" && "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]] && break
  sleep 0.1
done

[[ "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]]

echo "Second container ID: $SECOND_ID"

STARTED=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}')
c sh -c \
  'printf "%s  %-11s  Kubernetes status started=%s\n" "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" replacement "$1" >> /state/events' \
  sh "$STARTED"

echo "Waiting 3 seconds for some probes to happen..."

sleep 3

echo "Event log:"

c cat /state/events
```

Save as repro.sh and here are the results of me running it:

```
$ ./repro.sh --k3s
2026-08-04T08:27:19Z  initial      container started
2026-08-04T08:27:19Z  initial      startup probe: success
2026-08-04T08:27:20Z  initial      liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:27:21Z  initial      liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:27:22Z  initial      liveness probe: failure
2026-08-04T08:27:22Z  initial      received SIGTERM
2026-08-04T08:27:22Z  replacement  container started
2026-08-04T08:27:23Z  replacement  Kubernetes status started=true
2026-08-04T08:27:23Z  replacement  liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:27:24Z  replacement  startup probe: failure

```

```

2026-08-04T08:37:37Z  initial      container started
2026-08-04T08:37:38Z  initial      startup probe: success
2026-08-04T08:37:39Z  initial      liveness probe: success

2026-08-04T08:37:41Z  initial      received SIGTERM
2026-08-04T08:37:41Z  replacement  container started
2026-08-04T08:37:41Z  replacement  Kubernetes status started=true
2026-08-04T08:37:42Z  replacement  liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:37:43Z  replacement  startup probe: failure

```

```
$ ./repro.sh --kind
2026-08-04T08:39:36Z  initial      container started
2026-08-04T08:39:37Z  initial      startup probe: success
2026-08-04T08:39:38Z  initial      liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:39:39Z  initial      liveness probe: success
2026-08-04T08:39:40Z  initial      liveness probe: failure
```

comments.body: i would like to work on this. it is legacy issue and triggered due to feature gate "ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart" is set to "deprecated" and disabled by default.
/sig node

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

The bug is definitely important enough, but at this point we had two versions of kubernetes with this regression. Let's fix it as fast as we can and cherry-pick. For 1.37 - if we will have a fix fast we can ask release team, if not it will land in 1.37.1

A few quick questions:

1. Is readiness behaves the same way? Or it is being set to false when container is killed?
2. Should we actually change the Started to false when container is killed?
3. Does this affect the behavior when the same scenario, but there is also a kubelet restart happening at the same time? Is there a possibility of a race condition between the API server status update and the actual `Started` state of a container?

My understanding is as follows:

> * Is readiness behaves the same way? Or it is being set to false when container is killed?

Once the kubelet observes that a container is no longer running, its `Ready` status is reset to `false`. A new container ID also starts with the readiness probe’s initial `Failure` result. `Ready` does not appear to be affected by this particular bug.

> * Should we actually change the Started to false when container is killed?

Similarly, `Started` should be `false` for a terminated container or a new container instance. `Started` belongs to a specific `ContainerID`, which was the behavior before `ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart` was introduced. Our proposed fix is to avoid inheriting `Started` when the container ID changes. This preserves the previous behavior for container restarts.


> 3\. Does this affect the behavior when the same scenario, but there is also a kubelet restart happening at the same time? Is there a possibility of a race condition between the API server status update and the actual `Started` state of a container?

Yes, there is a race when the container and the kubelet restart around the same time. The API status may still contain `Started=true` for the old container ID while the container runtime reports a new ID. Our proposed fix preserves `Started` only when the old and current `ContainerID` values match. This addresses the race while retaining the intended behavior for a kubelet restart. We will also add an e2e test case to verify this scenario.

Clarification to my questions:

1. If Ready being set to false when container is killed, should Started also be set to false? I can understand the argument that this was never set to false and we need to keep the behavior.
2. What if API server was unavailable for some time while container was being restarted AND kubelet also restarted. Will it pick up the old "Ready" state then from older container? Should we protect against this as well? (this will be hard to write test for)

> * If Ready being set to false when container is killed, should Started also be set to false? I can understand the argument that this was never set to false and we need to keep the behavior.

Once the kubelet observes from the runtime that the container is no longer running, `UpdatePodStatus` computes both `Ready=false` and `Started=false`. During graceful termination, while the runtime still reports the container as running, these values may remain true. We intend to preserve this behavior.



> 2\. What if API server was unavailable for some time while container was being restarted AND kubelet also restarted. Will it pick up the old "Ready" state then from older container? Should we protect against this as well? (this will be hard to write test for)

Yes, I think the scenario you described may also reuse stale readiness state. Suppose the API server records container A as Ready=true; while the API server is unavailable, container A is replaced by container B; the kubelet then restarts. Container B may have started before the new kubelet process, so the current code may classify it as a container that survived the kubelet restart. It may consequently preserve readiness based on the stale Pod Ready condition and skip setting the readiness probe’s initial Failure result.

The Started/ContainerID check protects containers with a startup probe because container B remains Started=false until its startup probe succeeds. However, it does not fully protect containers that only have a readiness probe. I think we should apply the same identity rule when preserving readiness: only preserve the previous readiness state and skip the initial probe result when the API status and runtime status refer to the same ContainerID. If the IDs differ, the container should be treated as a new instance, without inheriting the previous instance’s Started or Ready state.

Since this is a separate failure mode from the current startup-probe regression, I think we can track it separately and address it in v1.38.

> 2. What if API server was unavailable for some time while container was being restarted AND kubelet also restarted. Will it pick up the old "Ready" state then from older container? Should we protect against this as well? (this will be hard to write test for)

Yes, it does. I reproduced it on kind v1.36.1 with a readiness-only pod, the replacement container came up `ready=true` inherited from the old container and stayed that way until its own probe ran after `initialDelaySeconds`. Filed #141473 with the repro and a proposed fix. Agree with keeping it separate from #141342 so that one stays minimal for the cherry-picks.

This bug should not be closed with the merge of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141342 as we will need to track cherry-picks of it.

@HirazawaUi do you want to send cherry-picks?
@SergeyKanzhelev Yes, this fix needs to be backported to the older branches. The cherry-picks have already been completed. ref: #142041 #142042 #142043

title: Memory Manager pod-scope restore compares container blocks with the pod request
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager, after a kubelet restart, Memory Manager finds a restored container allocation and calls `regenerateHints` with that container's blocks and the whole Pod memory request.

For a multi-container Pod, those values differ, so `regenerateHints` returns no hint instead of restoring the Pod's previous NUMA hint. This can cause an existing Pod to fail admission under `restricted` or `single-numa-node`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-scope hint restoration should use the restored pod-level allocation and preserve the previous NUMA hint.

### How can we reproduce it?

Use a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory resources and two containers, allocate it with static Memory Manager, restart from the checkpoint, then call `GetPodTopologyHints`. The current code returns no regenerated hint because it compares one container's blocks with the Pod request.

title: [Failing test] apisnoop-conformance-gate red since 2026-07-23: getLifecycleAPIGroup untested — pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml is not consumed by the gate
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

- `apisnoop-conformance-gate` (periodic, every 3h)
- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-conformance#apisnoop-conformance-gate
- https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate

### Which tests are failing?

The gate itself:

```
==================
UNTESTED ENDPOINTS
getLifecycleAPIGroup

==================
ERROR: You have 1 untested endpoints
==================
```

### Since when has it been failing?

First red build: [2080099338675032064](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080099338675032064) (2026-07-23 01:15 UTC).
Last green build: [2080053868456054784](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080053868456054784) (2026-07-22 22:14 UTC).
Every run since has failed (~60 consecutive builds as of 2026-07-30), and `testgrid-num-failures-to-alert: '1'` means this alerts on every run.

### Reason for failure

#137050 (merged 2026-07-23 00:33 UTC, 42 minutes before the first red build) added the `lifecycle.k8s.io/v1alpha1` group (EvictionRequest). The group discovery path `/apis/lifecycle.k8s.io/` has no version in it, so its operation `getLifecycleAPIGroup` registers as **stable** in apisnoop even though the group only serves an alpha version. No conformance test can hit it (the group is not served in a default/conformance cluster), so the gate flags it as an untested eligible endpoint.

#137050 anticipated this and added `getLifecycleAPIGroup` to [`test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml) — **but the `apisnoop-conformance-gate` job never reads that file**. The gate (snoopdb image) only loads `ineligible_endpoints.yaml`:

- [`303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql) fetches only `test/conformance/testdata/ineligible_endpoints.yaml`
- the untested list is `conformance.new_endpoint` = stable endpoints in the latest release minus `ineligible_endpoint` ([`207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql), [`203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql))
- [`docker-entrypoint.sh`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/docker-entrypoint.sh) exits 1 if that list is non-empty

`pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` is only consumed by:
- test-infra's [`experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py) (the `conformance-audit` jobs in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-arch/conformance-audit.yaml`)
- the apisnoop web UI ([`apps/web/src/lib/constants.js`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/web/src/lib/constants.js))

### Anything else we need to know?

- #140923 was filed for this failure and closed as a duplicate of #140523, but #140523 tracks adding EvictionRequest CRUD tests — that cannot turn this gate green while the group is alpha-only (the endpoint is not served in a conformance cluster, and alpha APIs cannot have conformance tests). #140897 was closed unmerged. So nothing currently open unblocks the job.
- Precedent for exactly this situation is an entry in **`ineligible_endpoints.yaml`** (the file the gate does consume). `getInternalApiserverAPIGroup`, `getResourceAPIGroup`, and `getStoragemigrationAPIGroup` all have entries there with reason *"The endpoint is part of a group that has no stable endpoints yet, reporting as a stable endpoint in apisnoop."* (see also kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop#859, the identical failure for `storagemigration`).

Proposed fix:

1. **Short term (unblocks CI):** move `getLifecycleAPIGroup` from `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` to `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` with the same reason/link as the existing `get*APIGroup` entries, and remove it once `lifecycle.k8s.io` serves a stable version with conformance coverage (#140523).
2. **Longer term:** make snoopdb's gate also honor `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` (kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop), so the documented escape hatch actually applies to `apisnoop-conformance-gate`, or document that only `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` gates CI.

cc @atiratree @kannon92

/kind failing-test
/sig architecture
/sig node
/wg node-lifecycle
/priority important-soon
author: dims

If you have questions or suggestions related to my behavior, please file an issue against the [kubernetes-sigs/prow](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prow/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository.
</details>
/assign @dims
FYI, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141043 is adding the endpoint tests

I created a few PRs to fix this for apisnoop and audit_log_parser.py jobs:

- [ ] 1. kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop#1035 - apisnoop
- [ ] 2. test-infra - bump the snoopdb image pin in
      `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-arch/conformance-gate.yaml`
- [ ] 3. kubernetes/test-infra#37599 - `audit_log_parser.py` (used by *-audit-kind-conformance and e2e-kind-audit prow jobs)
- [ ] 4. kubernetes/kubernetes#141109 - the yaml entries, once both
      checkers derive it. Held until the rest land.

A little background:

Both apisnoop and @dims aud_log_parser.py decide whether an endpoint is stable by looking for the
words "alpha" or "beta" in it. Neither word is in `/apis/lifecycle.k8s.io/`, so it reads as stable. The group only serves
`v1alpha1`.

The group endpoints are ones you call to ask a group which versions it has, so it
never carries a version itself. Every group starts alpha, and alpha groups are
off by default, so nothing exercises the endpoint and it gets reported as
an untested GA endpoint.

The fix is to look below the group which versions it serves instead of reading
only the group name. These changes cover arrivals and graduations both, with nothing to
maintain by hand going forward.

comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm
🤖 please dig into this. look deep into each ci job that failed by pulling down logs and figure out why things are flaky.

## Triage: `ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial` — three unrelated failure modes, not one flake

I pulled logs for **every** failing build in the GCS-retained window (2026‑07‑11 → 07‑29) and classified each by root cause. The "cluster doesn't come up" framing conflates **three independent problems**. The specific build linked in the issue is only the least interesting one.

### Failure-mode breakdown (27 reds inspected in the window)

| Mode | Count | What actually happened | Class |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. t2a VM STOCKOUT** | ~9 | GCE can't allocate the `t2a-standard-2` VM in `us-central1-a`; VM never boots | Infra/capacity |
| **B. 3h suite hang** | ~16 | VM boots, ginkgo launched over SSH, then **node goes silent** — prow hard-kills at the 180m decoration timeout | The real bug |
| **C. Single reboot/static-pod test fail** | ~2 | Suite runs to completion, 1 of ~190 specs fails | Known flake, arch-independent |

### Mode A — the build in the issue is a pure GCE stockout (not k8s)
The linked build [2082290551972958208](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2082290551972958208) ran only ~7.5 min and ended with:
```
ERROR: (gcloud.compute.instances.create) ...
code: ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED_WITH_DETAILS
message: A t2a-standard-2 VM instance is currently unavailable in the us-central1-a zone.
         Consider ... us-central1-f, us-central1-b ... (state:STOCKOUT ...)
```
The [job config](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/node-kubelet.yaml) pins `--gcp-zone=us-central1-a` and `t2a-standard-2` (real arm64 hardware, `k8s-infra-prow-build` cluster — **not emulated**). Arm `t2a` capacity in a single zone is thin, so ~1/3 of the reds are just GCE telling us to pick another zone. **Fix:** multi-zone fallback (the error literally names `us-central1-f`/`-b` as having capacity) or a zone rotation in the image-config. This is self-resolving and not a code regression.

### Mode B — the dominant failure: the suite silently hangs until prow kills it at 3h
This is what's actually worth fixing and produced the long streaks (e.g. **07‑15→07‑17: ~14 consecutive reds**; 07‑22: 5 reds). Signature in every Mode‑B build, e.g. [2081745699879260160](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2081745699879260160):
```
... ssh ... ./ginkgo -focus="[Serial]" ... e2e_node.test ...      <- suite launched over SSH
{"level":"error","msg":"Process did not finish before 3h0m0s timeout"}   <- prow entrypoint kill
```
Decisive evidence — **artifacts of a hung build vs a healthy one**:
- Hung build artifacts: `build-log.txt`, `junit_runner.xml` (empty), `metadata.json` — **and nothing else**.
- Healthy build ([2082472497290153984](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2082472497290153984)): full per‑node tree — `serial-1.log`, `kubelet.log`, `containerd.log`, `*-ginkgo.log`, `junit_ubuntu01.xml`.

So the node boots, ginkgo starts over SSH, and then **no test output ever streams back and no per-node logs are ever collected** — the node/SSH channel wedges mid-run and the runner blocks until the 180m guillotine. Because the kill is external, there is **no junit and no serial console to post-mortem** — that's the core diagnosability gap.

Two config facts that make this worse and are independently fixable:
- **Timeout mismatch:** decoration `timeout: 180m` but kubetest2 is passed `--timeout=4h0m0s` and ginkgo `-timeout=24h`. The inner timeouts can never fire — prow's 180m always wins, guaranteeing a log-less kill instead of a graceful ginkgo timeout that would dump node logs.
- Every Mode‑B log shows early `ssh: connect ... port 22: Connection refused` / `Permission denied (publickey)` during boot (retried OK), consistent with a flaky serial/SSH path on these t2a images rather than a specific test.

**Recommended next step (owner: SIG Node):** align the timeouts so ginkgo self-terminates and uploads node logs *before* the 180m kill (set kubetest2/ginkgo timeout well under 180m), so the next hang produces a `serial-1.log`/`kubelet.log` to root-cause. Right now every hang is an evidence black hole.

### Mode C — a known, arch-independent test flake (not arm-specific)
The 2 builds that ran to completion failed a single spec at `mirror_pod_test.go:930` ([2080897853596635136](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2080897853596635136)) or `static_pod_test.go` ([2078655240525058048](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-ubuntu-serial/2078655240525058048)) — kubelet-restart/mirror-pod timing. **This reproduces on native amd64:** `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial` build [2082439532740874240](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial/2082439532740874240) failed the *same* `mirror_pod_test.go:930` spec on 07‑29. So this is not an arch/"slow VM" issue — it's the previously-tracked static/mirror-pod flake family (cf. #137737). The amd64 native serial job is otherwise ~all green, which **rules out a code regression** as the cause of the arm64 reds — the arm64-specific pain is Modes A and B (infra), not test code.

### Bottom line
- **Not a single flake, and not a k8s code regression.** No commit-window bisect applies — the amd64 native equivalent is green.
- **~60% of reds = Mode B** (suite hangs → 3h prow kill, no logs). This is the real actionable item and needs the timeout re-alignment above so it becomes diagnosable.
- **~33% = Mode A** (t2a stockout in `us-central1-a`) — fix with multi-zone fallback.
- **~7% = Mode C** — the existing static/mirror-pod test flake, arch-independent.

If someone can land the timeout fix, the next Mode‑B occurrence will actually leave a `kubelet.log`/serial console behind and we can finish the root cause. Happy to open the test-infra PR for the timeout alignment + zone fallback if SIG Node wants it.

title: CPU Manager AllocatePod re-allocates restored pod CPUs after kubelet restart
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, static CPU Manager is not idempotent across kubelet restart.

After restart, pod-level CPU assignments are restored from the checkpoint. Existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod(AddOperation)`. In `allocatePodForAdd`, the pod-scope path does not check whether a complete pod-level allocation was already restored. It allocates again from the default CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment.

This causes two deterministic failure modes:

- If the remaining default CPU set cannot satisfy the same request again, kubelet rejects an existing Pod after restart.
- If enough CPUs remain, CPU Manager assigns a second CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment, while the original CPUs stay removed from the default set, effectively leaking exclusive CPUs.

Examples with 1 reserved CPU and a Pod requesting 2 CPUs:

```text
4 CPUs:
restored pod cpuset:     1-2
restored default cpuset: 0,3
readmission error:       not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1

6 CPUs:
pod cpuset:              1-2 -> 3-4
default cpuset:          0,3-5 -> 0,5
readmission error:       <nil>
```

The current path is here: [`allocatePodForAdd`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L397-L440). It calls `allocateCPUs` and `SetPodCPUSet` without consulting the restored pod allocation.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level CPU Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

If a complete pod-level allocation was restored from checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the restored pod CPU set, container assignments, and default CPU set. It should not allocate a second CPU set or reject the existing Pod because of its own restored reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestCPUManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static CPU Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager, 1 reserved CPU, and either 4 or 6 single-threaded CPUs.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level request/limit of 2 CPUs and 1 container.
4. Start CPU Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Add the container so the pod/container assignments are checkpointed.
6. Recreate CPU Manager with the same checkpoint dir to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Verify the pod CPU set, container assignment, and default CPU set were restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod(AddOperation)` again.
9. Verify the restored state is unchanged.

Observed results:

- On 4 CPUs: `not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1`
- On 6 CPUs: the restored pod CPU set changes from `1-2` to `3-4`, and the default CPU set changes from `0,3-5` to `0,5`

### Anything else we need to know?

This is the CPU Manager counterpart of #140906.

This is separate from #129078 / #129079. Those concern the older container-level `full-pcpus-only` SMT validation path. This reproducer does not enable `full-pcpus-only`; it exercises the pod-level allocation path introduced by #134768.

`PodLevelResourceManagers` was promoted to Beta and enabled by default for Kubernetes 1.37 in #140573.

### Kubernetes version

`master` commit `5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35`

title: No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination
body:
### What happened?

#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

### What did you expect to happen?

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

### Anything else we need to know?

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.0
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

</details>

Gap exists on master and all supported branches.

### Cloud provider

<details>

N/A

</details>

### OS version

<details>

title: kubelet: stopping a probe worker does not cancel an in-flight exec probe
body:
### What happened?

Stopping a probe worker does not cancel a probe that is already executing. `worker.stop()` does a non-blocking send on `stopCh`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L204-L211

and `run()` only selects on `stopCh` between probes, after `doProbe` returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L186-L201

So when `RemovePod` / `CleanupPods` / `StopLivenessAndStartup` stops a worker, an exec probe that is mid-flight keeps running against a container that is being killed. It ends only when its own `TimeoutSeconds` elapses, and `runProbeWithRetries` will retry up to `maxProbeRetries` (3) if the attempt errors, so the worst case is roughly `3 * TimeoutSeconds` after `stop()`. `TimeoutSeconds` is user-controlled, so that can be minutes. The worker also records the result of that last probe after it was told to stop.

Between #130487 (v1.35.0) and #140882 this happened to be papered over: workers inherited the pod worker's sync context, which the pod worker cancels at teardown, so in-flight execs died promptly. That was not a fix, it was the cause of #140881. The same cancellation also killed every readiness probe for the entire grace period, which is the much worse bug. #140882 detaches the worker context with `context.WithoutCancel` and restores the pre-1.35 behavior, which reinstates this gap.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659050743.

### What did you expect to happen?

`stop()` cancels the probe that is currently executing, and the worker goroutine exits promptly instead of waiting out `TimeoutSeconds`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Pod with an exec readiness probe whose command blocks (`sleep 300`) and `timeoutSeconds: 60`, plus `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1`. Delete the pod while a probe is in flight and watch `--v=4` kubelet logs: the `Exec-Probe runProbe` for that worker has no matching completion until the timeout fires, well after the container is gone.

### Anything else we need to know?

Suggested fix: give each worker its own context derived from the (detached) manager context and cancel it from `stop()`, roughly:

1. In `newWorker`, `w.ctx, w.cancel = context.WithCancel(ctx)`.
2. `run()` uses `w.ctx` for `doProbe` and adds `<-w.ctx.Done()` to the select.
3. `stop()` calls `w.cancel()` in addition to signalling `stopCh`, so an in-flight `ExecSync` is cancelled.

That keeps the worker lifecycle owned by the prober manager instead of the pod worker, which is what #140882 is after, while still bounding shutdown.

Worth checking as part of this whether cancelling mid-probe can record a spurious result. `doProbe` throws away errored results today, which is what made #140881 invisible, so a cancelled probe should not flip readiness either way. A test for "stop() during an in-flight probe records no result" would be good to have alongside.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.0
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

</details>

Present on master and on release-1.35 / release-1.36 once #140882 is backported.

comments.body: 🤖 please dig into this!

## Suite-timeout in `ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary` — capacity exhaustion, not a probe regression

**TL;DR:** Cluster [`3aa867c5…`](https://go.k8s.io/triage#3aa867c5ba978edcc4ae) is **not** a bug in the liveness/startup-probe tests. It is a **whole-suite ginkgo timeout** (`[TIMEDOUT] A suite timeout occurred`). The `container_probe.go` specs named in the signature are *victims*, not the cause — they're simply the slowest specs, so they're the ones still running when the deadline fires. The real problem: this canary job runs **all of NodeConformance in ~75 min of ginkgo budget, and the suite has grown to the point where it no longer reliably fits.** It fails intermittently whenever the run is a bit slower than average.

### Evidence

**1. The failure is a suite deadline, not an assertion.** In the newest red build [`2081212180027412480`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary/2081212180027412480) (SHA `24a5b063a5`, cos-beta, containerd 2.2.5):
```
Ran 570 of 1283 Specs in 4513.584 seconds
FAIL! - Suite Timeout Elapsed
```
`4513s ≈ 75.2 min`. Ginkgo is invoked with `--timeout=75m` (`ginkgo.timeout=1h14m59s`), wrapped in `timeout -k 30s 5400s`. 24 specs report `[TIMEDOUT]` in that single run — the mark of the *suite* clock expiring, not one test hanging. The `context canceled` on `getting pod` is ginkgo tearing the node down, not a kubelet/probe error.

**2. Green runs pass with almost no margin.** Recent SUCCESS builds:
| Build | Runtime | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| [`2081296486347313152`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary/2081296486347313152) | 3852s | /4500s |
| [`2081233824569626624`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary/2081233824569626624) | 4058s | /4500s |
| [`2081191042714963968`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary/2081191042714963968) | **4396s** | /4500s |

Green passes land at 85–98 % of budget. Any run a few minutes slower tips over. This is the textbook signature of a suite that has outgrown its timeout — **pass/fail is decided by run-to-run timing noise, not by code correctness.**

**3. The suite is growing.** Spec count has climbed steadily:
- Jul 12 ([`2076329600698290176`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-node-canary/2076329600698290176)): `will run 581 of 1217 specs` — already timing out
- Jul 19–20: `581 of 1224`
- Jul 26: `581 of 1283`

`+66 total specs in two weeks`, while the 75m budget is unchanged. The failures in this cluster stretch back to **at least Jul 12** — this is chronic capacity exhaustion, **not** an onset tied to a single recent PR.

**4. Why probe tests are always the ones caught.** The named specs (`should *not* be restarted …`) call `runLivenessTest` with a **fixed 240 s (4-minute) wait** (`0x37e11d6000` = 240s in the goroutine dump) to prove a restart does *not* happen — `container_probe.go:1806/1819`, sleeping in a `time.Sleep`-driven poll loop (`container_probe.go:1856`). They are among the longest-running specs in the suite, so probabilistically they are the ones in flight when the global clock expires. That's selection bias, not causation — the cluster also sweeps in `containers-lifecycle`, GRPC-probe, and restartable-init specs for the same reason.

### Job config (from `test-infra`)
`config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-testing/kubetest-canaries.yaml`: `interval: 1h`, cluster `k8s-infra-prow-build` (real HW, not emulated), `--test_args=--nodes=8 --focus="[NodeConformance]" --skip="[Flaky]|[Serial]"`, outer `--timeout=90m`, inner ginkgo `--timeout=75m`, VM has only **2 CPU / 4 Gi** running 8 parallel ginkgo processes. It's a **canary** job (`kubekins-e2e:latest-master`, `image-config-canary.yaml` → cos-beta), i.e. an early-warning lane — chronic flake here is comparatively low-severity but real.

### Classification
**Infrastructure/capacity flake — not a code regression.** No commit-window bisect is warranted: there is no clean green→red boundary (it's been intermittently red since ≥Jul 12), and green/red runs carry unrelated SHAs. The driver is `total NodeConformance runtime ≥ ginkgo 75m budget`, aggravated by steady spec growth and a small (2 CPU) VM.

### Suggested fixes (for SIG Node)
- **Raise the ginkgo budget / outer timeout**, or bump parallelism/VM size, so p99 runtime has real headroom (currently <5 % on good runs).
- **Or trim/shard** the NodeConformance set on this canary lane, or give the multi-minute "should *not* be restarted" probe specs a tighter observation window.
- This will recur and worsen as specs are added — a timeout bump is a stopgap; sharding is the durable fix.

I did **not** find an existing tracking issue for the node-canary suite timeout specifically (searched kubernetes/kubernetes) — #140943 appears to be the first. Worth `/sig node` + `/kind flake` and routing to whoever owns the canary lane's timeout budget.

*(Read-only triage; nothing was posted or modified.)*

body:
Title
Ensure Credential Pulled Images tests still flaking with "pulled record ... never appeared" after 
#138527/
#138642

Body

Hitting this on kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial - pretty sure this is the same flake as 
#136546/
#138527, just came back.

Testgrid: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-kubelet#kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial

A few sub-tests under Ensure Credential Pulled Images ... [FeatureGate:KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages] are failing, all through the same shared BeforeEach helper (tempRemoveImagePulledRecord in test/e2e_node/util_kubeletconfig.go):

util_kubeletconfig.go:133] Unexpected error: the file with the pulled record for the image ID never appeared:
<context.deadlineExceededError>: context deadline exceeded
Quick rundown of what that helper does: it polls every 1s for up to 5s waiting for kubelet to write an ImagePulledRecord at /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-<hash>, then moves it aside so a later step can check kubelet's behavior when the record's missing. If nothing shows up in 5s, it just fails.

#138527 got closed by 
#138642, but looking at that PR, it only added debug logging to this wait loop - didn't touch the 5s timeout or actually figure out why the record's sometimes missing. So this was never really fixed, just made easier to see happening.

And that's actually how I found something new - the extra logging from 
#138642 caught this in a recent run (2026-07-25, ~12:40 UTC) that wasn't visible back when 
#138527 was filed:

util_kubeletconfig.go:116] failed to stat file ".../pulled/sha256-c0a25c4ccec43320c35febdf68a46e03b3f9323eada881535d78d91aa9962741": ... no such file or directory
util_kubeletconfig.go:128] contents of "/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled": map[
  .../pulled/sha256-fbeb66043fabeed6f125049e44aef32e0b8f9e657a240b5a2091b292bab530f2:
    {"kind":"ImagePulledRecord", ..., "lastUpdatedTime":"2026-07-25T14:26:20Z", ...}
]
So at the moment it fails, the pulled/ directory isn't actually empty - there's a record in there, just for a different image, written ~23 minutes earlier by (presumably) an earlier sub-test in the same run. The record this specific check is waiting for just never shows up in the 5s window.

That makes me think this isn't pure slowness - more likely kubelet just doesn't write a new ImagePulledRecord at all when the image's already cached from an earlier sub-test in the same run, and the poll is timing out waiting for something that was never coming. Would be good to get sig-node's take on whether that's expected - if so, the fix is probably on the test's assumptions, not the timeout.

Checked the last 10 Testgrid columns for this job (~07-24 to 07-26) - failed 3/10 times, 6/20 over a longer window, so it's a real recurring thing, not a one-off. One specific run if useful: prow job 2080994746846679040 (2026-07-25, ~12:40-14:49 UTC), 2 sub-tests failed with this exact error.

🤖 please dig into this

## Root cause: PR #140350 un-skipped three heavyweight `[Slow]` StatefulSet tests that then time out — this is a **test-selection regression, not a product bug**

### TL;DR
On **2026-07-10** the `feature.StatefulSet` label was removed from the "Deploy clustered applications" tests (CockroachDB / MySQL / ZooKeeper) in [PR #140350 "Drop unnecessary sig-apps e2e features"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140350) (@soltysh, merged 14:05 UTC). Those tests were **skipped** before and now **run** in jobs that filter by `Feature:` — where they consistently time out at ~620s waiting for the app pods to come up. Cluster [`08ffb694…`](https://go.k8s.io/triage#08ffb694187fb53f5d54) is this, across three jobs.

### Regression boundary (job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary`)
| | Build | Started | SHA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Last green | [`2075496600431497216`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2075496600431497216) | 2026-07-10 08:25Z | `0fe889a7` |
| First red | [`2075617650255335424`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2075617650255335424) | 2026-07-10 16:26Z | `a473cbba` |

Solid red streak ever since (all 40+ builds through 7/24). Commit window `0fe889a7..a473cbba` = 6 PRs; only #140350 touches these tests.

### Smoking gun — junit shows the flip precisely
- **Green build junit:** `[sig-apps] StatefulSet Deploy clustered applications [Feature:StatefulSet] should creating a working CockroachDB cluster [Slow]` → **`status="skipped"`**
- **Red build junit** ([`2080456944…`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-alpha-beta-features-canary/2080456944480423936)): same test, now **without** the `[Feature:StatefulSet]` tag → **`status="failed" time="620"`**, error:
  ```
  [FAILED] Failed waiting for pods to enter running: context deadline exceeded
  k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/framework/statefulset/wait.go:63
  ```

### The change ([diff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140350/files))
`test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go`:
```diff
-	f.Describe("Deploy clustered applications", feature.StatefulSet, framework.WithSlow(), func() {
+	f.Describe("Deploy clustered applications", framework.WithSlow(), func() {
```
plus deletion of `feature.StatefulSet`/`feature.StatefulUpgrade` from `test/e2e/feature/feature.go`.

**Mechanism:** the kind canary job selects with `LABEL_FILTER: "Feature: isSubsetOf OffByDefault && !Deprecated && !Flaky && !Serial"` (`config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-testing/kubernetes-kind-ci.yaml`). With `[Feature:StatefulSet]` present (not an off-by-default gate), the test was excluded; strip the label and it now satisfies the filter and executes. The two kops jobs skip `[Feature:…]` classically, so the same relabel un-skips them there too.

### Breadth confirms it's the tests, not infra
Same three tests, same signature, failing concurrently across all three jobs in the cluster — kind-alpha-beta-features-canary plus [`e2e-ci-kubernetes-kops-cos-gce-slow-canary`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/e2e-ci-kubernetes-kops-cos-gce-slow-canary/2080482366580592640) and `e2e-ci-kubernetes-kops-al2023-aws-slow-canary`. The BeforeEach (client, namespace, service account) succeeds; only the app-pods-running wait times out. This rules out node/registry/kind-startup infra failure and rules out a code regression in a component — nothing in the StatefulSet controller changed in the window.

### Classification
**Real, datable test regression** (onset 7/10, single causative PR) — but the defect is in **test gating**, not in Kubernetes itself. These CockroachDB/MySQL/ZooKeeper deployments are known-heavy and were intentionally feature-gated so they only run where opted in; the cleanup PR removed the gate without accounting for the label-filter jobs that relied on it.

### Suggested fix directions (for sig-apps / @soltysh)
- Re-gate the "Deploy clustered applications" block (restore a `[Feature:…]`/off-by-default label or tag them `[Flaky]`/`[Serial]` so the canary filters exclude them), **or**
- Add a job-level skip for these three tests, **or**
- If they are meant to run, raise the StatefulSet running timeout for these apps.

No existing tracking/fix/revert PR found as of this triage. cc @soltysh @pohly (job owner, `testgrid-alert-email: patrick.ohly@intel.com`).

title: Memory Manager AllocatePod re-applies restored pod allocations after kubelet restart
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, the static Memory Manager restores pod-level assignments from its checkpoint when kubelet starts. The existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod` with `AddOperation`.
﻿
`AllocatePod` does not check whether the Pod already has a restored allocation. It calculates the request again and applies it to a machine state which already includes that Pod's reservation.
﻿
Depending on the remaining capacity, this can:
﻿
- reject an existing Pod during post-restart admission because its own allocation is no longer considered free;
- extend or change the previously selected NUMA affinity;
- reserve the same memory a second time, reducing `Free` and increasing `Reserved` and `NumberOfAssignments` again.
﻿
The Pod and container block entries are overwritten, but the additional machine-state accounting remains and is checkpointed.
﻿
﻿

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level Memory Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

When a complete allocation for the Pod has been restored from the checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the existing pod allocation, container assignments, NUMA affinity, and machine state. It should not consume capacity again or reject the Pod because of its own reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestMemoryManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static Memory Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory requests and limits and one container.
4. Start Memory Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Save the pod blocks, container blocks, and machine state.
6. Recreate Memory Manager with the same checkpoint directory to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Start the new manager and verify that the state was restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod` again with `AddOperation`, as post-restart admission does.
9. Verify that the call succeeds and all restored state remains unchanged.

With the current implementation, step 8 either accounts the Pod again or fails when there is not enough unreserved capacity to satisfy the same request a second time.

Using a single-container Pod keeps this reproducer separate from pod-scope hint regeneration behavior for multi-container Pods.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

commit 2192afa9f369883debb4bd43a1f9177aeab80a8e

Not provider-specific.

title: [Failing Test] pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master failing on all PRs: VM provisioning can't install OpenSSH (WU error 0x80244022)
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are failing?

None. The job dies during Azure VM provisioning, before checking out or testing anything. Zero test results are produced.

### Since when has it been failing?

Since at least 2026-07-23 ~16:00 UTC. The prow job history shows 0 successes across all PRs since then (a mix of FAILURE and ABORTED); before that the job was mostly green with occasional flakes.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/directory/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The harness (`sigs.k8s.io/windows-testing/scripts/enable_ssh_windows.ps1`) installs OpenSSH on the freshly provisioned Windows VM via `Add-WindowsCapability -Online`, which pulls the capability from Windows Update. That call is failing on every VM:

```
Add-WindowsCapability : Add-WindowsCapability failed. Error code = 0x80244022
```

`0x80244022` is `WU_E_PT_HTTP_STATUS_SERVICE_UNAVAIL`: the VM cannot reach Windows Update (or WU is returning 503). As a result sshd is never installed:

```
Get-Service : Cannot find any service with service name 'sshd'.
ssh: connect to host <vm-ip> port 22: Connection timed out
```

Every run fails identically on a different VM/IP, so this is not a flake; it is either a Windows Update/Azure-side outage or an image/network change affecting the harness's WU access.

Example runs (from kubernetes/kubernetes#140882, three consecutive failures with identical signature):

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080325276394328064
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080328164998909952
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080330379864051712

### Anything else we need to know?

The job is in the required presubmit set, so this blocks merges on every kubernetes/kubernetes PR. Hardening options regardless of the upstream outage: bake the OpenSSH capability into the VM image instead of installing it from Windows Update at provision time, or add retry/fallback (e.g. the Win32-OpenSSH release zip) in `enable_ssh_windows.ps1`.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig windows
/sig testing
