</details>
🤖 please dig into this

## Root cause: WAS APIs graduated `GenericWorkload` to Beta, but the alpha node-e2e job only enables `AllAlpha` — so the Beta parent is off while its Alpha dependents are on

Your read of the issue is exactly right. Here is the full chain with evidence.

### What breaks and why
The job aborts in `initialize feature gates` because five Alpha feature gates are enabled while their required parent `GenericWorkload` is disabled:

```
WorkloadWithJob / DRAWorkloadResourceClaims / CompositePodGroup /
TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling / PodGroupPreemptionPolicy
  → depends on features that are disabled: [GenericWorkload]
```

The dependency map in `pkg/features/kube_features.go` declares these as hard deps on `GenericWorkload`:
- `WorkloadWithJob: {GenericWorkload}` (kube_features.go:2742)
- `DRAWorkloadResourceClaims: {DynamicResourceAllocation, GenericWorkload}` (:2458)
- `CompositePodGroup: {GenericWorkload, TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling}` (:2416)
- `TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling: {GenericWorkload}` (:2714)
- `PodGroupPreemptionPolicy: {GenericWorkload}` (:2604)

All five dependents are **Alpha**; `GenericWorkload` was **Alpha in 1.35** and got **promoted to Beta at 1.37 with `Default: false`**:
```go
GenericWorkload: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.35"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},   // <-- new
},
```

The alpha-features node-e2e job passes **`--feature-gates=AllAlpha=true`** (with `EventedPLEG=false,PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI=true`) — **no `AllBeta=true`** (`test-infra/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/node-kubelet.yaml`, the `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features` tab). So `AllAlpha` flips the five Alpha dependents on, but since `GenericWorkload` is now **Beta** (not Alpha) it stays off → the dependency validator rejects the set and the whole suite exits before any test runs.

Note the contrast: the CRI-proxy job at node-kubelet.yaml:1210 uses `AllAlpha=true,AllBeta=true` and would *not* hit this; it's specifically the alpha-only tabs (`alpha-features` / `alpha-slow-features`) that break.

### Causative PR — confirmed by exact build boundary
**PR [#140184](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140184) "Graduate WAS APIs to beta"** (@tosi3k), commit `3ddd5a74e67`, merged **2026-07-21 16:03 UTC**.

Bisected on the periodic itself:

| Build | Started (UTC) | k8s SHA | Contains `3ddd5a74e67`? | `[GenericWorkload]` error? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [2079477169288908800](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features/2079477169288908800) | 07-21 08:03 | `74c594bf1a` | **NO** | **absent** |
| [2079839944150355968](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features/2079839944150355968) | 07-22 08:04 | `5478128c02` | **YES** | **present** |

The error signature appears in the first build that includes the merge and is absent in the one just before it — a clean onset that lines up with the 07-21 16:03 UTC merge time.

(The job was already red on other days for unrelated reasons — e.g. green on 07-17 — so this is a *new, distinct* failure mode layered on a flaky tab, not the tab's only problem. The feature-gate error blocks the entire suite regardless.)

### Blast radius
This will hit **every job that enables `AllAlpha=true` without also enabling `GenericWorkload`** (or `AllBeta` where applicable). At minimum the two sig-node tabs share the pattern:
- `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`
- `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-slow-features`

Worth grepping test-infra for other `AllAlpha=true`-without-`AllBeta`/`GenericWorkload` jobs (kind alpha jobs, etc.) — the issue author's suspicion that it affects other areas of testgrid is well-founded.

### Fix options (no existing fix PR found as of this triage)
1. **Simplest / job-side:** add `GenericWorkload=true` (or `AllBeta=true`) to the alpha-features node-test-args in `node-kubelet.yaml`. This is the classic remedy when an Alpha feature's parent graduates to Beta-but-default-off.
2. **Code-side:** in the WAS-beta PR, whichever component owns these gates could make the Alpha dependents self-consistent, or `GenericWorkload` could be treated as implicitly enabled when any dependent is on.

Given the graduation just landed, option 1 in test-infra is the fastest unblock; a SIG-scheduling / wg-workload-aware-scheduling call on the intended long-term shape is warranted. cc the PR author @tosi3k who has the most context.

/sig node
/wg workload-aware-scheduling

title: Exec readiness probes silently broken during graceful pod termination since v1.35 (probe context canceled at teardown)
body:
### What happened?

Since v1.35.0, exec readiness probes stop working the moment a pod begins graceful termination. Every probe attempt fails client-side with `rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled`, the prober discards errored results, and the pod's `Ready` condition stays frozen at whatever it was before termination began. A pod whose readiness probe starts failing during its grace period is never marked NotReady.

This is a regression from #130487 (`chore(kubelet): migrate prober to contextual logging`, commit b6f6731ab61, first released in v1.35.0). Probe workers previously ran on `context.Background()`. They now inherit the pod worker's sync context via `probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `kubelet.SyncPod`, and `pod_workers.go` cancels that context as soon as teardown begins ("Cancelling current pod sync"). Every subsequent CRI `ExecSync` fails immediately. In a 60s grace period I logged 61 consecutive canceled probes.

Only exec probes are affected. The HTTP, TCP, and gRPC probers don't take the ctx.

### What did you expect to happen?

Readiness probes keep running during graceful termination, and a failing probe flips the pod Ready condition to False within a few probe periods. This worked before 1.35 (see the delete-path output in #124648, filed against ~1.30, where READY drops during Terminating).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Pod with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60` running busybox with a script that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps TERM to `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, and idles. Readiness probe: exec `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.

1. Wait for Ready=True.
2. `kubectl delete pod <pod>` and sample `.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status` once per second.

Observed on kindest/node:v1.35.0: Ready stays True for the entire 59s until the containers die. Kubelet events show `Readiness probe errored and resulted in unknown state: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled` repeating once per probe period (capped at 25 by event spam filtering).

Note: assert on the pod Ready condition, not the EndpointSlice. The deletionTimestamp withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug.

### Anything else we need to know?

Mechanism, confirmed at `--v=4`:

1. `pod_workers.go` cancels the pod sync context at teardown start (`status.cancelFn()`, "Cancelling current pod sync").
2. Probe workers were started with that context (`kl.probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `SyncPod`; `go w.run(ctx)` in `prober_manager.go`). Ironically this call site sits right above the #113606 TODO warning about exactly this class of problem.
3. `runProbe` passes the ctx into `newExecInContainer`, so `ExecSync` fails instantly with grpc `Canceled`.
4. `worker.doProbe` treats probe errors as "throw away the result", so `results.Failure` is never recorded and `SetContainerReadiness` never fires.

```

Worker lifetime is already managed by its own stop channel; `WithoutCancel` keeps the logger. With that two-line change on v1.35.0, the same repro flips Ready to False 1s after the delete. | kubelet | Ready during 60s graceful delete |
|---|---|
| stock v1.35.0 | True the whole time (bug) |
| v1.35.0 + #139167 | True the whole time (unchanged) |
| v1.35.0 + `WithoutCancel` fix | False at 1s |

Related: this is the dominant cause behind #124648's symptom on current versions, and it makes #139167 a no-op as written (its new branch is gated on phase Failed/Succeeded, which a gracefully deleted pod never hits while containers run; on the eviction path its extra probes hit the same canceled context). The `ready = !workerExists` latching issue described by @smarterclayton on #116965 is real but only reachable once this is fixed. No e2e covers readiness during pod deletion; the merged "readiness probe while in preStop" NodeConformance test only exercises the liveness-kill path, where no teardown occurs, which is how this shipped green. title: Serial node e2e jobs failing since 2026-07-22: kubelet panics at startup when PodLevelResources is disabled (PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting)
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

All serial node e2e jobs that run the CPU Manager or Memory Manager suites:

- ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers
- ci-node-crio-resource-managers
- ci-kubernetes-node-swap-ubuntu-serial
- ci-node-crio-swap-serial
- ci-containerd-node-e2e-serial-ec2
- ci-containerd-node-arm64-e2e-serial-ec2
- presubmits pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager and pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager-kubetest2 (for PRs rebased on master)

### Which tests are failing?

The first failure lands in the CPU Manager and Memory Manager suites that disable the PodLevelResources feature gate. After that, every later [Serial] test in the run fails in its BeforeAll or BeforeEach step with:

```
[FAILED] Failed to get successful response from /configz: context deadline exceeded
In [BeforeAll] at: k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e_node/kubeletconfig/kubeletconfig.go:186
```

Triage clusters (126 and 51 test names, same root cause, split only by ginkgo phase):

- https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?xjob=azure%7Ckops%7Ccrio%7Cautoscaling%7Ccapz%7Cci-kubernetes-verify%7Ccluster-api%7C-cos-%7Cfedora%7Cwindows%7Clocal-e2e%7Calpha-enabled-default%7Cci-gcp%7Cdocker-docker%7Cdocker-containerd%7Cci-minikube%7Ckvm-docker%7Cci-cloud-provider-gcp%7Cnpd-%7Cagentic-sandbox#fe142f553034eead5bbc
- https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?xjob=azure%7Ckops%7Ccrio%7Cautoscaling%7Ccapz%7Cci-kubernetes-verify%7Ccluster-api%7C-cos-%7Cfedora%7Cwindows%7Clocal-e2e%7Calpha-enabled-default%7Cci-gcp%7Cdocker-docker%7Cdocker-containerd%7Cci-minikube%7Ckvm-docker%7Cci-cloud-provider-gcp%7Cnpd-%7Cagentic-sandbox#2624ca6d5446537c85a5

### Since when has it been failing?

Since 2026-07-22. The last green build ran commit faba7e6a94df (merged 01:11 UTC). The first failing builds ran commit 39c618b5c30c (merged 04:09 UTC).

The clusters also contain builds from 2026-07-15 to 2026-07-17. That was the same failure mode, caused by #137150 and fixed by #140631. See the history section below.

### Reason for failure

The kubelet panics at startup while loading the config file the test wrote:

```
panic: failed to merge global and in-flight KubeletConfiguration while setting defaults,
error: PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting is enabled, but depends on features that are
disabled: [PodLevelResources]
```

Mechanism:

1. #140514 (merged 2026-07-22 02:55 UTC) added the feature gate `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting`, enabled by default at Beta, with a declared dependency on `PodLevelResources` in `pkg/features/kube_features.go`.
2. `configureCPUManagerInKubelet` and `configureMemoryManagerInKubelet` in test/e2e_node set `PodLevelResources: false` in the kubelet config for some test variants, and do not disable the new gate.
3. `SetDefaults_KubeletConfiguration` (`pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go:72`) merges the config gates into a copy of the global gates with `SetFromMap`. The dependency check fails and the code panics.
4. systemd restarts the kubelet, it panics again on the same config, and /configz returns 503 through the API server proxy until the test times out. Every later Serial test in the run then fails the same way.

Evidence: [prow build](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers/2079792906901655552) and the [kubelet.log with the panic](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers/2079792906901655552/artifacts/n2d-standard-32-cos-125-19216-532-25-913c732d/kubelet.log).

History: this is the second time this exact pattern broke these jobs. #137150 added `PodLevelResourcesFixKubeletQOSClass` (also enabled by default, also depending on PodLevelResources) and broke the same jobs from 2026-07-15 to 2026-07-17. #140631 fixed the tests by disabling that gate by name, so the fix does not cover the new gate. The presubmit that runs these suites (pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager) is optional and did not run on #140514.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is not only a CI problem. Any kubelet config file that sets `featureGates: {PodLevelResources: false}` now crashes the kubelet at startup, and disabling a Beta gate is a normal thing for a cluster admin to do.

Two possible fixes:

- Short term, repeat #140631 for the new gate: also set `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting: false` next to the existing lines in `test/e2e_node/cpu_manager_test.go` and `test/e2e_node/memory_manager_test.go` when the test disables PodLevelResources.
- Longer term, stop the kubelet from panicking here. Either the dependency check should treat a gate that is only enabled by default as off when its dependency is off, or config loading should return an error instead of panicking. Without that, every future gate that depends on PodLevelResources and ships enabled by default will break these jobs again.

/kind failing-test
/kind regression
/sig node
/priority critical-urgent

title: Changing batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index annotation causes the job controller to miscalculate pods needed to run
body:
### What happened?

The simplest way to reproduce this problem is to follow these steps:
1. Create an Indexed Job with completions: 2 and parallelism: 1, for example. The numbers don't matter here that much.
2. When the first pod is running, modify the following annotation `batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index` from 0 to 1.
3. Observe the job controller does its job by creating 0 index once more. 

The final state is that the 0th index (as created by the controller) runs twice, whereas the supposedly created 1st index never run. 


### What did you expect to happen?

Modifying `batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index` should not affect which indexes are actually run by the system.

## Triage: `TestReconstructedVolumeShouldUnmountSucceedAfterSetupFailed` — intrinsic test‑harness flake, not a product regression

**TL;DR** — This is a **timing‑dependent flake in the unit test itself**, not a code regression in `pkg/kubelet/volumemanager`. The test issues **single‑shot `reconcile()` calls**, and the unmount it waits for gets gated behind the 500 ms `nestedpendingoperations` backoff left over from the deliberately‑failed mount. When the machine is slow/contended, that one unmount call is rejected and never retried, so `waitForUnmount` exhausts its ~12 s backoff and fails. It is the same long‑standing flake family already tracked in **#137387 (`triage/accepted`, sig/storage)** and the earlier Windows failure **#137468 / fix PR #137671**.

### Mechanism (from the triage signature)
The failure cluster's error text ends with exactly this sequence ([cluster `35437cd389b1999da8bc`](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html#35437cd389b1999da8bc)):

```
E … nestedpendingoperations.go:348] Operation for "{volumeName:fake-plugin/pv …}" failed.
    No retries permitted until 2026-07-16 18:38:53.38… (durationBeforeRetry 500ms).
    Error: MountVolume.SetUp failed … : csiRPCError
    reconciler_test.go:2033: Timed out waiting for pod "pod1uid" to be unmount from volume "fake-plugin/pv".
--- FAIL: TestReconstructedVolumeShouldUnmountSucceedAfterSetupFailed (12.23s)
```

Chain of events:
1. The test's `SetUpHook` forces `SetUp` to return `csiRPCError`. The first `reconciler.reconcile(ctx)` runs the mount in a goroutine; the failure registers a **500 ms exponential backoff keyed by `volumeName` (`fake-plugin/pv`)** in `nestedpendingoperations`.
2. The test deletes the pod and calls `reconciler.reconcile(ctx)` a **second, single time** (`reconciler.go`: `reconcile → unmountVolumes`). The unmount is a *new* operation but shares the same volume key, so it is subject to that 500 ms gate. If the second reconcile fires inside the backoff window, the unmount is **rejected — and there is no reconcile loop to retry it** (the test calls `reconcile()` directly, not `Run()`).
3. `waitForUnmount` then just polls ASW state that never changes. Its `retryWithExponentialBackOff` (Duration 100 ms, Factor 3, Steps 6 ≈ **12.1 s**) runs out — matching the observed 12.2–12.4 s FAIL durations exactly.

The `SetUpCallCount==1` wait added in the March fix (below) guarantees the mount *goroutine* ran, but does **not** synchronize against the 500 ms operation backoff that gates the subsequent unmount — so the race remains.

### Why this is not a July‑8 regression
- The issue's "since 2026‑07‑08" onset build is [ci-kubernetes-unit/2074869853222604800](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-unit/2074869853222604800), SHA `16e45f3b5e6`. The only product changes to `pkg/kubelet/volumemanager` / `operationexecutor` near that date — `476fa233a26` (Jul 20) and `b62df1d3926` (Jul 9) — are **not even in that build**; the newest one that is (`8ad339756cd`, SELinuxMount GA, Jun 24) is unrelated to the reconstructed‑unmount path.
- The test's own last two touches long predate the onset: `bd7c78107f1` (PR #136603, merged **Feb 3**) and `53bd956a457` (PR #137671, merged **Apr 23**). The `waitForUnmount` helper and the `reconcile()`‑then‑poll structure are unchanged since April.
- The flake predates July by months: **#137387** (opened Mar 4, `triage/accepted`) records the same test flaking on `ci-kubernetes-unit`, `-ppc64le`, and `-s390x` back to February. "2026‑07‑08" is when this reporter's cluster window opened, not a code‑change onset.

In the current triage data the cluster only shows `pr:pull-kubernetes-unit` builds; the periodic `ci-kubernetes-unit` reds cited in the issue have rolled out of the retention window, but the mechanism is arch/job‑independent (it's pure Go‑runtime scheduling timing), consistent with it surfacing across amd64/ppc64le/s390x.

### Answer to @ffromani (sig-node vs sig-storage)
Lean **sig/storage**, matching the precedent: the code lives under `pkg/kubelet/volumemanager` (hence the auto `sig/node` label), but it exercises volume reconstruction / unmount and the FakeVolume plugin, and the pre‑existing accepted flake **#137387** for this exact test is labeled **sig/storage**. Suggest `/sig storage` (keep node cc'd) and de‑duping against #137387.

### Suggested fix (deflake, test‑only)
Make the unmount robust to the mount backoff instead of relying on a single reconcile:
- drive the second phase with a short **reconcile loop / retry** so the unmount is re‑attempted once the 500 ms backoff expires (mirroring how the real `reconciler.Run()` loop behaves), or
- advance/clear the operation backoff for the volume before the unmount reconcile, or
- have `waitForUnmount` call `reconciler.reconcile(ctx)` on each poll iteration rather than polling passive state.

Any of these removes the 500 ms‑window race without touching product code.

### Corroborating links
- Issue: [#140823](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140823)
- Prior accepted flake (same test): [#137387](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137387)
- Windows failure + prior race "fix": [#137468](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137468) / PR [#137671](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137671) (`53bd956a457`)
- Reconstructed‑unmount origin: PR [#136603](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136603) (`bd7c78107f1`)
- Triage cluster: [`35437cd389b1999da8bc`](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html#35437cd389b1999da8bc)

**Classification: flake (test‑harness timing race), not a product regression.** Recommend `/kind flake`, re‑home to sig/storage, and dedupe with #137387.

---
*🔬 Automated triage on behalf of @dims, generated by Claude with the `k8s-ci-triage` skill. May contain mistakes — verify before acting.* <!-- k8s-bot:auto -->

The classification looks right, but the gate is `operationPending`, not the 500ms backoff. `unmountVolumes` skips the volume with `continue` before it ever reaches `UnmountVolume`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2a5a1c06c4bb33424a8253d876a094cc01957b07/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler_common.go#L150-L153

Reproduced with a 600ms sleep in `SetUpHook`, deliberately longer than the backoff:

```
reconciler_test.go:2033: Timed out waiting for pod "pod1uid" to be unmount from volume "fake-plugin/pv".
--- FAIL: TestReconstructedVolumeShouldUnmountSucceedAfterSetupFailed (12.71s)
```

The existing `SetUpCallCount == 1` wait does not close this, because the counter is incremented before the hook runs, so it returns while the mount operation is still pending.

Fix: wait for the operation to not be pending before the second `reconcile()`. Test-only. Happy to send it.

/assign

/triage accepted

title: Memory Manager pod scope drops hugepage requests used only by regular init containers
body:
### What happened?

With the static Memory Manager and pod-level Topology Manager scope, `getPodRequestedResources` drops a memory resource type when that resource is requested by a regular init container but by no app container.
﻿
A minimal example is:
﻿
- a regular init container requests `memory: 1Gi` and `hugepages-1Gi: 2Gi`;
- the app container requests `memory: 1Gi`, but does not request `hugepages-1Gi`.
﻿
The calculated pod request is:
﻿
```text
map[memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The expected result is:
﻿
```text
map[hugepages-1Gi:2147483648 memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The init container still receives an individual hugepage memory block because its resources are processed separately, but the pod allocation and global NUMA capacity do not account for that block. This can produce incorrect topology hints and leave the Memory Manager machine state with more available hugepage capacity than actually assigned.

### What did you expect to happen?

getPodRequestedResources` should calculate each managed resource independently across the union of resource names requested by:
﻿
- app containers;
- restartable init containers;
- regular init containers.
﻿
For every resource name, the existing init-container and long-running-container maximum semantics should then be applied. A resource must not be omitted merely because no app container requests that resource type.
﻿
In the example above, both `memory` and `hugepages-1Gi` must be included in topology hint generation, pod memory blocks, and NUMA machine-state accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add the following case to `Test_getPodRequestedResources` in `pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager/policy_static_test.go`:

`{
	description: "resource requested only by a regular init container",
	pod: getPodWithInitContainers(
		"",
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "app-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "init-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
						hugepages1Gi:      resource.MustParse("2Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
	),
	expected: map[v1.ResourceName]uint64{
		v1.ResourceMemory: 1 * gb,
		hugepages1Gi:      2 * gb,
	},
},
`

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager -run Test_getPodRequestedResources -count=1

Thanks for filing this issue.
The problem at hand seems legit. But I can't help but think about the larger and older issue about releasing resources required only by init containers (context: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131764 and the linked issues and ramifications).
Now: at glance this just seem a legit issue, the pod shape _should indeed_ be the `max(max(initContainers), sum(sidecarContainers, appContainers))` but still we should spend some time checking how it feeds back in the "lost resources" issue.

At the moment of writing we are at the very very last hours of the 1.37 cycle. Since we determined this is not a regression I'm intentionally deferring the PR review after code freeze. I won't object if other reviewers/approvers want to push it through though.

Thanks for the triage. On the lost-resources interaction: this fix only brings hugepages into the same max() accounting that memory already gets at pod scope, so the reservation-outliving-init shape is pre-existing rather than something the fix adds — before it, the init-only sizes were simply invisible at pod scope, which under-reserves the NUMA node rather than over-holds it. Any release-after-init mechanism coming out of that line of work should then apply to memory and hugepages uniformly. After-freeze timing for the PR is completely fine.

> Thanks for the triage. On the lost-resources interaction: this fix only brings hugepages into the same max() accounting that memory already gets at pod scope, so the reservation-outliving-init shape is pre-existing rather than something the fix adds — before it, the init-only sizes were simply invisible at pod scope, which under-reserves the NUMA node rather than over-holds it. Any release-after-init mechanism coming out of that line of work should then apply to memory and hugepages uniformly.

You are right. Your fix does the correct thing. The reasons why I'm treading carefully are different and related to the system behavior as whole:
1. the **correct** accounting your PR fixes is expected to cause some huge pages to get "lost" - reserved, not in use. The current **wrong** code avoids this by side effect and **accidentally** "releases" the hugepages as side effect. Therefore it can make it obvious some broken user deployments are broken, but still surprise users
2. related to the above: we need to document we have another "resource lost" case, and arguably one severe as much as the "CPU leak" case which was already raised quite a few times, but which is hard to fix.

Out of experience, kubernetes is very strongly affected by [Hryum's law](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Hyrum%27s_law), so caution is warranted when we change, (even correcting! even with an obvious fix!) the observable behavior.
It is possible that a release note/doc is all we need. But we need to evaluate, preferably without a tight deadline :)

Agreed on both points, and no rush from my side. One data point for the evaluation: the reservation-outliving-init shape already applies to memory and to hugepage sizes shared with app containers (the max() against init containers was already in place for those), so this fix only extends it to sizes requested exclusively by init containers — which bounds the set of deployments that could observe the change to a fairly narrow corner. Happy to expand the release note to spell out the behavior change, and to help document this as the hugepage variant of the "lost resources" case once you get to the evaluation.

title: kubelet configures pod sandbox resource limits incorrectly
body:
While generating CRI pod sandbox config  ([calculateSandboxResources](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/90904cf220ea10fa6c9c04b5e17f89dc49ef8e92/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_linux.go#L48)) we calculate limits as sum of declared container limits. If some contianers skip setting the limit, we currently count that 0. Instead, we need to treat missing limits as unlimited like what we do while setting pod cgroups  ([ResourceConfigForPod](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c59911870d649f7eb308ac1e267e6055a1b4033e/pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go#L192-L214))

/kind bug
/sig node

comments.body: some discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140009#discussion_r3620382780

After code freeze, I'd like to open a discussion about changing the `resourcehelper.PodLimits` function to automatically omit limits for some resources when they aren't set on every container. I don't think we ever want that for CPU & memory, but I think we always want it for EphemeralStorage. For the rest, I'm not sure.
/assign

I have added the change in `PodLimits()`, but kept the fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141014 intentionally narrow to target sandbox resource calculation. The new option is opt-in, so the other callers are unaffected.

Going through the rest of the `PodLimits()` callers, I see the same incorrect accounting in other places:
1. Eviction manager - ephemeral storage eviction limit in [podEphemeralStorageLimitEviction](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2db862797c5d97de96e2bc36999aaba5fad0533a/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L572) 
2. Quota - we currently count partial limit sum toward quota in [podComputeUsageHelper](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2db862797c5d97de96e2bc36999aaba5fad0533a/pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods.go#L294)
3. emptyDir sizing - the volume size limit is derived from the same partial sum in [AddPodToVolume](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2db862797c5d97de96e2bc36999aaba5fad0533a/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/cache/desired_state_of_world.go#L316) .

I would prefer to handle those in separate PRs so that impact of the change can be evaluated independently.
cc @ndixita to ensure consistency with pod and container level settings.

> I would prefer to handle those in separate PRs so that impact of the change can be evaluated independently.

+1. We need to document the impact on the workloads clearly.

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

Follow up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140810#issuecomment-5122071861. Digging deeper into and the impact of fixing the calculation in `PodLimits()` (with some help from Google Antigravity for analysis):

The bug in `PodLimits()` only affects cpu, memory, and ephemeral-storage. These are the only resources where an unset limit in the spec means **unbound** and not zero. Any fix must apply only to these 3 resources. Hugepages and extended resources, where an unset limit means zero should remain unaffected.

Behavior change per consumer, using a running example:
— pod with 2 contianers c1, c2. 
— `c1` declaring `limits: {cpu: 2, memory: 256Mi, ephemeral-storage: 1Gi}`
— `c2` declaring no limits

**1. Pod sandbox resources (CRI, [`calculateSandboxResources`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_linux.go#L48))**
- **Current behavior:** sandbox config reports `cpu: 2 / memory: 256Mi` as the pod's limit even though `c2` may burst to node capacity. Runtimes that size the guest from this field (like Kata Containers) get an undersized VM.
- **With fix:** sandbox limits are unset (unlimited), consistent with the pod cgroup set by the kubelet ([`ResourceConfigForPod`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go#L180)).
- **Impact:** Pods that relied on partial-sum sizing get the runtime's default sizing at the next sandbox creation.

**2. Eviction manager — pod-level ephemeral-storage check ([`podEphemeralStorageLimitEviction`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L571))**
- **Current behavior:** ephemeral-storage limits have no cgroup enforcement, they are enforced entirely by the kubelet eviction manager which periodically runs three sequential checks per pod (for emptyDir, pod level limits, container level limits in [`localStorageEviction`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L516)), any of which immediately evicts the whole pod. This fix only impacts the pod-level check. The pod-level eviction threshold is the partial sum (1Gi from c1). The pod is evicted when *total* usage (c1 + c2 + emptyDirs) exceeds it, even when c1 is within its own limit (1Gi) and the usage comes from c2.
- **With fix:** no eviction because of pod-level checks if c1's own usage is less than the 1Gi limit. The container-level limit is correctly enforced by the container-level check (the whole pod is evicted if c1 exceeds it).
- **Impact:** Usage in undeclared places (c2) no longer evicts the pod at a threshold derived from c1's limit. c1 gets to use its full declared limit, measured only against its own usage. Workloads that relied on one container's limit acting as a de-facto pod-wide cap become unbounded at pod level.

**3. ResourceQuota — `limits.cpu` / `limits.memory` / `limits.ephemeral-storage` usage**
- **Namespace has a quota on `limits.cpu` or `limits.memory`** (e.g. `limits.cpu: 10`):
  - **Current behavior:** the example pod cannot be created at all — quota admission separately requires every container to declare the limit ([`Constraints()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/quota/v1/evaluator/core/pods.go#L129)), so creation fails with `must specify limits.cpu for: c2`. 
  - **With fix:** Pod rejection behavior does not change. The only change is accounting for pre-existing pods: today the example pod counts `cpu: 2` of the 10; with the fix it counts 0.
- **Namespace has a quota on `limits.ephemeral-storage`** (e.g. `limits.ephemeral-storage: 50Gi`):
  - **Current behavior:** We currently do not have a constraint that all containers must specify a limit when quota exists, so the example pod is admitted and counts `1Gi`. But the current eviction manager behavior (2 above) keeps this bounded as kubelet evicts the pod once total usage exceeds the same `1Gi` partial sum, so the pod is bounded by the amount it is charged for in quota.
  - **With fix:** the pod is still admitted counts 0 and has no pod-level bound. On kubelet it is unbound if c1 stays within limit (With fix for (2)). 
- **Impact:**  Pod effectively escapes quota if **ANY** of its containers skips setting the limit unless we include constraints similar to cpu/memory limit in quota manager (even now we have this gap, but only if **ALL** the containers in a pod skip setting limit for ephemeral storage).

**4. emptyDir sizing (volume manager [`AddPodToVolume`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/cache/desired_state_of_world.go#L261))**
- **Current behavior:** when the kubelet mounts a disk-backed emptyDir, it records a maximum size for the volume: the smaller of the emptyDir's own `sizeLimit` and the pod's ephemeral-storage limit — which today is the partial sum (1Gi in the example, shrinking a 2Gi `sizeLimit`).
- **With fix:** when any container skips the limit, only the emptyDir's own `sizeLimit` is recorded.
- **Impact:** None. This value is used only for usage tracking, not enforcement.


**5. Pod-level resources status ([`getEffectiveAllocatedResources`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a76f2bbb5a67c4a0142f49f5b40423905c356e86/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2188))**
- **Current behavior:** pod-level status limits show the partial sum while the pod is pending. Once running, the status flips to cgroup-derived values, which are unlimited.
- **With fix:** omitted limits are simply not reported — consistent between pending and running phases, and with the actual pod cgroup. Pods that set a pod-level limit are unaffected: the pod-level value takes precedence, per resource.
- **Impact:** Status no longer reports a limit the kubelet does not enforce;

title: EvictionRequest: fix first sync race
body:
### What happened?

As mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137050#discussion_r3615804000 by @jpbetz, we should fix a race where a different controller can race the main controller to do illegal state initialization during the first sync.

> I think the first sync can bypass the anti-spoofing machinery. This gate only applies when oldStatus != nil, and none of the time checks below require state == Active, so the initializing write can pre-populate startTime and completionTime on Inactive entries too. With completionTime already set, the heartbeat deadline check is skipped on each later flip, so a single actor with status write can walk the whole responder chain to Completed in seconds without any responder acting, then set the final conditions.



### What did you expect to happen?

Should the first sync require non-Active entries to be name and priority only instead of setting the whole struct? A test would be valuable.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Fast controller tries to race the evictionrequest-controller

title: [Failing Test] Windows e2e node CPUManager specs failing since 2026-07-17 (windows-e2e-node-master)
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

- `ci-kubernetes-e2enode-windows-master` (every run since 2026-07-17T23:50 UTC; last green 2026-07-17T15:49 UTC)
- `pull-kubernetes-e2enode-windows` (every PR run since 2026-07-19, regardless of PR content)

### Which tests are failing?

All 12 `[sig-windows] [Feature:CPUManager] [Feature:Windows]` specs in `test/e2e_node_windows`, e.g.:

- `should not set CPU affinity on a burstable container` — fails with `burstable container must not receive exclusive CPU affinity: got 0 CPUs (host has 8)`
- `should set CPU affinity with exactly 1 CPU for a single-container pod` (and the 2/3-CPU, multi-container, init-container, and strict-cpu-reservation variants) — all `Timed out after 30.000s` waiting for affinity to appear.

`getWindowsContainerCPUAffinity` reads `ContainerStatus().Status.Resources.Windows.AffinityCpus` via CRI and gets an empty set for every container, i.e. the kubelet is no longer applying any Windows CPU group affinity (`WindowsCPUAndMemoryAffinity` / static CPU manager path via `PreCreateContainer` → `AffinityCpus`).

Because the failing specs each burn 30–77s and the suite is run as plain `go test` (10m default timeout), cmd/go kills the process (`*** Test killed: ran too long (11m0s)`), so junit/ginkgo reports are lost and the job surface just shows a timeout. Fix for that masking: kubernetes-sigs/windows-testing PR adding an explicit `--timeout`.

### Since when has it been failing?

Onset between periodic runs 2078145122851098624 (green, started 2026-07-17T15:49:43Z) and 2078266162692493312 (first red, started 2026-07-17T23:50:41Z).

### Reason for failure (regression window analysis)

kubernetes/kubernetes merges in the window (green clone ~16:04 UTC → red clone ~23:55 UTC):

- #140682 (job controller dead-code removal), #140667 (scheduler unit test), #140150 (docs), #138833 / #138831 (kube-proxy ipvs/ipset prealloc, linux-only), #140497 (coredns manifest bump)

None touch kubelet, CRI, winstats, or the Windows tests → the k/k commit window is effectively empty.

Everything else pinned/unchanged across the boundary:

- kubernetes-sigs/windows-testing: no commits since 2026-07-09
- containerd: pinned 1.7.16
- Go on the VM: 1.26.4 on both sides of the boundary
- test images (busybox 1.37.0-2, pause 3.8): pinned digests

The one moving part is the Azure VM image: `MicrosoftWindowsServer:WindowsServer:2022-datacenter-core-smalldisk-g2:latest`. The first red run's node reports `KernelVersion: 10.0.20348.5386` (July 2026 WS2022 cumulative update; July Patch Tuesday was 2026-07-14, and marketplace image rollout lands ~that week). Green runs never dump Node Info so the prior build isn't in the logs, but the timing matches the image rollout window exactly.

Working hypothesis: the WS2022 July 2026 CU (OS build 20348.5386) changes behavior under the kubelet's Windows CPU affinity path — either winstats CPU topology discovery (`GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx`) returning something the CPU manager can't use, or HCS/job-object group affinity application/reporting — so no `AffinityCpus` ever reach the container.

### Suggested next steps

1. Repro on an Azure VM with the current image; collect kubelet.log (job currently only scps `c:/Logs/*.xml`).
2. Pin the job image to the previous exact version (`az vm image list --all` for the sku, use `:<previous-version>` instead of `:latest`) to confirm/unblock CI.
3. Compare winstats topology output between 20348 builds.

title: `TestVolumeAttachLimitExceededCleanup` flakes on Windows CI with `context deadline exceeded`
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are flaking?

TestVolumeAttachLimitExceededCleanup

### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `954ac21c6c8b2bc77666373d5c4f5b68603a8e50` (2025-09-03), which introduced the test in PR #133357.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140657/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2079304403352817664

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test creates 500 pods and expects all of them to reach `PodFailed` state within a 30-second timeout. On Windows CI this is insufficient due to:

1. **Mutex contention** — `FakeRuntime.GetPod` and `FakeRuntime.GetPodStatus` are called via `fakeCache.GetNewerThan` for each pod, each acquiring the `FakeRuntime` mutex. With 500 pods this results in ~1000 serialized lock acquisitions.
2. **Status manager contention** — `SetPodStatus` is called twice per pod (once for `PodPending`, once for `PodFailed`), each acquiring the `statusManager` mutex (~1000 acquisitions).
3. **Disk I/O** — `makePodDataDirs` performs 3 `os.MkdirAll` calls per pod (1500 total mkdir operations), which is slower on Windows CI.

The 30s timeout is exceeded before all 500 pods can be processed through the `podWorkerLoop` → `SyncPod` → `rejectPod` → `SetPodStatus(PodFailed)` pipeline.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Relevant SIG(s)

title: DRA: AdminAccess consumes counters
body:
### What happened?

The DRA allocator does not exempt admin-access requests from the counter-availability check.
For a partitionable device that's already allocated, the pool's available counters have the owner's consumption subtracted, and the admin candidate then reserves the device's full consumption a second time, so the allocation fails with "insufficient counters" unless the counter set can fit the device twice.

### What did you expect to happen?

`AdminAccess` claim to get allocated without requiring or consuming counter capacity

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```

index 2c5ed97e5dd..ac876e669ba 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go
@@ -1645,6 +1645,42 @@ func TestAllocator(t *testing.T,
 				deviceAllocationResult(req0, driverA, pool1, device2, true),
 			)},
 		},
+		// A monitoring claim requests admin access to a partitionable device
+		// whose counters are fully consumed by the claim that owns it. Per the
+		// AdminAccess API ("They ignore all ordinary claims to the device with
+		// respect to access modes and any resource allocations"), the admin
+		// allocation must succeed: admin access does not consume any resources
+		// itself.
+		"admin-access-allocated-partitionable-device": {
+			features: Features{
+				AdminAccess:          true,
+				PartitionableDevices: true,
+			},
+			claimsToAllocate: func() []wrapResourceClaim {
+				c := claimWithRequest(claim0, req0, classA)
+				c.Spec.Devices.Requests[0].Exactly.AdminAccess = ptr.To(true)
+				return []wrapResourceClaim{c}
+			}(),
+			allocatedDevices: []DeviceID{
+				MakeDeviceID(driverA, pool1, device1),
+			},
+			classes: objects(class(classA, driverA)),
+			slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
+				sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverA,
+					device(device1, nil, nil).withDeviceCounterConsumption(
+						deviceCounterConsumption(counterSet1, map[string]resource.Quantity{capacity0: one}),
+					),
+				),
+				sliceWithCounterSets(slice2, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverA,
+					counterSet(counterSet1, map[string]resource.Quantity{capacity0: one}),
+				),
+			),
+			node: node(node1, region1),
+			expectResults: []any{allocationResult(
+				localNodeSelector(node1),
+				deviceAllocationResult(req0, driverA, pool1, device1, true),
+			)},
+		},
 		"separate-claims-share-device-admin-access": {
 			features: Features{
 				AdminAccess: true,

comments.body: /assign
/sig node

I looked at the counter case here and think the same exemption is needed in a few more spots, so I'm noting them in case they help scope a complete fix (the counter-check skip in #140739 covers the counter part).

Capacity: `CmpRequestOverCapacity` runs for an admin request in the ExactCount pre-check (`allocateOne`), in `AllocationMode: All` selection, and in `allocateDevice`. On an `allowMultipleAllocations` device an admin request also generates a ShareID and adds to `allocatingCapacity`, so it can briefly hold capacity that a later ordinary request in the same Allocate call then misses.

Compatibility groups: `checkAndConsumeCompatibilityGroups` also runs for an admin request, so an admin device's groups fold into the running intersection and can make a later ordinary request incompatible.

Exclusivity: a dedicated admin device is still inserted into `allocatingDevices` (the guard there is `!allowMultipleAllocations` only). The comment just above it reads "unless we do admin access", but the code doesn't check that, so a later ordinary request sees the device via `deviceInUse` and the outcome depends on claim order.

Since a persisted admin result is skipped on the next scan, the behavior also differs depending on whether the admin claim is allocated in the same pass or already stored.

Would it make sense to treat AdminAccess as accounting-neutral across the search rather than only in the counter check? Same-claim admin dedup could use separate state instead of the shared `allocatingDevices` marker. Glad to help with tests if it's useful.

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

## DRA ubuntu OOM — triage: real regression, onset 2026-07-17, prime suspect PR #140543

### What's failing
All four **ubuntu** DRA node-e2e periodics fail fast; **cos** variants stay green.

| Job | Status | Mem limit |
|---|---|---|
| `ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra` | 🔴 red since 07-17 00:59Z | 6Gi |
| `ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra` | 🔴 red since 07-17 00:59Z | 6Gi |
| `ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features` | 🔴 red since 07-17 00:59Z | 6Gi |
| `ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features` | 🔴 red since 07-17 01:00Z | 6Gi |
| `ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-cos-dra` / `-2-0-cos-dra` | ✅ **green** | 6Gi |

### Regression boundary (both ubuntu jobs, identical)
- **Last green:** [build 2077830294626373632](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra/2077830294626373632) — started 07-16 18:58Z, k8s package `v1.37.0-alpha.3.383+9714bafcc4515d`
- **First red:** [build 2077921134619136000](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra/2077921134619136000) — started 07-17 00:59Z, k8s package `v1.37.0-alpha.3.403+55f9bc555944f8`

Clean onset — 5 consecutive greens before, 100% red after. This is a **regression, not a flake**.

### Failure signature
The prow build **pod is OOM-killed** (6Gi cgroup limit) ~65s in, killing the tester subprocess:
```
F0717 01:00:56 node.go:498] failed to run ginkgo tester: signal: killed
Error: exit status 255   (junit_runner.xml: time=65.2s, failures=1)
```
The pod dies so early that **no ginkgo/node artifacts are produced** (`artifacts/` contains only `junit_runner.xml` + `metadata.json`) — the OOM happens during local setup, before the remote e2e suite gets going.

### Commit window
`started.json` on both boundary builds only pins `kubernetes/test-infra`, but the moving part is the **k8s test package** (`.383 → .403`).
- **test-infra window** (`617110e..04ddafd`): a single Windows-only PR ([#37455](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/37455)) — **ruled out**, touches only `sig-windows` configs.
- **k8s window** (`9714bafc..55f9bc55`): the only DRA-relevant change is **[PR #140543 "dra: use cdispecs-go to manage cdi instead of handcrafting it"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140543)** (merged 07-16 **20:29Z** — inside the window; commit `13ddcc0a`). It adds the `tags.cncf.io/container-device-interface/specs-go` vendored dependency and rewrites the DRA test-driver CDI generation + `dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin/metadata.go`.

### Assessment — leading suspect with one open question
PR #140543 is the **only DRA-touching change** in the window and it rewrites exactly the CDI/test-driver path these jobs exercise, so it is the prime suspect. **However, two facts mean this needs confirmation before it's called definitive:**
1. **cos-dra runs the identical k8s package and stays green** — only the ubuntu image-config differs (`pipeline-1-29`, pinned by [#134819](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134819)).
2. The OOM is on the **prow build pod** (6Gi), not the remote GCE test node — so a test-driver change running remotely can't obviously explain a *local* pod OOM unless it changes the local orchestration/log-buffering path or the ubuntu remote node now errors early and floods logs.

This split suggests the true trigger is a **PR #140543 × ubuntu-image interaction** pushing the pod over its 6Gi ceiling, rather than a pure code bug. No revert or fix-forward PR exists yet; no other tracking issue found.

### Suggested next steps
- **Confirm causality:** revert-or-rerun #140543 against an ubuntu-dra job, or re-run the first-red package on cos vs ubuntu side-by-side.
- **Unblock CI now:** bump the ubuntu-dra pod `memory` limit (currently 6Gi in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/dra-ci.yaml`) to see whether it's a hard OOM-loop or a modest overshoot — cheap mitigation while root cause is confirmed.
- cc PR author/approvers **@alaypatel07 / @pohly / @liggitt** and **@bart0sh / SIG-node** given the ubuntu-only, pod-side OOM.

@alaypatel07 can you please look?

Just out of curiosity what is the difference between this job run https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140543/pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077029398942322688 that was successful on the PR and the periodic jobs that are failing?
🤖 please answer the question from @alaypatel07 in the previous comment :)

## Re: @alaypatel07's question — why the PR run passed but the periodics OOM

Short answer: the two aren't testing the same situation, and the failure is **Ubuntu-image-specific, not a k8s-code regression**. The COS DRA periodics run the *exact same k8s binary* and stay green — which exonerates PR #140543 (my earlier automated suspicion was wrong; details below).

### 1. The successful PR run predates the onset

The run you linked ([pull-...-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077029398942322688](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140543/pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077029398942322688)) executed **2026-07-14 14:29 UTC**. The periodic OOM onset is **2026-07-17 00:59 UTC** (`started.json` timestamps). So that green presubmit ran ~2.5 days *before* the breakage started — it never saw the failing condition.

Boundary on `ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra`:
| Build | Result | Started | k8s binary (`job-version`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [2077830295435874304](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077830295435874304) | 🟢 SUCCESS | 07-16 18:58Z | `v1.37.0-alpha.3.383+9714bafcc4515d` |
| [2077921134786908160](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077921134786908160) | 🔴 FAILURE | 07-17 00:59Z | `v1.37.0-alpha.3.403+55f9bc555944f8` |

### 2. The decisive difference: Ubuntu vs COS, not the code

At the *same* boundary, holding the k8s binary fixed:

| Job | Image | 07-17 00:59Z run | k8s binary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `...-2-0-ubuntu-dra` | Ubuntu (`pipeline-1-34-amd64`, floating) | 🔴 OOM | `...403+55f9bc555944f8` |
| `...-1-7-ubuntu-dra` | Ubuntu | 🔴 OOM | `...403` |
| `...-2-0-cos-dra` | COS (`cos-125-lts`, pinned) | 🟢 SUCCESS | **`...403+55f9bc555944f8`** |
| `...-1-7-cos-dra` | COS | 🟢 SUCCESS | `...403` |

Both COS jobs ran the **identical** `v1.37.0-alpha.3.403+55f9bc555944f8` binary and passed, while both Ubuntu jobs OOM'd on it. Since PR #140543's code is in that binary and runs on COS too, **#140543 (and the k8s commit window generally) cannot be the cause.** The only variable that tracks the red/green split is the VM image family: Ubuntu floats to latest (`pipeline-1-34-amd64`, `image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"`), COS is pinned to `cos-125-lts`.

### 3. What the OOM actually is

The Prow pod (6Gi limit, identical for ubuntu and cos) is OOM-killed ~60s in, during ginkgo **tester startup, before any spec runs** — [build-log](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077921134786908160/build-log.txt):
```
Will use ginkgo flags as: --nodes=1 --label-filter="DRA && ... !Flaky" ...
F0717 01:00:53  node.go:498] failed to run ginkgo tester: signal: killed
```
The red build produces only `junit_runner.xml` + `metadata.json` (no node serial/kubelet logs) — it dies before meaningful test execution, consistent with a pod-level OOM in the orchestration step, not a test assertion.

### 4. Secondary config differences (not the OOM cause, but why presubmit ≠ periodic)

- **Binaries:** presubmit uses `--build-binaries --repo-root=.` (compiles the PR); periodic uses `--use-binaries-from-package` from `latest-fast.txt`.
- **Test scope:** presubmit label-filter has `!Slow`; the periodic does **not** — periodics additionally run `Slow`-tagged DRA tests. (Irrelevant to *this* OOM since it dies pre-spec, but it's a real difference.)
- Same 6Gi mem limit, same image-config on both.

### Conclusion

- **Not a k8s regression, not #140543** — proven by COS passing on the same binary. Please disregard the earlier bot post that named #140543 as prime suspect; the COS cross-check refutes it.
- **Root cause is the floating Ubuntu image** (`pipeline-1-34-amd64` in `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`) tipping the 6Gi Prow-pod limit over during orchestration, starting 07-17. COS is unaffected because it's pinned.
- **Suggested fix directions:** bump the memory limit on the four `*-ubuntu-dra*` periodics (COS/others use 6Gi fine, but Ubuntu now needs more), and/or pin the Ubuntu `image_family` the way COS pins `cos-125-lts` so a new base image can't silently regress the job. Owners per job config: eduard.bartosh@intel.com, patrick.ohly@intel.com.

The one check that would make this definitive: diff the Ubuntu image version between the last green (07-16 18:58Z) and first red (07-17 00:59Z) VM — but the red run OOMs before it records the image name, so a re-run with a raised limit (or an image pin) is the fastest confirmation.

## Re: @dims — "diff the Ubuntu image version between last green (07-16 18:58Z) and first red (07-17 00:59Z) VM"

I dug into the logs. **The premise can't hold the way it's framed — there is no "first red VM" to diff against, because the red builds die in the Prow pod *before any GCE VM is created or any Ubuntu image is even selected.*** That itself is the key finding, and it rules the Ubuntu image out as the trigger.

### What the boundary builds actually show
Same job, `ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra`:

| | Build | Result | Reached image-list? | Reached "Creating instance"? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Last green** 07-16 18:58Z | [2077830295435874304](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077830295435874304) | SUCCESS | ✅ yes | ✅ yes |
| **First red** 07-17 00:59Z | [2077921134786908160](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra/2077921134786908160) | FAILURE | ❌ **no** | ❌ **no** |

The **entire** red `build-log.txt` is 3,870 bytes and ends at:
```
I0717 00:59:56  node.go:490  Running command ".../e2e_node.test" [ "remote" ... ]
I0717 00:59:56  run_remote_suite.go:87  Will use ginkgo flags as: --nodes=1 ...
F0717 01:00:53  node.go:498  failed to run ginkgo tester: signal: killed
Error: exit status 255
```
It never lists images, never picks one, never calls `Creating instance`. The `signal: killed` is the Prow pod's `e2e_node.test`/ginkgo child being **OOM-killed on the build host** (matches the cluster's "Job pod was OOM killed" banner). All four ubuntu-DRA reds — both containerd 2.0 and 1.7, both plain and alpha-beta — have the **identical 3.8 KB log and identical `signal: killed`** verdict. None reach VM creation.

### The image the *green* VMs booted (the only side that has a VM)
- `...-2-0-ubuntu-dra` and `...-alpha-beta`: `ubuntu-gke-2404-1-34-amd64-v20260714`
- `...-1-7-ubuntu-dra`: `ubuntu-gke-2204-1-29-v20260714`

The green build's image listing shows `v20260714` was already the newest image in the pinned family (`pipeline-1-34-amd64`, project `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`) **and it stayed newest through the red runs** — no new Ubuntu image published in the 07-16→07-17 window. So even if the reds had reached VM creation, they'd have selected the **same `v20260714` image the greens passed on.**

### The image config didn't move either
`jobs/e2e_node/containerd/containerd-release-2.1/image-config-ubuntu.yaml` (`image_family: pipeline-1-34-amd64`) was untouched — `git log 617110e..04ddafd -- jobs/e2e_node/` (the exact test-infra SHAs from the two builds' `started.json`) returns **zero commits**.

### What *did* change across the boundary
The only moving part is the **k8s CI package** the pod downloads and runs locally:
- green `v1.37.0-alpha.3.383+9714bafcc4515d` → first red `v1.37.0-alpha.3.403+55f9bc555944f8`

The OOM is in the host-side `e2e_node.test` binary during ginkgo bootstrap, which is consistent with the earlier triage pointing at a k8s-side change in that package window (prime suspect PR [#140543](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140543)), **not** an Ubuntu image bump.

### Bottom line
- **Ubuntu image is not the culprit** — greens and (would-be) reds resolve to the same `v20260714`; no image or image-config change occurred in the window.
- The regression is the **host-side e2e_node.test process getting OOM-killed before VM provisioning**, tied to the k8s CI-package delta (`.383 → .403`), which lines up with the previously-identified suspect PR. The Ubuntu-image diff is a dead end by construction: the red side never got far enough to have a VM.

🤖 you took 3 turns at diagnosing this problem so far and we are not anywhere near a solution. review again using multiple agents looking at various aspects.

## DRA ubuntu OOM (#140701) — multi-agent re-review: root cause is a **1 Gi Prow-pod memory limit** on the host runner, not a k8s code regression

I re-ran this with parallel agents on four independent angles (OOM mechanism, job/pod config, ubuntu image diff, PR #140543). They converge, and I verified the crux directly against the live pods. **New facts that correct the earlier triage in this thread:**

### 1. The pod memory limit is **1 Gi**, and it was *reduced* from 6 Gi on 2026-06-22
The earlier analysis assumed 6 Gi (that's what a **stale** test-infra checkout showed). The **actually-deployed** pods run at **1 Gi**. From the real `podinfo.json`:

| Build | Job | `test` container limit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2077830295435874304` (07-16 18:58Z, last green) | 2.0-ubuntu-dra | **1Gi** | ✅ |
| `2077921134786908160` (07-17 00:59Z, first red) | 2.0-ubuntu-dra | **1Gi** | ❌ OOMKilled |
| `2077921134874988544` (07-17 00:59Z) | 2.0-**cos**-dra | **1Gi** | ✅ |

`origin/master` `dra-ci.yaml` confirms `memory: 1Gi` for these node-e2e jobs. The reduction landed in [`0a5cb1dd85`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/commit/0a5cb1dd85) + [`ed5ed26b86`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/commit/ed5ed26b86) — *"DRA: reduce resource requirements for E2E node jobs"* (I & II), Patrick Ohly, 2026-06-22. **1 Gi is the ceiling being hit.**

### 2. What OOMs, and where — the *host-side* runner, before any VM exists
No `go build` happens (periodics download prebuilt binaries via `--use-binaries-from-package`). The killed process is the **`e2e_node.test remote` orchestrator on the Prow pod itself** (PID 45/53). From the red `podinfo.json`: `"reason":"OOMKilled"`. The entire red `build-log.txt` is 17 lines and dies ~58s after start, *before instance creation*:
```
run_remote_suite.go:87] Will use ginkgo flags as: --nodes=1 --label-filter="DRA && ..."
F node.go:498] failed to run ginkgo tester: signal: killed
```
No `Creating instance`, no per-node `tmp-node-e2e-*/` artifacts → **the VM was never provisioned.** The green build sails past this same line to `Creating instance` → `Ran 38 of 1220 Specs … SUCCESS`.

### 3. The COS cross-check exonerates the k8s code (and PR #140543)
At the **same** timestamp, **same 1 Gi limit**, **same k8s test package** `v1.37.0-alpha.3.403+55f9bc555944f8`, `ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-**cos**-dra` reaches `Creating instance {image:cos-125-...}` and passes (`SUCCESS! 38 Passed`). Since PR #140543's code ships in that same package and runs fine on COS, **#140543 is not the cause** — the earlier "prime suspect #140543" call is refuted. The k8s payload is a red herring for the OOM.

### 4. The only differentiator is the ubuntu image-config path
Diffing the two jobs' args, **the sole difference** is `--image-config-file=…/image-config-ubuntu.yaml` (ubuntu, family `pipeline-1-34-amd64`, regex `.*[^-cgroupsv1]$`) vs the COS config. Everything else — 1 Gi limit, `--parallelism=1`, `e2-standard-2`, label filter, timeout — is identical. So the ~1 Gi is exceeded specifically in the **ubuntu image-resolution / ginkgo-bootstrap** phase the host runner performs before instance creation. The ubuntu image family pin itself has **not** changed since 2026-06-18; the last green resolved `ubuntu-gke-2404-1-34-amd64-v20260714`, and the family auto-rolls to the newest daily image (COS is pinned to `cos-125-lts`).

### Why it held until 07-16 then broke 07-17
1 Gi was live and *passing* on 07-16, so the June memory cut is the underlying fragility, not the trigger. A tipping factor on 07-17 pushed the ubuntu-only host path over 1 Gi — most likely the test-package growth across `.383→.403` **and/or** a newer image accreting in the `pipeline-1-34-amd64` family (the red run dies before logging its image, so it can't be pinned from CI). Either way the ubuntu variant sits right at the 1 Gi edge that COS clears comfortably.

### Recommended fix (no PR exists yet)
Raise the `memory` limit/request back up for the four `*-ubuntu-dra*` node-e2e periodics in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-node/dra-ci.yaml` (COS is fine at 1 Gi; ubuntu needs more headroom) — i.e. partially revert the 06-22 reduction for the ubuntu variants. cc @pohly (author of the resource-reduction commits) @alaypatel07. title: CPUManager distribute-cpus-across-cores relies on CPU numbering order instead of topology
body:
## What happened?

The `distribute-cpus-across-cores` CPU manager policy option (KEP-4176, alpha since v1.31) does not correctly spread CPUs across physical cores on systems where sibling thread CPU IDs are contiguous (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

The spread algorithm in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` sorts CPUs numerically within each socket:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    for _, socket := range a.sortAvailableSockets() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInSockets(socket).UnsortedList()
        sort.Ints(cpus)
        result = append(result, cpus...)
    }
    return result
}
```

This assumes that numerically-sorted CPU IDs naturally interleave across physical cores. That assumption holds on systems where the BIOS/firmware enumerates all first threads before second threads (e.g., core 0 thread 0 = CPU 0, core 1 thread 0 = CPU 1, ..., core 0 thread 1 = CPU 8, core 1 thread 1 = CPU 9), but fails when sibling threads have contiguous IDs (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3).

With contiguous siblings, `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` produces the same CPU order as `sortAvailableCPUsPacked()`, and the spreading has no effect — both allocate sibling threads together.

## How to reproduce

On any system with contiguous sibling CPU IDs (common in VMs/QEMU, and some bare-metal configurations):

```
$ lscpu | grep Thread
Thread(s) per core:  2

$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/topology/thread_siblings_list
0-1
$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/topology/thread_siblings_list
2-3
```

Enable the CPU manager with `distribute-cpus-across-cores`:
```
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--feature-gates=CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true
--cpu-manager-policy-options=distribute-cpus-across-cores=true
```

Create a Guaranteed pod requesting 4 CPUs. The allocated cpuset will be contiguous (e.g., `1-4`), hitting only 2-3 physical cores instead of spreading across 4 separate cores.

The kubelet logs confirm the option is active:
```
"created with configuration" options={"DistributeCPUsAcrossCores":true,...} cpuGroupSize=2
```

## Expected behavior

Requesting 4 CPUs on a system with 8 cores × 2 threads should allocate 1 thread from each of 4 different physical cores (e.g., CPUs 0, 2, 4, 6), regardless of whether sibling IDs are contiguous or non-contiguous.

## Root cause

The algorithm uses `sort.Ints()` on CPU IDs as a proxy for topology-aware spreading. It should instead use the core topology information already available in `cpuAccumulator.details` to explicitly round-robin across cores:

```go
func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int {
    var result []int
    coresCPUs := make(map[int][]int)
    maxThreads := 0
    for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
        cpus := a.details.CPUsInCores(core).SortedList()
        coresCPUs[core] = cpus
        if len(cpus) > maxThreads {
            maxThreads = len(cpus)
        }
    }
    // Round-robin: pick thread 0 from all cores, then thread 1, etc.
    for t := 0; t < maxThreads; t++ {
        for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() {
            if t < len(coresCPUs[core]) {
                result = append(result, coresCPUs[core][t])
            }
        }
    }
    return result
}
```

This approach works regardless of CPU numbering because it explicitly iterates cores and picks one thread per core before doubling up.

## Additional context

- The KEP-4176 example topology assumes non-contiguous siblings (CPUs 0 and 6 as siblings), which is common on many server BIOSes that enumerate all thread-0 CPUs before thread-1 CPUs, but is not guaranteed.
- QEMU/KVM always produces contiguous sibling IDs (thread ID in lowest APIC bits), making this feature untestable in virtual environments.
- The Linux kernel topology documentation notes the "alternative enumeration" (non-contiguous siblings) depends on BIOS MADT ordering and explicitly states "we do not trust BIOSes to enumerate packages in a consistent way."
- Tested on Kubernetes v1.35.6 with `DistributeCPUsAcrossCores: true` confirmed in kubelet logs.

/kind bug

Hi @ffromani, 

While reading the Design Details section of the KEP, I had one question about the proposed CPU ordering algorithm.

From the example in the KEP, the new ordering changes from:

`socket → core → cpu`

to effectively:

`socket → cpu`

using the example topology where the resulting CPU order becomes:

`0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11`

This works because, in that example, selecting CPUs in numerical order also happens to select one logical CPU from each physical core first.

My question is: does the implementation rely on this logical CPU numbering, or does it explicitly use the CPU topology (socket/core/thread relationships) reported by the Kernel to guarantee spreading across physical cores regardless of how logical CPUs are numbered?

For example, on some systems, sibling threads may be numbered differently `(e.g. "0/1" instead of "0/15" or "0/16")`, so I wanted to understand whether the example in the KEP is purely illustrative, while the implementation remains topology-aware for all supported architectures.

For reference, this is the KEP I'm referring to:

[KEP-4176: New CPUManager Static Policy which spread hyperthreads across physical CPUs to better utilize CPU Cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4176-cpumanager-spread-cpus-preferred-policy)

Thanks! I'm looking forward to working on this.

Hi @OchukoWH, thanks for picking this up!

To answer your question directly: the current implementation relies on logical CPU numbering, not topology. The spread sort in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` does `sort.Ints()` on all CPU IDs within a socket and picks from the front — it doesn't use the core topology information available in `cpuAccumulator.details`.

We confirmed this by testing on a system with contiguous sibling numbering (core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3 etc). With `DistributeCPUsAcrossCores: true` confirmed active in kubelet logs, requesting 4 CPUs on 8 cores × 2 threads allocated cpuset `1-4` — hitting only 2-3 physical cores instead of spreading across 4.

The KEP example topology happens to have non-contiguous siblings (CPUs 0 and 6 sharing a core), which is common on server BIOSes that enumerate all thread-0 CPUs before thread-1 CPUs. But this MADT/BIOS enumeration order is not guaranteed — VMs (QEMU/KVM), some bare-metal configs, and potentially non-x86 architectures use contiguous sibling IDs.

The fix should replace the numeric sort with explicit topology-aware round-robin using `CPUsInCores()`, which is already available in the accumulator. Happy to help review if you'd like to discuss the approach.

Thanks @lyarwood  for the clarification.
I was already thinking of implementing it based on the topology information, but I wanted to clarify the behavior because of what I saw in the KEP.

I'll work on the implementation and let you know once it's ready for review.
Thanks again for the explanation!

> To answer your question directly: the current implementation relies on logical CPU numbering, not topology. The spread sort in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` does `sort.Ints()` on all CPU IDs within a socket and picks from the front — it doesn't use the core topology information available in `cpuAccumulator.details`.

Correct, and there likely are other instances of the same approach - naively sorting IDs using `sort.Ints()` which we should check and fix, in the same PR or in followups (I'd prefer in a single PR)

title: Kubelet allocates system-reserved CPU to pod when cpu-topology is hybrid
body:
### What happened?

Following CPU topology (hybrid i.e. cores with id `0-28` are hyper-threaded and `32-43` are single-threaded) was given.
```
Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700
CPU(s):                28
On-line CPU(s) list:   0-27
Core(s) per socket:    20
Socket(s):             1
NUMA node(s):          1
```

For pod with 2 guaranteed CPUs, kubelet allocated `0-1` cpuset, despite `0` was explicitly reserved for system purposes. Kubelet was launched with following flags: `--kubelet-flags="--cpu-manager-policy=static --reserved-cpus=0`. 

Here are some kubelet logs:
```
I0710 16:32:08.192397  353056 policy_static.go:185] "Reserved CPUs not available for exclusive assignment" reservedSize=1 reserved="0" reservedPhysicalCPUs="0-1"
...
I0710 16:32:45.032352  353056 policy_static.go:556] "Allocate start" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1"
I0710 16:32:45.032419  353056 policy_static.go:675] "AllocateCPUs" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1" numCPUs=2 socket=null
I0710 16:32:45.035206  353056 policy_static.go:708] "AllocateCPUs" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1" result="0-1 aligned=<uncore:true>"
I0710 16:32:45.037033  353056 policy_static.go:621] "Allocate end" pod="default/test-7fb87c954c-n8gtr" podUID="35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb" containerName="testcnt1"
```

Then, kubelet was **restarted**, but it can't boot again due to invalid state:
```
I0713 16:37:04.270175  593834 state_mem.go:143] "Updated default CPUSet" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint.CPUManager state memory" cpuSet="2-27"
I0713 16:37:04.270195  593834 state_mem.go:161] "Updated CPUSet assignments" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint.CPUManager state memory" assignments="{\"35863126-0027-47ff-90f9-8684692a19bb\":{\"testcnt1\":\"0-1\"}}"
I0713 15:37:04.270215  593834 state_checkpoint.go:182] "restored state from checkpoint" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint"
I0713 16:37:04.270227  593834 state_checkpoint.go:183] "defaultCPUSet" logger="CPUManager state checkpoint" defaultCpuSet="2-27"
E0713 16:37:04.270257  593834 policy_static.go:303] "invalid state, please drain node and remove policy state file" err="not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
E0713 16:37:04.270266  593834 cpu_manager.go:263] "Policy start error" err="not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
E0713 16:37:04.270277  593834 kubelet.go:1837] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="start cpu manager error: not all reserved cpus: \"0\" are present in defaultCpuSet: \"2-27\""
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet allocates 2 CPUs that do not interfere with reserved CPUs. After restart kubelet starts smoothly.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start local cluster using `hack/local-up-cluster.sh` script with proper flags set.
```console
CPUMANAGER_POLICY="static" KUBELET_FLAGS="--reserved-cpus=0" hack/local-up-cluster.sh
```
2. Deploy the pod with guaranteed CPU resources
```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: '2'
    memory: "2Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: '2'
    memory: "2Gi"
```
3. Kill the cluster and try to start it again.

### Anything else we need to know?

this is a byproduct of kubelet assuming all the cores are identical and symmetrical, and it's one of the many ways this bubbles up.
We know since a long time the kubelet hw model is very, very simple (simplistic, it may be argued). The real unknowns which affects priority and severity are:
1. how to fix incrementally?
2. how often does this issue manifest in practice

nevertheless, the bug is real. Starting with `backlog` cautiously.

what an incremental fix would look like. The hybrid CPU topology case does
highlight a limitation in the kubelet’s simplified hardware model, so it

environments.

</details>
/triage accepted

Update: it turns out [there _are_ jobs that are supposed to be running these tests](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/65f8776e04fed715922c6c4c32f5460a4840329e/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-network/sig-network-gce.yaml#L339-L418), but the results don't show up in the testgrid, so... I guess that means they aren't getting run? But I don't understand why...
@bowei can i work around this, happy to share thoughts

I dug into the current state of these jobs and the tests appear to be running and reporting fine:

- Four periodics focus on `[Feature:PerformanceDNS]` every 6 hours: `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-coredns-performance`, `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-kubedns-performance`, and their `-nodecache` variants ([config](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-network/sig-network-gce.yaml)).
- The [latest coredns-performance run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-coredns-performance/2078108371096965120) (2026-07-17) passed, and its junit shows the spec `[sig-network] [Feature:PerformanceDNS] Should answer DNS query for maximum number of services per cluster [Serial]` actually executed (764s), so the focus regex is matching, not passing trivially.
- The results do show up on TestGrid: [sig-network-gce](https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-network-gce) has all four tabs green, and the `gce-coredns-performance` tab has the test row populated continuously back through at least 2026-07-02 (58 passes, 2 failures around July 13-14 in the last 60 columns).

So the tests don't seem to need reinstating. The open question is rather why the coverage tool in kubernetes/test-infra#37410 reported them as never run: these periodics carry the `prow.k8s.io/refs.org: kubernetes` / `prow.k8s.io/refs.repo: kubernetes` labels, so as far as I can tell they should pass its job filter. That part is probably worth following up on that PR instead.

> these periodics carry the `prow.k8s.io/refs.org: kubernetes` / `prow.k8s.io/refs.repo: kubernetes` labels, so as far as I can tell they should pass its job filter

Ah! But they didn't last week. That got fixed in https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37310. So it seems like that was the problem, and the tests should get picked up in the next run of the tool.

Thanks for the analysis @nicknikolakakis
