comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon

I'd like to investigate this flaky test. I'll start by reproducing the failure, reviewing device_plugin_failures_pod_status_test.go, and tracing how the device health status propagates from the device plugin to the pod status to determine whether the issue is in the implementation or the test itself
@sohankunkerkar we have release v1.37.0-alpha.3 scheduled for today, do you think it is a blocker for the release?
/assign

I don't think this is a release blocker. I'm seeing about a 5% flake rate (1 out of the last 20 runs), caused by a pre-existing, non-blocking channel send in the device manager that can drop health updates under CI load. This doesn't appear to be a 1.37 regression, but I'll defer to @harche on this one.

I tracked this down. It is a kubelet bug in the device manager, not a problem in the test itself.

When a device plugin reports a health change, [`genericDeviceUpdateCallback`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L293-L346) resolves the affected pod via [`getPodAndContainerForDevice`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/pod_devices.go#L184-L198), which matches on the device ID alone across all pods and all resources. Device IDs are only unique per resource, and every spec in [`device_plugin_failures_pod_status_test.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/test/e2e_node/device_plugin_failures_pod_status_test.go#L131) registers its device as `testdevice` under a randomized resource name. The CI jobs run several parallel ginkgo processes against one kubelet, so when two of these specs run close together the lookup can land on the other spec's pod, and Go map iteration order makes it a coin flip. The notification then syncs the wrong pod, and the pod that actually owns the unhealthy device only picks up the new status at the next periodic sync, up to a minute later, which loses the race against the test's 60 second timeout.

The kubelet log from failing run [`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd/2074205743732494336`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd/2074205743732494336) shows it directly: the device for resource `test.device/device-plugin-failures-3083` goes unhealthy at 19:47:40 (`Processed device updates ... healthyCount=0`), but the forwarded sync event carries the pod UID of the previous spec's pod from namespace `device-plugin-failures-5477`. The correct pod got its Unhealthy patch at 19:48:43 via the periodic sync, 2.4 seconds after the test gave up.

I reproduced it on a GCE Ubuntu 24.04 VM with containerd by running just the two `Device Plugin Failures Pod Status` specs concurrently against a stock kubelet:

```
ginkgo -nodes=2 -focus="Device Plugin Failures Pod Status" e2e_node.test -- \
  --kubelet-config-file=test/e2e_node/jenkins/default-kubelet-config.yaml \
  --container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock \
  --prepull-images=false --node-name $(hostname) --report-dir=/tmp/results
```

It failed on the first iteration with the exact signature above and the same wrong pod UID routing in the kubelet log. With the lookup scoped by resource name the same loop passed 10 consecutive iterations, and every health flip was routed to the pod in the matching namespace. Fix is up in #140323.

Worth noting this can affect real workloads too, since two device plugins that happen to use the same device ID (for example both naming a device `gpu0`) would misroute health notifications the same way. The status still corrects itself on the next periodic sync, so the impact is a delayed pod status update.

On the release question: this is a latent bug in the Beta ResourceHealthStatus feature rather than a new regression in the alpha.3 payload (nothing in the device manager or these tests changed when the flaking started), so I do not consider it a release blocker.

title: Evaluate node stability risks and support hybrid workload Memory QoS in KEP 2570
body:
/sig node
/kind feature

### Problem: KEP-2570 `memory.min` Introduces Node Stability Risks & Bin-Packing Regressions

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

#### 1. The `memory.min` Bin-Packing Problem

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

#### 2. Behavioral Shifts and Starvation

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

#### 3. Node-Level Enforcement Breaks Mixed Workloads

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads. Administrators cannot safely run a latency-sensitive database (requiring strict `memory.min` protection) alongside an elastic web application on the exact same machine. Applying `memory.high` globally means a large workload might be aggressively throttled well before it consumes its physical free capacity. This node-level rigidity defeats the purpose of high-density Kubernetes colocation.

---

### Proposed Solution: The Tiered Protection Architecture

We propose modifying the Memory QoS architecture to establish `memory.low` as the global default baseline, while allowing opt-in escalation for hard protections via node-level flags or per-pod APIs (DRA).

#### 1. The Baseline: Map All Requests to `memory.low` (Soft Protection)

Instead of forcing Guaranteed pods to `memory.min`, the Kubelet should map all pod memory requests (Guaranteed and Burstable) to `memory.low` by default.

* **Maximum Elasticity & Bin-Packing:** This protects memory during normal operations, but during a catastrophic node-level emergency, the kernel retains the flexibility to reclaim idle cache rather than hitting a hard boundary that triggers artificial OOM kills.
* **Industry Validation:** This matches the `fbtax2` architecture utilized at scale by Meta, which explicitly favors `memory.low` because it is "work-conserving" and safely handles system memory overcommit without thrashing.
* **CRI Visibility:** Mapping to `memory.low` successfully populates the CRI payload, satisfying local node agents instantly without API server queries.

**Action Item:** Expand `memoryReservationPolicy` to include a `SoftReservation` mode (or update the default behavior of `TieredReservation`) where all requests are mapped to `memory.low`.

#### 2. Node-Level Hard Protection (Explicit Opt-In)

For specialized, dedicated hardware pools (e.g., dedicated database nodes), administrators should be able to explicitly toggle `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation` to universally map Guaranteed workloads to `memory.min`.

* **Action Item:** Ensure that even when `memory.min` is enforced, the Kubelet redundantly populates `memory.low` with the same value in the CRI payload so node daemons retain a uniform schema regardless of the enforcement mechanism.

#### 3. Long-Term Vision: Per-Pod Memory QoS via DRA

Because Kubelet-level enforcement is too blunt for hybrid clusters, fine-grained hard memory locks (`memory.min`) and custom proactive throttling thresholds (`memory.high`) should be managed via **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)**.

* **Industry Validation:** Organizations like Alibaba Cloud already recognize the upstream limits of KEP-2570, resorting to external Koordinator agents and custom annotations to inject per-pod Memory QoS policies.
* **Action Item:** Transition application cgroup routing out of Kubelet defaults. The Kubelet should focus on protecting the node (`kube-reserved`), while users request strict memory isolation via DRA `ResourceClaims` that instruct the container runtime to append `memory.min` or `memory.high` on a per-pod basis.

---

### Discussion Request for SIG-Node (July 7, 2026)

We would love to get SIG-Node's feedback on:

1. Shifting the baseline cgroups v2 mapping strategy from `memory.min` to `memory.low` for Guaranteed & Burstable workloads to prevent aggressive OOM starvation.
2. The viability of expanding `memoryReservationPolicy` to give administrators explicit `SoftReservation` / `HardReservation` choices in the upcoming beta cycles.
3. The long-term roadmap for offloading specialized, per-pod Memory QoS configurations (like hard locking and custom throttling factors) to Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

title: kubelet HTTP probe logs probe `httpHeaders` (Authorization / Cookie / API keys) at -v=4
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:160-173
case p.HTTPGet != nil:
    req, err := httpprobe.NewRequestForHTTPGetAction(p.HTTPGet, &container, status.PodIP, "probe")
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(4).Info("HTTP-Probe failed to create request", "error", err)
        return probe.Unknown, "", err
    }
    if loggerV4 := logger.V(4); logger.Enabled() {
        port := req.URL.Port()
        host := req.URL.Hostname()
        path := req.URL.Path
        scheme := req.URL.Scheme
        headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders              // <-- raw PodSpec headers
        loggerV4.Info("HTTP-Probe", "scheme", scheme, "host", host, "port", port,
            "path", path, "timeout", timeout, "headers", headers, "probeType", probeType)  // <-- sink
    }
    return pb.http.Probe(req, timeout)
```

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet/prober`, sets `-v=4`, builds an HTTP liveness probe with `Authorization: Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token`, calls the real `(*prober).runProbe`, and the fake HTTP prober returns `Success` — proving the leak happens **before** the request executes and does not require probe failure. Cleans up after itself; no cluster needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/prober/zz_poc_probe_header_leak_test.go"
SECRET="Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package prober

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"net/http"
	"testing"
	"time"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
	kubecontainer "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/container"
	"k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/probe"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSuccessHTTPProber struct{}

func (pocSuccessHTTPProber) Probe(_ *http.Request, _ time.Duration) (probe.Result, string, error) {
	return probe.Success, "ok", nil // probe SUCCEEDS — leak is pre-request, not failure-only
}

func TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	if flag.CommandLine.Lookup("v") == nil {
		klog.InitFlags(nil)
	}
	if err := flag.Set("v", "4"); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	pb := &prober{http: pocSuccessHTTPProber{}}
	_, _, err := pb.runProbe(
		context.Background(),
		liveness,
		&v1.Probe{ProbeHandler: v1.ProbeHandler{HTTPGet: &v1.HTTPGetAction{
			Path: "/healthz",
			Port: intstr.FromInt32(8080),
			HTTPHeaders: []v1.HTTPHeader{
				{Name: "Authorization", Value: "Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"},
			},
		}}},
		&v1.Pod{},
		v1.PodStatus{PodIP: "127.0.0.1"},
		v1.Container{Name: "app"},
		kubecontainer.ContainerID{Type: "test", ID: "container"},
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	klog.Flush()
}
GOEOF
OUT="$( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet/prober -run TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 )"
printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep 'HTTP-Probe' || true
if printf '%s\n' "$OUT" | grep -F "$SECRET"; then
  echo "VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs"
else
  echo "NOT VULNERABLE: secret header not observed in logs" >&2; exit 1
fi
```

Expected: a `prober.go` `HTTP-Probe` log line containing the secret in the `headers` field, followed by the `VULNERABLE` confirmation:

```text
I0702 11:32:34.631974 2674209 prober.go:173] "HTTP-Probe" scheme="http" host="127.0.0.1" port="8080" path="/healthz" timeout="0s" headers=[{"name":"Authorization","value":"Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"}] probeType="Liveness"
VULNERABLE: kubelet HTTP probe Authorization header leaked into verbose logs
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of probe-configured credentials to kubelet verbose logs. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_prober_http_probe_header_log_leak`.
- It is **distinct** from the recorded `kubelet_http_probe_header_log_leak` (sink `pkg/probe/http/http.go:119`, failure-only). This report's sink is `pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:173` (pre-request), so successful probes leak too. Both are already separately recorded in the knowledge base.
- Affects HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probes; requires kubelet `-v>=4`. `TCP`/`Exec`/`GRPC` probes do not carry `httpHeaders` at this sink.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ git describe --tags
v1.37.0-alpha.2-121-ga0b6070d29d   # current master; reproducer verified at a0b6070d29d
```

</details>

Linux 5.15.0-139-generic # probe test is OS-independent
```

title: Excessive "Label not found" V(4) logs for optional container annotations flood kubelet logs and cause rapid disk space consumption
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs with `--v=4` (a common debug level), the log is continuously flooded with lines like:

```plaintext
I0627 08:10:30.787761    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 08:10:30.787766    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 08:10:30.787771    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
...
I0627 09:00:34.694549    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 09:00:34.695552    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 09:00:34.695745    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
```

In a kubemark cluster, this was observed to run continuously and consume disk space rapidly, with approximately 220 pods (2 containers per pod) running on each node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Logging "Label not found" for optional annotations at V(4) might be too verbose, since these labels are typically absent for many containers. It would be better to raise the log level so it doesn't appear during typical debug verbosity, or perhaps consider removing the line entirely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run kubelet with --v=4.
2. Schedule a high density of pods on the node (e.g., ~200 pods), whose containers have no preStop handler, no ports, and whose pod has no deletionGracePeriodSeconds (i.e. almost every pod).
3. Observe the three "Label not found" lines being emitted continuously during pod syncs, consuming disk space rapidly.

### Anything else we need to know?

> Commit [ab839c93](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/ab839c93ff85072b2cc289a5826f61ff409b937a)

In `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/labels.go`, the "Label not found" logs are emitted by `getInt64PointerFromLabel` and `getJSONObjectFromLabel` whenever a label is absent.

These labels are only written conditionally in `newContainerAnnotations`:

`podDeletionGracePeriodLabel` — only if `pod.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds != nil`
`containerPreStopHandlerLabel` — only if `container.Lifecycle.PreStop != nil`
`containerPortsLabel` — only if `len(container.Ports) > 0`
Since these conditions are not met for most containers, the labels are expected to be missing. However, `getContainerInfoFromAnnotations` is called on every status lookup, triggering the log on the normal path.

This test was just changed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139920/changes#diff-ab13d9c7ec3ceec3024ca3eaea2d912d3236e81872d81d49212faf34defbdd37

Please revert or fix the flaky test ASAP.

/cc @dom4ha
/assign @brejman
🤖 let's dig deep into https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?pr=1&text=TestPodGroupScheduling#b7e5d9678c5463ad2d1d and figure out why.
Looks like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140111 is open to try to address this

## Root cause: flaky ordering assertion introduced by #139920 (the same PR liggitt already flagged)

I dug into the triage cluster [`b7e5d9678c5463ad2d1d`](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?pr=1&text=TestPodGroupScheduling#b7e5d9678c5463ad2d1d) and confirmed the flake is a **test-harness race**, not a scheduler regression. Here's the evidence.

### What's failing
Cluster spans 5 jobs (arm64 has the most hits: `ci-kubernetes-integration-arm64-master[14]`, plus `-master`, `-master-s390x`, `-fieldsv1string`, and the `pull-kubernetes-integration` presubmit). Every failure carries the same signature:

```
podgroup_test.go:652: step 3 (Create 5 pods belonging to the gang) failed:
    failed to ensure queueing order of pod mut-p5: context deadline exceeded
```

It hits `TestPodGroupScheduling/gang_pods_are_unschedulable_due_to_lack_of_space,_then_scheduled_when_minCount_is_decreased`.

### Regression boundary (confirmed by SHA)
- Oldest red arm64 build `2071621898961162240` (2026-06-29) → `repo-commit` **`2533a7c0234bdbf55120e424d5840bfc169c09ac`**
- That is exactly the merge commit of **[#139920 "Validate matching priorities when scheduling pod groups"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139920)** (merged 2026-06-29 14:38 UTC, author @brejman, squash commit `bafd5e85734`).

The flake onset (6/29, per liggitt's graph) lines up precisely with this merge. This is the [same PR liggitt already identified](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139920/changes) — my independent bisection corroborates it.

### The actual bug (why it flakes)
#139920 added the `CreatePodsInOrder` helper in `stepsframework.go`, which after creating each pod polls for the scheduler to have "observed" it:

```go
err := wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(ctx, 100*time.Millisecond, 10*time.Second, ...) {
    _, ok := testCtx.Scheduler.SchedulingQueue.GetPod(p.Name, p.Namespace, p.Spec.SchedulingGroup)
    if ok { return true, nil }
    // pod may have gotten queued and scheduled between the polls
    return podScheduledFn(ctx)   // <-- requires pod.Spec.NodeName != ""
}
```

The condition is unsatisfiable for `mut-p5` in this specific test:
1. `GetPod` only finds a pod while it sits in the active/backoff/unschedulable queues (`getEntityFromAnyQueue`, `scheduling_queue.go:1549`). Once the scheduler pops the pod, attempts it, and moves it out, a 100 ms poll can miss the queued window entirely.
2. The fallback `PodScheduled` (`test/integration/util/util.go:669`) only returns true when `pod.Spec.NodeName != ""` — i.e. **actually bound to a node**. But this test case is deliberately over-capacity (5 pods × 1 CPU vs a 4-CPU node, `minCount=5`), so `mut-p5` is *never* scheduled by design.

So when the scheduler races ahead of the poller, neither branch ever becomes true and the helper dead-ends into `context deadline exceeded`. It's inherently timing-dependent, which is why it flakes rather than fails deterministically (and why arm64/s390x, being slower, hit it hardest).

### Fix already in flight
**[#140111 "flake: observe scheduling attempts in ordered pod creation"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140111)** (open, @brejman) directly addresses this. It replaces the `NodeName`-based fallback with a `podSchedulingAttempted` check that treats a `PodScheduled` condition of **either `True` or `False`** as proof the scheduler observed the pod — which is exactly the missing case for a permanently-unschedulable gang pod. Author reports 20× stress runs clean. This is the correct fix (not the assignment-only check the current code relies on).

### Recommendation
- **Fast-track / LGTM [#140111](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140111)** — it's the targeted fix and is already validated under stress. This is the path liggitt asked for ("revert or fix ASAP").
- No scheduler behavior change is needed; production `GenericWorkload`/`TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling` code paths are not implicated — the defect is entirely in the integration test's ordering helper.

cc @brejman @dom4ha — the boundary SHA (`2533a7c`) and the queue/poll race both confirm #140111 is the right remedy for #140149.

title: kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext.

At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393
manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header)
if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 {
    for k, v := range kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader {
        for i := range v {
            manifestURLHeader.Add(k, v[i])          // values copied into a plain http.Header
        }
    }
}
...
if kubeCfg.StaticPodURL != "" {
    logger.Info("Adding pod URL with HTTP header", "URL", kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, "header", manifestURLHeader)  // <-- sink
    config.NewSourceURL(logger, kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, manifestURLHeader, ...)
}
```

The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)

### What did you expect to happen?

`makePodSourceConfig` should not log the header values. The `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the `server.go:287-290` config-mask both express the intent that `StaticPodURLHeader` is secret; this code path bypasses both by logging a runtime copy. The sink should mask/drop the `header` field (e.g. log only that headers are present, or redact like the config-dump path does). Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet` that calls the real `makePodSourceConfig` with a custom `logr` sink capturing klog output, sets `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret`, and asserts the secret appears in the captured logs. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/zz_poc_staticpodheader_logleak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package kubelet

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-logr/logr"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
	kubeletutil "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/util"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSink struct{ buf *bytes.Buffer }

func (s *pocSink) Init(logr.RuntimeInfo)          {}
func (s *pocSink) Enabled(int) bool               { return true }
func (s *pocSink) Info(_ int, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) Error(err error, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg, err}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) WithValues(kv ...interface{}) logr.LogSink { return s }
func (s *pocSink) WithName(string) logr.LogSink              { return s }

func TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	ctx := klog.NewContext(context.Background(), logr.New(&pocSink{buf: &logs}))

	const secret = "Bearer static-pod-url-secret"
	kubeCfg := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
		HTTPCheckFrequency:  metav1.Duration{Duration: time.Hour},
	}
	deps := &Dependencies{PodStartupLatencyTracker: kubeletutil.NewPodStartupLatencyTracker()}

	if _, err := makePodSourceConfig(ctx, kubeCfg, deps, "node-a", func() bool { return true }); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("makePodSourceConfig: %v", err)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(logs.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in logs:\n%s", logs.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs\n%s", logs.String())
}
GOEOF
( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet -run TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 | grep -E 'VULNERABLE|Adding pod URL|PASS|FAIL|ok ' )
```

Expected: printed lines show the secret in the kubelet log output, then `PASS`:

```text
VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs
    Adding pod URL with HTTP header URL http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml header map[Authorization:[Bearer static-pod-url-secret]]
--- PASS: TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak (0.00s)
ok  	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet
```

i.e. the `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret` value is logged verbatim by `Adding pod URL with HTTP header`.

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials to kubelet logs, at default verbosity. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_staticpodurlheader_log_leak`.
- Distinct from `kubelet_configz_staticpodurlheader_leak` (the `/configz` JSON path, different sink and code path) — both leak the same `StaticPodURLHeader` field but via different endpoints; both capitalize on the fact that `makePodSourceConfig`/`setConfigz` bypass the `datapolicy`/config-mask that `server.go:287-290` applies.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` are not affected.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ git describe --tags
v1.37.0-alpha.2-121-ga0b6070d29d   # current master; reproducer verified at a0b6070d29d
```

title: kubelet /configz leaks --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys)
body:
### What happened?

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```go
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```go
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops an in-package Go test that calls the real `setConfigz` + `configz.InstallHandler`, hits the handler with `GET /configz`, and asserts the secret header is in the JSON response. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
DIR="$ROOT/cmd/kubelet/app"
F="$DIR/zz_poc_configz_leak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package app

import (
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"k8s.io/component-base/configz"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
)

func TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader(t *testing.T) {
	const name = "poc-configz-leak"
	const secret = "Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"
	cz, err := configz.New(name)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("register: %v", err)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() { configz.Delete(name) })

	kc := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "https://manifests.example.invalid/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
	}
	if err := setConfigz(cz, kc); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("setConfigz: %v", err)
	}

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	configz.InstallHandler(mux)
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	mux.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/configz", nil))
	if rec.Code != http.StatusOK {
		t.Fatalf("status=%d body=%s", rec.Code, rec.Body.String())
	}
	if !strings.Contains(rec.Body.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in /configz body:\n%s", rec.Body.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: /configz body contains %q", secret)
	t.Logf("body: %s", rec.Body.String())
}
GOEOF
go test ./cmd/kubelet/app -run TestPOCConfigzLeaksHeader -count=1 -v
```

Expected: test **passes**, and the `body:` line shows
`"staticPodURLHeader":{"Authorization":["Bearer POC_STATIC_POD_HEADER_TOKEN"]}` — the header value in cleartext. (Against a real node: `curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <kubelet-token>" https://<node>:10250/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.staticPodURLHeader'`.)

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials via an authenticated kubelet endpoint. It is a credentials/config exposure issue — any caller already trusted to read `/configz` (ops, monitoring, support) gains the manifest-auth credentials, which they were not meant to receive.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` (file source) are not affected.

title: EasyCLA blocks website main to dev branch-sync PRs on kubernetes-prow[bot] merge commits
body:
### What happened?

Weekly "Merge main branch into dev-1.37" sync PRs against `kubernetes/website` fail the **EasyCLA** check with `Missing CLA Authorization`, and the only committer flagged is the bot identity `kubernetes-prow[bot]`.

These sync PRs merge `main` into the release dev branch, which by design pulls in the merge commits that Prow created when merging earlier PRs. EasyCLA evaluates every commit author in the PR, finds the `kubernetes-prow[bot]`-authored merge commits, and reports them as not covered by a signed CLA. Every human contributor on the branch passes; only the bot fails.

Key detail: in the same EasyCLA report, the older bot identity **`k8s-ci-robot` (name "Kubernetes Prow Robot") passes** the CLA check, while the newer GitHub App identity **`kubernetes-prow[bot]` fails**. So merge commits that used to be authored by the CLA-authorized `k8s-ci-robot` are now authored by `kubernetes-prow[bot]`, which has no CLA association - that identity change appears to be what newly breaks these sync PRs.

Examples:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/56271 — EasyCLA `fail`. `k8s-ci-robot` ✅ (e.g. `373112ed5c7fe7c2a5e502bb61b3aad9b917cf87`), but `@kubernetes-prow[bot]` ❌ (35 merge commits, e.g. `1797afad91da7d36ecf0ca3ed975a71e6716a860`).
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/56300 — fresh sync PR, same failure on the same bot identity.

This blocks the routine weekly branch sync during the v1.37 cycle: `tide` reports "Not mergeable. Needs ... cncf-cla: yes" because the bot commits aren't CLA-authorized.

### What did you expect to happen?

Merge commits authored by `kubernetes-prow[bot]` that arrive via a `main` → `dev-*` sync merge should not block EasyCLA / the `cncf-cla: yes` label - the same way the older `k8s-ci-robot` identity is already treated - so the routine weekly branch sync can proceed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Follow the [documented weekly branch-sync flow](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/blob/master/release-team/role-handbooks/docs/Release-Timeline.md#weekly-branch-sync-prs) for `kubernetes/website`: fetch `upstream/main` and `upstream/dev-1.37`, fast-forward `dev-1.37`, then `git merge upstream/main` onto a `merged-main-dev-1.37` branch.
2. Push the branch and open a PR targeting `dev-1.37`.
3. The merge brings in `kubernetes-prow[bot]` merge commits from `main`.
4. EasyCLA runs and reports `Missing CLA Authorization`, flagging only `@kubernetes-prow[bot]` (while `k8s-ci-robot` on the same PR passes).

### Anything else we need to know?

Rebasing/squashing is not a viable fix here: the entire purpose of the sync PR is to carry `main`'s merge history into the dev branch, so dropping those bot merge commits would defeat the sync. Looking for guidance on the right path - e.g. giving `kubernetes-prow[bot]` the same CLA treatment that `k8s-ci-robot` already has (allowlisting the bot identity in EasyCLA), an admin merge/override for sync PRs, or a different recommended sync procedure that avoids carrying bot-authored merge commits.

Filing as a tracking issue per advice in Slack to get direction from the owning SIG. Marking priority critical-urgent for now since it blocks the v1.37 weekly docs branch sync; happy to lower it once a fix path is confirmed.

title: Kubelet emits transient `object "<ns>"/"<name>" not registered` (FailedMount) on cold start
body:
## What happens

On kubelet start/restart (node reboot, kubelet upgrade, cold node join), pods that mount secret
or configMap volumes intermittently fail to mount with a `FailedMount` event:

```
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "sec" : object "bootrace-min"/"s37" not registered
```

It is transient and clears on the volume reconciler's next pass, but delays pod startup and
generates many `FailedMount` events at scale (node reboots, node-pool upgrades).

## Environment

- Kubernetes: reproduced on v1.31.14; symptom reported across 1.22–1.27 (see related issues).
- Node: 2 vCPU Linux, containerd, single-node kubeadm cluster.

## Reproduce

Small node (e.g. **2 vCPU**), kubelet `maxPods` raised to fit the pod count: create N pods each
mounting its **own distinct** secret + configMap, then restart kubelet a few times. A *shared*
object does not reproduce; the objects must be distinct.

```bash
./repro.sh                 # 150 distinct-object pods, 6 kubelet restarts (defaults)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# USAGE: ./repro.sh [NUM_PODS] [RESTARTS] [SETTLE_SECS]   (defaults: 150 6 25)
# ENV:   NS, NODE, RESTART_CMD="sudo systemctl restart kubelet"
# Requires kubectl + ability to restart kubelet on the node. Raise kubelet maxPods to fit NUM_PODS.
set -uo pipefail
N="${1:-150}"; R="${2:-6}"; SETTLE="${3:-25}"
NS="${NS:-bootrace-min}"
RESTART_CMD="${RESTART_CMD:-sudo systemctl restart kubelet}"
NODE="${NODE:-$(kubectl get nodes --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '$2=="Ready"{print $1; exit}')}"
[ -z "$NODE" ] && { echo "ERROR: no Ready node; set NODE=<name>"; exit 1; }

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: Secret\nmetadata: {name: s%d, namespace: %s}\nstringData: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: ConfigMap\nmetadata: {name: c%d, namespace: %s}\ndata: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do cat <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: p$i, namespace: $NS, labels: {app: bootrace-min}}
spec:
  nodeName: $NODE
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: sec, mountPath: /etc/sec, readOnly: true}
    - {name: cm,  mountPath: /etc/cm,  readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: sec, secret: {secretName: s$i}}
  - {name: cm,  configMap: {name: c$i}}
---
EOF
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null

for t in $(seq 1 120); do
  run=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$run" -ge "$N" ] && break; sleep 4
done
echo "Running: $run / $N"

total=0
for b in $(seq 1 "$R"); do
  kubectl -n "$NS" delete events --all >/dev/null 2>&1
  eval "$RESTART_CMD"
  sleep "$SETTLE"
  hits=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount \
           -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.message}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'not registered')
  total=$((total + hits))
  printf 'restart %2d/%d | FailedMount "not registered": %d\n' "$b" "$R" "$hits"
done
echo "TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: $total"
echo "Cleanup: kubectl delete ns $NS"
```
</details>

### Sample output (single-node, 2 vCPU, 150 distinct-object pods)

```
restart  1/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 14
restart  2/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 4
restart  3/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 58
restart  4/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 46
restart  5/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 15
restart  6/6 | FailedMount "not registered": 6
TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: 143
```

Inspect: `kubectl -n bootrace-min get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount | grep 'not registered'`

## Related issues

- #105204 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.22–1.23)
- #119361 — Sporadic "MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume ... not registered" (1.27)

title: Kubelet UID-qualified exec/run routes ignore mismatched pod UID during pod resolution
body:
### What happened?

While investigating kubelet streaming endpoints, I noticed that the UID-qualified `exec` and `run` routes do not appear to enforce the supplied pod UID during pod resolution.

Routes:

```
/exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
/run/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
```

parse and forward the UID, but the underlying lookup prefers the pod full name whenever it is available.

As a result, a request using a stale or mismatched UID can still resolve successfully to the currently running pod with the same namespace/name.

I initially treated this as a potential security concern and performed a deeper investigation of the authorization path.

After tracing the complete request flow multiple times, I could not identify any authorization bypass or privilege escalation. Authorization is already enforced before these handlers, so the observed behavior appears to be a correctness/consistency issue rather than a security issue.

I have reproduced and re-verified this behavior twice using the existing runtime tests and local code tracing.

### What did you expect to happen?

When a UID-qualified kubelet route is used and a non-empty pod UID is supplied, the request should require both:

- pod full name
- pod UID

to match the current pod.

For example:

```
Pod:
namespace: default
name: demo
uid: new-uid

Request:
/exec/default/demo/old-uid/container
```

should be rejected instead of resolving to the recreated pod.

This would also make the behavior consistent with the existing `attach` and `port-forward` implementations, which explicitly reject UID mismatches.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The existing runtime test already documents the lookup precedence.

Run:

```bash
go test ./pkg/kubelet/container \
-run 'TestPodsFindPod/find_by_full_name_takes_precedence' \
-count=1 -v
```

The test demonstrates that:

```
Pods.FindPod("pod1_ns1", "uid2")
```

returns the pod identified by its full name even when the supplied UID belongs to a different pod.

Relevant request flow:

```
HTTP /exec/{namespace}/{pod}/{uid}/{container}
        ↓
getExec()
        ↓
GetExec()
        ↓
findContainer(...)
        ↓
Pods.FindPod(podFullName, podUID)
        ↓
FindPodByFullName(...)
```

I reproduced this behavior twice during investigation and obtained the same result both times.

### Anything else we need to know?

Additional investigation:

- Traced the complete kubelet exec/run request path.
- Compared behavior with `attach` and `port-forward`.
- Verified that authorization occurs before the streaming handlers.
- Verified that this does **not** appear to introduce RBAC bypass, privilege escalation, or tenant isolation issues.

Behavior comparison:

| Operation | UID validation |
|-----------|---------------|
| exec | UID effectively ignored |
| run | UID effectively ignored |
| attach | explicit UID mismatch check |
| port-forward | explicit UID mismatch check |

I also searched for existing issues and local history using:

- FindPod
- GetExec
- RunInContainer
- kubelet exec UID
- UID mismatch
- pod recreation

and could not find an existing report covering this specific behavior.

If this behavior is considered unintended, I'd be happy to prepare a focused PR together with regression tests.

Repository investigation against current kubernetes/kubernetes main branch.

No running cluster was required for reproduction.

Not applicable (local source investigation).


### OS version

```console
Local development environment (Windows).

Behavior verified through source analysis and focused Go tests.

title: DRA-backed extended resources do not report ResourceHealthStatus in PodStatus
body:
### What happened?

When a Pod uses an extended resource backed by Dynamic Resource Allocation, kubelet prepares the generated special ResourceClaim and injects the CDI devices, but it does not populate `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus` for those resources.
﻿
For DRA-backed extended resources, the container request is in `container.Resources.Requests`, not in `container.Resources.Claims`, so the health status update path never considers `pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.RequestMappings`.
﻿
As a result, DRA-backed extended resources can be prepared and passed into the container, but their health is not reflected in PodStatus.

### What did you expect to happen?

When `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled and a DRA plugin reports health for a device allocated via a DRA-backed extended resource, kubelet should publish that health in `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus`.
﻿
The reported status should correspond to the generated special ResourceClaim and request from `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus.requestMappings`.

**Status update / clarification on timing**

This fix was deliberately split across two releases:

**1.37 (done):** #139941 (merged 2026-07-22, [`78e971a4bc0`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/78e971a4bc0dc76845d7986495607ed6d5b616a7)) relaxed pod status validation so apiservers accept `claim:<claimName>/<requestName>` names resolved via `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus` — see [`matchesExtendedResourceClaimStatus` in validation.go at the merge commit](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/78e971a4bc0dc76845d7986495607ed6d5b616a7/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L9816). It intentionally did **not** add kubelet reporting. Quoting the [PR description of #139941](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139941):

> This prepares the API side first. Kubelet reporting for DRA-backed extended resource health is intentionally deferred to a follow-up release to avoid 1.37 kubelets writing pod status that could be rejected after downgrade to a 1.36 apiserver.

**1.38 (planned):** kubelet reporting of health for DRA-backed extended resources in `allocatedResourcesStatus`, tracked in #140060. Quoting the [issue description of #140060](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140060):

> For 1.38, revisit kubelet reporting for DRA-backed extended resources: add kubelet reporting for DRA-backed extended resource health once 1.36 rollback compatibility is no longer in scope

The reason for the split is version skew: per the [version skew policy](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/#kubelet), `kubelet` may be up to three minor versions older than `kube-apiserver` but **must not be newer** — so a 1.38 kubelet writing these names is only safe if 1.37 apiservers (its oldest supported peer during rollback) already accept them, which is what #139941 guarantees.

/remove-priority important-soon
/priority important-longterm

title: kubelet allocates hostUsers:false pod UID/GID range ending at UINT32_MAX, causing sandbox creation to fail indefinitely
body:
### What happened?

A pod using:

```yaml

spec:

  hostUsers: false
```
intermittently fails during pod sandbox creation when kubelet allocates the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

This maps container UID/GID 0..65535 to host UID/GID: 4294901760..4294967295
The final mapped value is:
```
4294967295 = 2^32 - 1 = UINT32_MAX
```

The pod then fails sandbox creation indefinitely with:
```
FailedCreatePodSandBox
failed to create network namespace for sandbox:
failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument
```

The affected pod never starts its init container or app container. Volume setup succeeds, but sandbox creation fails before container execution.

I have reproduced/observed this again with in same configuration on different cluster:
```
namespace: pim-adapter
pod: pim-adapter-akeneo-attributes-queue-cronjob-29701755-5blmf
```
The kubelet persisted user namespace state for this pod confirms the same terminal range:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```
The persisted kubelet state is from:
```
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/userns
```

Other hostUsers: false pods on the same node with non-terminal UID/GID ranges run successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either:

1. kubelet should not allocate a pod user namespace range that includes 4294967295 / UINT32_MAX, or
2. the runtime/kernel stack should successfully create the sandbox with this mapping, or
3. the pod should fail with a clear validation/allocation error instead of retrying sandbox creation indefinitely.

In particular, kubelet should probably avoid allocating the final 65,536-ID block:
```
4294901760..4294967295
```
if this range is not valid for pod user namespace mappings.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This appears to reproduce when kubelet assigns the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range to a pod using hostUsers: false.

Minimal pod property:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: userns-terminal-range-repro
  namespace: userns-terminal-range-repro
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "id && sleep 3600"]
```

The important condition is that kubelet allocates this persisted user namespace mapping:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

Validation steps on an affected pod:
```
NS=userns-terminal-range-repro
POD=userns-terminal-range-repro

kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='hostUsers={.spec.hostUsers}{"\n"}node={.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}uid={.metadata.uid}{"\n"}phase={.status.phase}{"\n"}'

POD_UID=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
echo "$POD_UID"
```
On the node where the pod is scheduled:
```
sudo cat "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Boundary check:
```
sudo jq -r '
  .uidMappings[0] as $u |
  .gidMappings[0] as $g |
  "uid_hostId=\($u.hostId)",
  "uid_length=\($u.length)",
  "uid_end=\($u.hostId + $u.length - 1)",
  "gid_hostId=\($g.hostId)",
  "gid_length=\($g.length)",
  "gid_end=\($g.hostId + $g.length - 1)",
  "uid_hits_uint32_max=\(($u.hostId + $u.length - 1) == 4294967295)",
  "gid_hits_uint32_max=\(($g.hostId + $g.length - 1) == 4294967295)"
' "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Observed output:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```

Check kubelet events/logs:

```
kubectl describe pod -n "$NS" "$POD" | grep -A8 -B4 'FailedCreatePodSandBox\|CreatePodSandbox\|failed to create network namespace\|noop process\|invalid argument'
```

```
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|CreatePodSandbox|FailedCreatePodSandBox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
```
sudo journalctl -u containerd --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|RunPodSandbox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
The failure occurs before CNI appears to run and before any init/app container starts.

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks like a boundary bug in the kubelet pod user namespace allocator or in validation of generated mappings.
The node can run other hostUsers: false pods successfully when kubelet assigns non-terminal ranges. Examples of working persisted mappings observed on the same node include:
```
{"hostId":416546816,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":1584726016,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4152492032,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4130734080,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":3823566848,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
```

The affected pod is from a CronJob/Job. In one observed case, the pod stayed stuck for approximately 2 days and accumulated more than 13,000 FailedCreatePodSandBox events. It happened on two different clusters with same CronJob/Job.

Relevant pod spec properties:
```
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
```

The affected workload does not use:
```
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostIPC: true
volumeDevices:
```
Relevant sysctls on the node:
```
user.max_user_namespaces = 62502
user.max_net_namespaces = 62502
```
Workaround:
```
hostUsers: true
```
or removing:
```
hostUsers: false
```
avoids the kubelet pod user namespace allocation path and prevents this failure for the affected workload.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# Observed Kubernetes version:

# v1.35.5-eks-0247562
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
AWS EKS

Self-managed node group
</details>

<details>

```console

Kernel: 6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.x86_64

</details>

<details>

<details>

runc: 1.3.4

<details>
The observed failure appears to happen before CNI execution:

RunPodSandbox fails with:
failed to create network namespace for sandbox:
failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument

Happy to work on a fix + test if sig-node thinks that's the right spot.

title: [kubelet] Why isn’t DRA prepare failure treated as a pod sync error?
body:
I noticed that DRA `PrepareDynamicResources` / `NodePrepareResources` failures appear not to be propagated as pod sync errors in kubelet. As a result, the retry seems to happen on the regular pod resync interval instead of the pod sync error backoff path.

I would like to understand whether this is intentional, and if so, what the design rationale is.

**code path**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1585-L1597

When PrepareDynamicResources fails,the function returns early, but it does not appear to mark the PodSyncResult as failed, for example via either:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1498-L1522

This matters because if result.Error() == nil, the kubelet will re-process the pod after the default sync interval (60s–90s). Otherwise, the pod is placed into the backoff queue and will be retried sooner. In our experience, the first few PrepareDynamicResources calls sometimes fail, forcing us to wait through several default sync periods, which significantly increases pod startup latency.

title: [kubelet] Calling UpdatePod on an untracked but terminated pod should mark it as terminated, not terminating
body:
The first call to `UpdatePod` for a failed (rejected) pod sets `terminatingAt` but doesn't set `termitatedAt` because we need to run `SyncTerminatingPod` to clean up:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L803-L812

However, the first time we enter the pod worker loop, I'm pretty sure we end up saying the pod can never start, and exit the worker loop:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1234

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1180

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1047-L1049

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1240-L1243

Unless I'm missing something, this looks like a bug with how we handle clean up in this case. But, if that cleanup isn't actually necessary, then maybe we can just set the `terminatedAt` timestamp immediately for the failed pod, which would cause it to be considered inactive.

Note: There is a test case that is suppose to cover this, but since the test uses a fake cache implementation that doesn't match the defaulting logic of the real cache, it skips over the code that generates the terminating sync status.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go#L750-L771

This was the intention, but there are some outstanding issues today:

Hi, I'd like to investigate and work on a fix for this.
From the pprof dump, the leak is rooted in context.(*cancelCtx).propagateCancel being held for ~918k contexts strongly suggesting that context.WithCancel is being called inside the startPodSync / pod worker loop in pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go but the returned cancel function is never called on certain code paths, causing child contexts to accumulate in the parent's children map indefinitely.

/kind bug

I investigated a bit more. This appears to be a **regression in Kubernetes 1.36** which was introduced on 2026-02-19 in this commit:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/e94e67337dfe4864665db25b3d3d1957c6234a92#diff-c6d21f5481c391a3f32bcfddf45c9c20132b2876e8be9690289474b76b71d809L1157-R1153

In `startPodSync`, the old version:

```
	// initialize a context for the worker if one does not exist
	if status.ctx == nil || status.ctx.Err() == context.Canceled {
		status.ctx, status.cancelFn = context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	}
	ctx = status.ctx
```

which reuses the existing context if possible, was replaced by:

```
	ctx, status.cancelFn = context.WithCancel(parentCtx)
```

which unconditionally creates a new context and leaks the old one.

title: DRA: allocator clears DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests too aggressively, widening a per-request config to the whole claim
body:
### What happened?

The DRA structured allocator post-processes allocated configs to drop a `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` list to `nil` when the config "applies to all requests" (the *empty means all* semantic). It decides this with a length comparison:

```go

for i := range allocationResult.Devices.Config {
    if len(allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests) {
        allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests = nil
    }
}
```

`len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)` is **not** equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim", because `config.Requests` entries may be sub-request references of the form `"<request>/<subRequest>"`  the allocator matches them that way a few lines earlier:

```go
subRequestName := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", request.Name, subRequest.Name)
if slices.Contains(config.Requests, subRequestName) { ... }
```

A config that references **N sub-requests of a single parent request** has `len(config.Requests) == N`. If the claim has **N top-level requests**, the lengths match even though the config covers only one of them  so its `Requests` is cleared and the config is silently re-scoped to **every** request in the claim.

The same defect is present in all three production implementations:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go` (the cleanup loop)
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`

### What did you expect to happen?

A config that references only sub-requests of one request should remain scoped to that request. `Requests` should be cleared to `nil` (the "applies to all" form) only when the config actually covers **all** top-level requests in the claim.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to the shared table in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` (`TestAllocator`) and run `go test ./structured/internal/experimental/ -run 'TestAllocator/repro-config-subrequests-not-all'` (fails identically for `incubating` and `stable`):

```go
"repro-config-subrequests-not-all": {
    features: Features{PrioritizedList: true},
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(
            requestWithPrioritizedList(req0,
                subRequest(subReq0, classA, 1),
                subRequest(subReq1, classB, 1),
            ),
            deviceRequest(req1, classA, 1), // second top-level request, unrelated to the config
        ).withConfigs(objects(
            // references BOTH sub-requests of req0 only; must NOT apply to req1
            deviceClaimConfig([]string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo")),
        )),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA), class(classB, driverB)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
        device(device1, nil, nil), device(device2, nil, nil),
    )),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{allocationResultWithConfigs(
        localNodeSelector(node1),
        objects(
            deviceAllocationResult(req0SubReq0, driverA, pool1, device1, false),
            deviceAllocationResult(req1, driverA, pool1, device2, false),
        ),
        []resourceapi.DeviceAllocationConfiguration{{
            Source:              resourceapi.AllocationConfigSourceClaim,
            Requests:            []string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, // expected: stays scoped to req0
            DeviceConfiguration: deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo"),
        }},
    )},
},
```

Device allocation comes out exactly as expected (`req-0/subReq-0` → `device-1`, `req-1` → `device-2`); the **only** difference is the config scope:

```text
expected: Requests: ["req-0/subReq-0", "req-0/subReq-1"]
actual:   Requests: nil      # == applies to ALL requests, including the unrelated req-1
```

title: Supporting concurrent processing of PLEG events is needed
body:
### What happened?

In kubelet, [GenericPLEG.Relist](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1cd0b215bb5ce2f723cde78660b5524ee3258dcb/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L289) periodically retrieves Pods/Containers from the container runtime and compares them with the information in memory to update the cache. When there are a large number of changes to containers on a single node (our production scenario already supports up to 300, although the default is currently 110 Pods), this process can take a significant amount of time, even exceeding 3 minutes. Therefore, we believe that parallel processing should be supported in this area.

In [GenericPLEG.Relist](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1cd0b215bb5ce2f723cde78660b5524ee3258dcb/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L289), updates to the cache can be processed concurrently.

comments.body: /sig node

Based on my testing, I do not think GenericPLEG relisting should take minutes at this scale. I have tested PLEG relisting on nodes with thousands of pods, and it worked well.

One important detail is that GenericPLEG does not call CRI status APIs for every pod on every relist. For pods whose container state has not changed, `reconcilePodRecord` only compares the old and current pod records and returns. It calls `GetPodStatus` only when events are generated or when the pod needs reinspection.

So if a single relist takes more than 3 minutes with around 300 pods, I would first focus on CRI latency in that environment.

Please check the latency of kubelet calls to the container runtime when the issue happens, especially `ListPodSandbox`, `ListContainers`, `PodSandboxStatus`, and `ContainerStatus`.

That should help determine whether the relist is blocked in the pod listing phase, or whether many pod/container changes in the same time window cause GenericPLEG to sequentially refresh per-pod status.

Parallelizing cache updates may help if many changed pods are blocked on slow status calls. However, I would first verify the CRI latency, investigate the root cause of that latency, and only then treat PLEG event processing concurrency as one possible contributing factor.
/triage needs-information

title: [SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health
body:
### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time. 

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IwONkeXSc2SG_EQMYGRSkfiSWNk8yWLpVhPm-LOTbGM) before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-metrics/failures-latest.html?include=node&sort=days&asc=0), but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/kettle/README.md), `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?sig=node)) to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community. 
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

/sig node
cc: @SergeyKanzhelev
author: mariafromano-25

/sig node

From today's CI meeting: 
- option 1: look into the source code of Dim's dashboard and make some edits to fit our triage process.
    --> consider: much longer investment in time and effort but could be longer standing solution for the group
- option 2: add the flaky label in test code if we see it fail for over xx amount of days. 
    --> consider: clearly outline how long until we add the label and how long it will take to fix.  
    --> [k8s flaky definition](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/10c089c55c543e702ba7eff26b1e038650fd5da2/contributors/devel/sig-testing/e2e-tests.md?plain=1#L554)

Any thoughts?

I was thinking about it. I have a feeling that splitting the dashboard into reasons will become a never-ending chase of additional dimensions. Keeping it green sounds like a better idea. So I think it is the good idea to start being more aggressive in applying the `[Flaky]` label to tests.

So the goal is to keep all the jobs green. And separately - track ownership and "time to fix" for all flakes. Maybe even cross link all `Flaky` labels with the tracking issues.

This separation will put the right ownership - CI group ownership of keeping test lanes green and finding owners for test failures. And specific components owners responsible for individual tests.

We can extend this model to test definitions by moving continuously failing tests to "Flaky" tab with associated tracking bug and an owner.

Some policy around not moving release blocking tests to Flaky or moving to Flaky and treat fixes as release blocking issues would be needed as well. Not that important for features that are not GA or not yet treated as release blocking.

Thanks for picking this up. The panic and my fix in #139698 both live in the DRA validation, `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go` (the `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep` modulo on the `DRAConsumableCapacity` capacity-request-policy path). That is `resource.k8s.io` group code; its OWNERS (pohly, klueska, bart0sh) carry the `wg/device-management` label, so it reads as SIG Node / WG Device Management to me rather than SIG API Machinery. The divide-by-zero is in the in-tree DRA validation itself, not in the shared apimachinery `Quantity` type it calls into. So the current `sig/node` label looks right to me, but you have a far better view of the SIG boundaries here, so I'm happy to follow whichever way you route it and keep the PR in step with the SIG and reviewers you prefer.

/assign

/triage accepted

Is it a regression? I am trying to apply the priority and see if we need a patch for previous releases

Not a regression as far as I can tell. The panic is in `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep` in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`, which runs `added % stepVal` without first rejecting a zero or non-positive step. That function and the rest of the `validRange.step` validation came in with the consumable-capacity work in commit `5ad969588d5d` ("KEP-5075: API updates"), which first shipped in v1.34. The modulo has been unguarded since that first commit (no earlier guard was removed), and the function is identical and still unguarded on release-1.34, release-1.35, release-1.36, and master. It doesn't exist before 1.34, so there was no prior release where this path handled a zero step correctly.

For the backport question, it tracks the `DRAConsumableCapacity` gate: alpha and off by default in 1.34 and 1.35 (with the gate off, the request-policy fields are dropped in PrepareForCreate before validation, so the path isn't reachable), and beta and on by default in 1.36. So it's reachable in a default 1.36 cluster, and on 1.34 and 1.35 only when the alpha gate is explicitly enabled. Since ResourceSlices are normally published by DRA drivers rather than arbitrary users, I read this as validation robustness rather than a broadly reachable DoS, though you have the better view on how to weigh that.

The fix in #139698 is a small additive guard with no behavior change for valid input, so it should cherry-pick cleanly to release-1.34, release-1.35, and release-1.36. I'm happy to open the cherry-picks for whichever of those you'd like once it merges. Just let me know how you'd prefer to proceed.

title: kubelet CleanSubPaths can leave pods stuck Terminating when subPath target stat returns ENOENT but mountinfo still has the mount
body:
### What happened?

A pod using a CSI volume with `volumeMount.subPath` got stuck in `Terminating`.

The workload container had already exited, but kubelet repeatedly failed during volume cleanup before calling CSI `NodeUnpublishVolume`.

Example kubelet logs:

```text
UnmountVolume started for volume "<pvc-name>" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/<driver>^<volume>")
Warning: mount cleanup skipped because path does not exist:
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx/3

Warning: mount cleanup skipped because path does not exist:
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx/5

Operation ... failed. No retries permitted until ...
Error: error cleaning subPath mounts for volume "<pvc-name>" ...
error deleting /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volume-subpaths/<volume-name>/xxxx:
remove .../xxxx: directory not empty
```
### What did you expect to happen?

If a subPath target path returns ENOENT but the mount is still present in mountinfo, kubelet should not skip cleanup and then fail on the parent directory with directory not empty.

Kubelet should either detect the stale/deleted mountpoint from mountinfo and attempt to unmount it, or re-check/re-walk remaining subPath entries before failing the parent directory removal.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We do not yet have a manifest-only reproducer. The key failure state is:

```text
a kubelet subPath bind target is still present in mountinfo,
but stat(2) on the subPath target returns ENOENT
```

I dug into one specific failure to figure out whether this is a flaky timeout or something real, and it's real — here's the root cause.

I traced build [`2099502935326068736`](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-containerd/2099502935326068736) (COS run, Sep 14 2026), where `RestartAllContainersWithKubeletRestarts` / "during startup" failed with `[FAILED] Timed out after 180.001s ... not all containers are running`.

**Timeline (from `containerd.log` / `kubelet.log` on the COS node):**

- `15:58:47.807` — test triggers `STEP: restarting kubelet`
- `15:58:47.907` — old kubelet process shuts down
- `15:58:48.037` — new kubelet process comes up
- `15:58:49.064` — new kubelet receives the pod fresh from the API server and treats it as "synced for the first time"
- `15:58:49.065` — new kubelet decides `"Pod is terminal"` → `"Pod directory completed naturally and should now terminate"`
- `15:58:49.065 – 15:58:50.172` — pod gets torn down in two passes: containers destroyed and volumes unmounted, then a housekeeping pass finds the pod "orphaned," destroys the last sandbox container, removes the cgroups, and broadcasts `"Pod removed"` at `15:58:50.171611`
- `16:01:52.986` — test finally times out waiting for "all containers running" — which was never going to happen, since the pod itself was already deleted just over 3 minutes earlier

**Root cause:**

Right before the kubelet restart, every container in the pod had a status like:
lastState.terminated{exitCode: 137, reason: "RestartingAllContainers", message: "The container is removed because RestartAllContainers in place"}


That's the feature's own signal for "this container isn't done — it's paused mid-coordinated-restart, please recreate it." The old kubelet process understood that and was actively recreating containers (it had already recreated `init` right before it got killed).

The new kubelet process doesn't. When it rebuilds pod state from scratch after restarting, it sees a pod whose containers all exited and applies its normal completion logic — it concludes the pod's work is done and deletes it, instead of resuming the restart.

So this isn't a slow-recovery issue, and no timeout value fixes it — the pod is gone well before the 180s wait even starts. The gap is specifically in how `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits`/`ContainerRestartRules` state survives a kubelet process restart; the "mid-restart, don't clean me up" intent doesn't seem to be checkpointed or restored when the pod worker rebuilds state fresh.

This likely explains the flakiness too — it would only reproduce when the kubelet restart lands in the narrow window where containers are marked "paused for restart" but not yet recreated. I've only deep-traced this one instance so far; haven't yet confirmed the other historical failures show the identical teardown pattern, but the failure signature (timeout at the exact 180s boundary) is consistent with it.

I'll pick this up and look into a fix for the pod-worker's restart-recovery path.

title: apiserver: return 4xx instead of 500 when pod runtimeClassName is empty
body:
### What happened?

The Kubernetes API Server returns HTTP 500 Internal Server Error when creating a Pod whose `spec.runtimeClassName` is set to an empty string.

The following request sets `spec.runtimeClassName` to `""`:

```bash
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":""}}'
```
Actual response:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "resource name may not be empty",
  "code": 500
}
```
The request is invalid or incomplete, but the API Server returns an internal server error.

### What did you expect to happen?

The API Server should return a client-side error, such as HTTP 400 Bad Request or HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity, instead of HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

Since `spec.runtimeClassName` is invalid when it is an empty string, the error should be reported as a validation error rather than an internal server error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a Kubernetes cluster with an affected version.
2. Start a local API proxy:

```bash
kubectl proxy --port=8001
```
3. Send the following request:
```bash
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":""}}'
```
4. Observe that the API Server returns HTTP 500:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "resource name may not be empty",
  "code": 500
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue was found during RESTful API fuzzing of the Kubernetes API Server.

The request is invalid because `runtimeClassName` is empty and the Pod body is incomplete. However, this should not be surfaced as HTTP 500. It appears that an empty `runtimeClassName` is propagated to runtime class lookup logic and reported as an internal error.

This behavior is reproducible in my tests on Kubernetes v1.33.1 and v1.36.0.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.36.0
Kustomize Version: v5.8.1
Server Version: v1.36.0
```
```console
