body:
### What happened?

When creating a ResourceClaim with 2 requests with 2 different device class that have a config, the config reported in the allocation devices status is not mentioning from which request the config is coming from. So the DRA-Drivers cannot identify the configuration belonging to the request it is supposed to handle.
```yaml

kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: my-resource-claim
spec:
...
status:
  allocation:
    devices:
      config:
      - opaque:
          driver: resource-driver.example.com
          parameters:
            test: example-0
        source: FromClass
      - opaque:
          driver: resource-driver.example.com
          parameters:
            test: example-1
        source: FromClass
      results:
```

No more **spec.template.metadata.creationTimestamp** field !
So upgrading cluster from 1.33 to 1.34 will trigger a rollout of pods managed by statefulset as the doc says about pod template.

"If you change the pod template for a workload resource, that resource needs to create replacement Pods that use the updated template."

> if you upgrade kubernetes version, it will recreate the pods, this is expected behavior

I think this is referring to the case where the control plane is only updated.

/sig api-machinery
/cc @liggitt

>if you upgrade kubernetes version, it will recreate the pods, this is expected behavior

I disagree. Control plane upgrade should NOT impact user workload especially for a change that is not marked as breaking change.

If I have a large cluster running some AI/ML training job using statefulset, upgrading to 1.34 means all my workload will be interrupted which is a real problem.

Thoughts? @liggitt @jpbetz @deads2k

I agree a control plane upgrade should not trigger workload rollouts. It looks like statefulsets use hashes of serialized statefulset template json as the indicator a change occurred, which is unfortunately fragile to any json-visible serialization changes under PodTemplate (as well as any field defaulting changes under pod template).

The creationTimestamp omitzero change presumed the field would always be populated server side, so would not change serialization in server responses, but that was only true for the root metadata.creationTimestamp.

Reverting the change would cause disruption in the opposite direction in 1.34 → 1.35 or 1.34.0 → 1.34.x upgrades, so I think we'll need to add a secondary check when statefulset is determining whether the latest revision is identical to the current state that checks if removal of `creationTimestamp:null` is needed to normalize for comparison.

/assign
/kind regression
/priority important-soon

xref previous issues with using exact json serialization / hashing for determining if a rollout or container restart was required:
* this issue for statefulset (fragile to json serialization and podtemplate field defaulting)
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/69445 (daemonset fragile to podtemplate defaulting, not fundamentally fixed in daemonset)
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/78633 (daemonset fragile to podtemplate defaulting, not fundamentally fixed in daemonset)
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/63814 (kubelet restarting containers based on json hash)
WIP fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135017
Fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135017 is ready for review
Fix is merged to master, cherry-pick to release-1.34 is at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135087 and will hopefully be included in the next 1.34 patch release
Reopening to track merge of the cherry-pick PR / restoration of release-1.34 behavior
@liggitt Since upgrading to k8s 1.34, if we merge the fix and then upgrade to a version that includes the patch, will it trigger a rollout of the sts workload?

> if we merge the fix and then upgrade to a version that includes the patch, will it trigger a rollout of the sts workload?

Nope, the fix makes sts stable against spurious rollouts in both directions
The missing test coverage identified in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/78904 would have helped catch / prevent this

Ok this has lead to nasty downtime for me. They are called stateful sets for a reason: they contain stateful data and now the entire state of the system had to be rebuilt from. the ground up. 1.34 has been available since august already, I don't understand how it took that long before anybody experienced this problem.

> They are called stateful sets for a reason: they contain stateful data and now the entire state of the system had to be rebuilt from. the ground up.

The stateful part is in the persistent volumes, and the stable identity of pods in the set, which were not impacted by this issue.

A rollout of a new revision of a statefulset replaces those individual pods, and could cause _disruption_ for applications which are sensitive to any pod in the set restarting or being replaced, but should not break stateful data...  if you are seeing state problems after a no-op rollout, I think that means _any_ upgrade of your nodes (which replaces pods) or _any_ update of your statefulset image or pod spec (which would roll out new pods) would have caused similar loss.

This issue went undetected because *most* statefulset applications are not sensitive to normal pod restart / replacement that occurs during a statefulset rollout.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135087 is merged and will be included in v1.34.2

title: No share ID in DRA kubelet plugin's API
body:
### What happened?

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

### Anything else we need to know?

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/4a625314cb46ed38018d05e17a397420335277eb.

PR:

title: PodReadyToStartContainers condition gets flipped  to true after image pull.
body:
### What happened?

According to documentation https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-has-network

> The PodReadyToStartContainers condition is set to True by the kubelet after the successful completion of sandbox creation and network configuration for the Pod by the runtime plugin. The kubelet can start pulling container images and create containers after PodReadyToStartContainers condition has been set to True.

What I am observing is that kubelet is flipping this condition to true after application container image is pulled. 
Also noticed kubelet patched pod with pod ip after image pull.

### What did you expect to happen?

PodReadyToStartContainers to flip to true as as soon as network ip is assigned and containerd sets up the sand box. To set up the sandbox, AFAIK containerd only needs pause container. It flips condition to ready here https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/7669bb4f04b7a2e88ab6da6c95720a5532c97174/internal/cri/server/podsandbox/sandbox_run.go#L290.

```
    for i in $(seq 1 35); do \

CMD ["sleep","3600"]
```

Looking at the test code in `test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go`, I've identified some potential timing issues:

## Observations:

1. **The `waitForPodDeferred()` function** (line 1276-1280) uses `f.Timeouts.PodStart` as the timeout, which may not be appropriate for deferred resize scenarios where resource allocation can take longer.

2. **Race condition between resource calculation and resize**: In all three deferred tests, there's a sequence like:
   - Calculate available node resources
   - Create/patch multiple pods
   - Wait for deferred status
   
   Between steps, other pods or system processes might consume resources, causing the expected "deferred" state to be different than anticipated.

3. **Test 1 potential issue** (line 691-817): The test calculates `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2` but then creates pod3 which might affect the actual available resources before the resize patch is applied.

## Suggested Fixes:

1. **Add retry logic with backoff** instead of a single wait
2. **Use a more appropriate timeout** - maybe `f.Timeouts.PodStartSlow` or a custom timeout for resize operations
3. **Add resource availability checks** right before the resize patch to ensure the test assumptions still hold
4. **Add logging** of actual vs expected resource values when the test fails

Would you like me to prepare a PR with these fixes? I can start with adding better logging and adjusting the timeout values.

/assign @oyiz-michael

I have some questions, maybe you can elaborate more on your observations

> The waitForPodDeferred() function (line 1276-1280) uses f.Timeouts.PodStart as the timeout, which may not be appropriate for deferred resize scenarios where resource allocation can take longer.

Why wouldn't PodStart be appropriate as a timeout? The allocation manager shouldn't take that long to run and decide whether to allocate or defer the resize. If it is actually taking longer than pod starting, we should try to find out why.

> Between steps, other pods or system processes might consume resources, causing the expected "deferred" state to be different than anticipated.

Deferred state is calculated based on the sum of other pod requests. Unless other pods are being created, deleted, or resized unexpectedly, I don't think it should change the deferred result. I think of the observations you listed, this one might be a feasible culprit. Have you found logs showing that other create/delete/resize operations are happening at the same time? 

> The test calculates nodeAvailableMilliCPU2 but then creates pod3 which might affect the actual available resources before the resize patch is applied.

I don't really understand this one. pod3's resources are calculated based off of `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2`, so `nodeAvailableMilliCPU2` necessarily needs to be calculated before creating pod3. Have you looked at the logs or anything to see if the resized calculation is wrong, and if so why does it only happen sometimes? 

I think we need a better understanding of what could be causing the issue before we start writing a PR. More logging is fine if you have looked at the logs and found a specific gap that prevents us from root causing the issue.

title: Static Memory Manager doesn't verify OS reported available huge pages during pod admission
body:
### What happened?

Hi there, 

We have configured the static memory manager to enable numa aware scheduling of our Guaranteed QoS pods. We run various workloads on an m6id.32xlarge 2 numa node system, which accepts both Guaranteed and non Guaranteed QoS pods. These pods run Java based applications which in turn are configured to use huge pages. 

We have noticed an issue that once the pod was scheduled, the JVM was not able to start as it was not able to reserve enough memory (8GB). The pod was configured with the following resource limits:
```
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
      requests:
        cpu: 6000m
        hugepages-2Mi: 8500Mi
        memory: 4000Mi
```

```
and the JVM failed with:

│ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to commit memory (Not enough space)                                                                                                                         │
│ [0.008s][error][gc] Forced to lower max Java heap size from 8192M(100%) to 4094M(50%)                                                                                                  ││ [0.008s][error][gc] Failed to allocate initial Java heap (8192M)                                                                                                                       ││ Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.                                                                                                                                      │
│ Error: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.
```

Upon inspection of the node, we noticed that one of the numa nodes are very short on available huge pages:

```
root@ip-10-31-22-160:/var/snap/amazon-ssm-agent/11320# cat /sys/devices/system/node/node*/meminfo | fgrep Huge
Node 0 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 0 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 0 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 0 HugePages_Free:  41168
Node 0 HugePages_Surp:      0
Node 1 AnonHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 ShmemHugePages:        0 kB
Node 1 FileHugePages:         0 kB
Node 1 HugePages_Total: 65536
Node 1 HugePages_Free:   1631
Node 1 HugePages_Surp:      0
```

which happens to be where this pod was assigned to. 

When we looked at what the memory controller thought as free memory is, we found that its much more than what the OS is reporting as free: 

```
    "1": {
      "numberOfAssignments": 12,
      "memoryMap": {
        "hugepages-1Gi": {
          "total": 0,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 0,
          "reserved": 0,
          "free": 0
        },
        "hugepages-2Mi": {
          "total": 137438953472,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 137438953472,
          "reserved": 121110528000,
          "free": 16328425472
        },
        "memory": {
          "total": 266247880704,
          "systemReserved": 0,
          "allocatable": 128808927232,
          "reserved": 31457280000,
          "free": 97351647232
        }
      },
```

I am no expert in this space but with a quick inspection of the memory controller code it looks like it assumes all pods on the node are running in Guarnateed QoS, it calculates what the free HP utilisation should be based on those but it doesn't take into account any best effort/burstable pods which can also use up huge pages, resulting in the startup failure we have seen. 

### What did you expect to happen?

At least the memory controller should look at what the OS is reporting as free memory and reject the pod admission/suggest an alternative numa node if the memory requirements at the time can't be satisfied with the amount of free memory available on the numa node. Also it could consider evicting best effort/burstable pods to free up more memory on a given numa node. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Given the following kubelet args:
```
--reserved-cpus=0-1,64-65 
--kube-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--system-reserved=memory=5Gi 
--reserved-memory=0:memory=10340Mi 
--memory-manager-policy=Static 
--topology-manager-scope=pod 
--topology-manager-policy=single-numa-node 
--feature-gates CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions=true,CPUManagerPolicyOptions=true,MemoryManager=true 
--cpu-manager-policy static 
--cpu-manager-policy-options full-pcpus-only=true 
--cpu-manager-policy-options strict-cpu-reservation=true 
```

on a 2 numa node system, schedule 2 pods onto said node, one with Burstable and another one with Guaranteed QoS. Both apps should reserve the pod's limits worth of huge pages on start Expect:

/var/lib/kubelet/memory_manager_state.free for numa node 1/2 to take the usage of the burstable pod into an account. 

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

```console
zoltanszel@MacBookPro ~> kubectl version

Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
```

comments.body:
/sig node
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

I need to review if memory manager assumes all pods requesting hugepages are guaranteed. Will review the KEP

Following up on this issue, I wrote down the current accounting flow and the open ownership question:
﻿
https://gist.github.com/AutuSnow/da03266ed23b727c9345128840859e99
﻿
The main distinction I am trying to preserve is between:
﻿
- admission accuracy: kubelet should not select a NUMA affinity which is already known to be unsatisfiable;
- isolation: workloads outside Memory Manager's scope cannot consume memory assigned to Guaranteed workloads.
﻿
Today Memory Manager only tracks Guaranteed Pods, while hugepage resources do not affect Pod QoS classification. This allows kernel-reported NUMA availability and Memory Manager's internal `Free` value to diverge.
﻿
Before proposing an implementation or KEP, I would like feedback on two points:
﻿
1. Should #134395 be addressed as a narrow admission/accounting fix?
2. If cross-QoS NUMA accounting is required, should Memory Manager own it, or should that state belong to another kubelet component?

title: preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits
body:
### What happened?

I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: sleep-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 120
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f sleep-job.yaml 
job.batch/sleep-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           6s         6s

NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Running   0          6s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods sleep-job-qh2qk
pod "sleep-job-qh2qk" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           24s        24s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          24s
```

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           59s        59s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          59s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           69s        69s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          69s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           2m19s      2m19s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          2m19s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Complete   1/1           2m21s      2m22s
```


### Anything else we need to know?

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits. Of course this won't work in a shell-less container which AFAIK is the reason the preStop sleep was introduced.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: exec-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: exec-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sleep", "120"]
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f exec-job.yaml 
job.batch/exec-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           4s         4s

NAME                 READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Running   0          4s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods exec-job-k62r4
pod "exec-job-k62r4" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           23s        23s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          23s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           55s        55s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          55s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           61s        61s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          61s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Complete   1/1           63s        64s
```


### Kubernetes version

Reproduced on KIND, but first observed on EKS 1.32.


But if you delete the pod, then yes, preStop will continue until finished.
I assume it's becasue this ctx can not capture if the signal of PID 1 exits: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go#L132-L145

I'm not familiar with this level's knowledge, let's wait for some sig-node folks to help :(

As far as I know, the current implementation doesn’t cancel the context when the container exits. I was curious why your original implementation [worked this way](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go#L138-L141), but looking at the original PR (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119026), it seems there weren’t many reviews from SIG Node, so this might have slipped through. That said, since the current behavior keeps the preStop hook running even after the main container has stopped, changing it now would likely be a breaking change. I’ll cc a few others who are more knowledgeable in this area.

/cc @SergeyKanzhelev @HirazawaUi

> This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.).

Do you really need to add a sleep in the preStop hook? When a Pod is deleted, its containers receive a SIGTERM, and if they don’t shutdown cleanly within terminationGracePeriodSeconds, they’ll be sent a SIGKILL. If the job implementation simply ignores SIGTERM, it should keep running until terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires (though this is best-effort and not a strict guarantee). Anyway, since a Pod can stop at any time for some reason (e.g. host error, node pressure), I think it’s safer to make the job idempotent or able to resume from intermediate checkpoints.

Agree fully. A SIGTERM handler and/or checkpointing are the more elegant and preferred solutions. They are not always possible, however, such as in the case of vendor-provided images. And even when we do control the application code, this would be much more effort to implement than simply adding 4 lines of YAML for a preStop sleep. One of those solutions is much easier to convince an app team to adopt than the other :)

In any case, I'm struggling to imagine a scenario where the sleep continuing after the process exits is desirable. And, for me, it is surprising behavior given that it is different from the `exec /bin/sleep` pattern that it was intended to replace.
/cc @esotsal

/triage accepted

We believe that your expectation is reasonable.

/cc @atiratree

Can you weigh in from the perspective of wg node lifecycle?

/cc @@AxeZhan

title: High-throughput container logs cause kubelet log rotation to hang, leading to unbounded 0.log growth (v1.27+ timestamp-based rotation)
body:
### What happened?

**What happened:**

In Kubernetes clusters running v1.27+, the new timestamp-based container log rotation mechanism (0.log.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS) fails to rotate logs for high-throughput containers (e.g., >50 MB/s). The 0.log file grows indefinitely (observed >12 GiB), even though containerLogMaxSize is set (e.g., 100Mi).

Kubelet’s log shows repeated "Adding new entry to the queue for processing" every containerLogMonitorInterval seconds, but no "rotateLog" or "rotateLog finished" logs for the affected container — indicating the rotation task never gets executed.

[Pasted Graphic 1.tiff](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22593110/Pasted.Graphic.1.tiff)

[Pasted Graphic.tiff](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22593115/Pasted.Graphic.tiff)

log config :  
containerLogMaxSize: 100Mi
containerLogMaxFiles: 5
containerLogMonitorInterval: 1s
containerLogMaxWorkers: 10



### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet should properly rotate container logs even under high-throughput logging workloads — specifically, the log rotation mechanism should not hang or fail to trigger when a container generates logs at a high rate. The 0.log file should be rotated once it exceeds containerLogMaxSize, preventing unbounded disk usage.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a pod that continuously writes logs at high throughput (e.g., ~100 MB/s),my yaml :
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-generator4dd
  namespace: lk
  labels:
    app: log-generator
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-generator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-generator
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: log-generator
        image: nginx:1.14.1-8.6
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        command: ["/bin/sh"]
        args:
          - -c
          - |
            echo "Starting TRUE 1GB/s log generator..."
            
            while true; do
              echo "$(date): Starting 1GB/s flood for 60 seconds..."
              
              for second in $(seq 1 60); do
                echo "$(date): Second $second - outputting 1GB..."
                
                timeout 1s dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=256 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' 'A' &
                timeout 1s dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=256 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' 'B' &
                timeout 1s dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=256 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' 'C' &
                timeout 1s dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=256 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' 'D' &
                wait
              done
              
              echo "$(date): 60GB flood completed, resting 30s..."
              sleep 30
            done
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "4Gi"
            cpu: "2000m"
          limits:
            memory: "8Gi"
            cpu: "4000m"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp-storage
          mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
      - name: tmp-storage
        emptyDir:
          sizeLimit: "512Mi"
      restartPolicy: Always

```

title: Lifecycle Hooks: PreStop httpGet hooks do not work with host networking
body:
### What happened?

Pods using both host networking and a `httpGet` preStop hook fail to execute the hook. If the same pods use pod networking, then the preStop hook succeeds.

The failure produces a Kubernetes event (potentially sensitive fields have been replaced by `...`):

<details>

author: bmacdonell-roblox

comments.body: /assign

Hi, @bmacdonell-roblox ,thank you for your reporting. I have reproduced the issue locally at HEAD. Currently, it appears that when a pod is configured with hostNetwork and an httpGet preStop lifecycle hook without specifying a host, this setup does not work as expected.

If you wish to use this functionality in the short term, you may configure the host field as follows:

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    httpGet:
      host: 127.0.0.1
      port: 80
      path: /
```
The core reason behind this issue can be traced back to the following critical piece of code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0bdf1f89c3a2eeac2a64ca29b93f552a4b601341/pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go#L149-L162

When Pod using `hostNetwork`, `containerManager.GetPodStatus` returns empty `status.IPs`
```
E0927 18:06:12.697255  125758 kuberuntime_container.go:763] "PreStop hook failed" err="failed to find networking container: &{f799f5cb-0f87-41b5-a57b-fcfc601e01a1 httpd default [] [0xc000e11180] [0xc000e11180] [id:\"a8c65989a9feaec291f0efc37e667442cc4463a1a22849c2a8ba3e2f89ea563a\" metadata:{name:\"httpd\" uid:\"f799f5cb-0f87-41b5-a57b-fcfc601e01a1\" namespace:\"default\"} created_at:1758967421585547002 network:{} linux:{namespaces:{options:{network:NODE pid:CONTAINER userns_options:{mode:NODE}}}} labels:{key:\"io.kubernetes.pod.name\" value:\"httpd\"} labels:{key:\"io.kubernetes.pod.namespace\" value:\"default\"} labels:{key:\"io.kubernetes.pod.uid\" value:\"f799f5cb-0f87-41b5-a57b-fcfc601e01a1\"} annotations:{key:\"kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration\" value:\"{\\\"apiVersion\\\":\\\"v1\\\",\\\"kind\\\":\\\"Pod\\\",\\\"metadata\\\":{\\\"annotations\\\":{},\\\"name\\\":\\\"httpd\\\",\\\"namespace\\\":\\\"default\\\"},\\\"spec\\\":{\\\"containers\\\":[{\\\"command\\\":[\\\"httpd\\\",\\\"-f\\\",\\\"-h\\\",\\\"/www\\\"],\\\"image\\\":\\\"busybox:latest\\\",\\\"lifecycle\\\":{\\\"preStop\\\":{\\\"httpGet\\\":{\\\"path\\\":\\\"/\\\",\\\"port\\\":80}}},\\\"name\\\":\\\"httpd\\\",\\\"ports\\\":[{\\\"containerPort\\\":80}],\\\"volumeMounts\\\":[{\\\"mountPath\\\":\\\"/www\\\",\\\"name\\\":\\\"data\\\",\\\"readOnly\\\":true}]}],\\\"hostNetwork\\\":true,\\\"volumes\\\":[{\\\"configMap\\\":{\\\"name\\\":\\\"data\\\"},\\\"name\\\":\\\"data\\\"}]}}\\n\"} annotations:{key:\"kubernetes.io/config.seen\" value:\"2025-09-27T18:03:41.253987393+08:00\"} annotations:{key:\"kubernetes.io/config.source\" value:\"api\"}] 2025-09-27 18:06:12.695446601 +0800 CST m=+555.788087135}" pod="default/httpd" podUID="f799f5cb-0f87-41b5-a57b-fcfc601e01a1" containerName="httpd" containerID="containerd://7a40ea604572a651154d9510147544a9e0d863b38e45cfcad1d62a8ac9feaed5"
```
/sig node

```
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    httpGet:
      host: 127.0.0.1
      port: 80
      path: /
```

Thanks, that's good to know! We had been working around it using an `exec` hook instead, but setting the `host` explicitly is a cleaner workaround.

> The core reason behind this issue can be traced back to the following critical piece of code:
> 
> [kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0bdf1f89c3a2eeac2a64ca29b93f552a4b601341/pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go#L149-L162)

That makes sense. What I haven't had time to figure out yet is why the lifecycle hooks are failing, while the `httpGet` liveness and readiness probes on the same pod are working - I would expect the lifecycle hooks and probes to share much of the same code.

host override was intentionally [created for this](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/):

> Here's one scenario where you would set it. Suppose the container listens on 127.0.0.1 and the Pod's hostNetwork field is true. Then host, under httpGet, should be set to 127.0.0.1. If your pod relies on virtual hosts, which is probably the more common case, you should not use host, but rather set the Host header in httpHeaders.

/sig auth
/sig network

to decide on what is the "correct" IP here. Especially with the host field restriction: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4940
/triage needs-information

> * The node IP might be publicly exposed, that seems is an unnecessary risk, and using it by default seem to contradict https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4940

No, the PSA is because we don't want people to be able to send probes to _unrelated_ IPs. Having it default to the primary node IP for hostNetwork pods does not contradict that.

> * A host can have multiple, dynamic, or virtual IP addresses

While that's true, a _hostNetwork pod_ has one official podIP (per family), which is the primary node IP. For example, if you have a Service that points to a hostNetwork pod, the Service will send traffic to that IP, whether or not that is convenient for you. (Maybe there should be a feature to be able to override the `podIPs` of hostNetwork pods.)

So IMO, preStop httpGet probes should probe the `podIP` by default, not 127.0.0.1. If you are explicitly making your hostNetwork pod only listen on 127.0.0.1, then you can also explicitly make your probes use `host: 127.0.0.1`. (This also doesn't conflict with KEP-4940; we had decided that `host: 127.0.0.1` for hostNetwork pods is a valid and supported use case, and at any rate, PSA also blocks hostNetwork pods, so you have to be bypassing it in this case anyway.)

> While that's true, a hostNetwork pod has one official podIP (per family), which is the primary node IP

This IP depends on multiple factors and flags, and in external cloud providers the assignment also depend on an external controller, that at scale can have significant latency, and this can not be solved because is by design.
This is a big problem for fast startup for hostNetwork pods that will use this feature will add a big penalty to the pod start, because the first checks will fail with "failed to find network status or pod IP for pod" if those addresses are not there.

In addition, hostNetwork pods are also typically used for node system components, that impact the node readiness, the impact on the node startup impact we'll be even worse.

> So IMO, preStop httpGet probes should probe the podIP by default

I do not disagree with you, my point is that beside PodIPs is more logical , IMO localhost is a better default because:
- it is simpler and faster and ubiquitous 
- it is more secure for kubelet to probe its own localhost address
- is less prone to errors with networking components , specially those that handle network policies ...

Actually, I would like to add another real-world usage scenario:

The container application uses `hostNetwork` but only listens on `POD_IP` for security reasons, e.g.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hostnetwork-podip-demo
  labels:
    app: hostnetwork-podip-demo
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet
  containers:
  - name: myapp
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - >
        ip=$(POD_IP);
        echo "App start, listening on $ip:8080";
        nc -lk -s $ip -p 8080 -e echo "hello from pod";
    env:
    - name: POD_IP
      valueFrom:
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: status.podIP
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
```
In this case, a preStop HTTP GET hook targeting `localhost:8080` would fail.

> This IP depends on multiple factors and flags, and in external cloud providers the assignment also depend on an external controller, that at scale can have significant latency, and this can not be solved because is by design.

Sure, and _in that case_, you can override the default. But most pods are not involved in bootstrapping the cluster, so we should choose a default based on what makes sense for them.

> IMO localhost is a better default

But your arguments mostly apply to hostNetwork pods as Service endpoints too, and we use the podIP there.

I feel like, even if localhost was more convenient in more situations, it would still be the wrong default because it's inconsistent. (Though I admit I don't really love that argument: "we have to be inconvenient here because we're inconvenient elsewhere".)

> This is a big problem for fast startup for hostNetwork pods that will use this feature

Well, we're talking about `preStop` here, and the problem doesn't apply to `postStart` because [`postStart`+`httpGet` doesn't work anyway](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133091#issuecomment-3097137762).

> The container application uses `hostNetwork` but only listens on `POD_IP` for security reasons, e.g., `--bind-address=$(POD_IP):8080`.
> 
> In this case, a preStop HTTP GET hook targeting `localhost:8080` would fail.

So, given that it currently doesn't work at all, we don't have to worry about breaking existing users. But yeah, this is still a problem: if `host` defaults to the pod/node IP and you want to override it to use localhost, you can say `host: 127.0.0.1`. But if `host` defaults to localhost and you want to override it to use the pod/node IP, you can't do it, because you don't know what that's going to be for sure until after you create the pod...

> if `host` defaults to localhost and you want to override it to use the pod/node IP, you can't do it, because you don't know what that's going to be for sure until after you create the pod

(Though, admittedly, being able to say something like `host: UseHostIP` or `host: UseSecondaryPodIP` would solve some use cases...)

> I feel like, even if localhost was more convenient in more situations, it would still be the wrong default because it's inconsistent. (Though I admit I don't really love that argument: "we have to be inconvenient here because we're inconvenient elsewhere".)

> In this case, a preStop HTTP GET hook targeting `localhost:8080` would fail.

ok, you have convinced me that "train has left the station" 

Thanks for the discussion

/triage accepted
/remove-triage needs-information
/priority important-longterm

title: Incorrect pod phase transition after node reboot with init containers
body:
### What happened?

A Pod with multiple init containers does not transition to the correct phase after a Node restart. I came across this issue while investigating the flaky test in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132930. For more information, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132930#issuecomment-3311419471.

The Pod phase is determined based on the ContainerStatus state of regular init containers, restartable init containers, and regular containers. For example, if there are any regular or restartable init containers that haven’t started yet, the Pod phase is considered Pending.

When a Node reboots, all containers in the Pod are restarted. In this case, the previous ContainerStatus state is preserved until the container actually restarts. As a result, if multiple init containers exist, the Pod phase incorrectly transitions to Running right after the first init container completes.

Here’s a rough timeline of what happens after a Node reboot:

1. Node reboots
1. Since all containers are stopped, if restartPolicy=Always, the Pod is considered Running because containers are being restarted
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1831-L1834
1. While a regular init container is running, the Pod phase becomes Pending
    https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1790-L1800
1. Once the regular init container exits, we fall back to step 2 and the Pod phase becomes Running again1. This flip-flop continues for each regular/restartable init container (Pending while running, Running once exited)

### What did you expect to happen?

Ideally, the Pod should remain in Pending until the regular containers have started (i.e. `podHasInitialized=true`). But we’ll need to carefully check that fixing this doesn’t break other scenarios outside of Node reboots.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

You can reproduce this issue by starting a Pod with multiple init containers similar to this Node E2E test case. And then deleting the PodSandbox to simulate a Node reboot.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0aeda7ba3766fe2fce2fa2e04c3fd37b8910efa3/test/e2e_node/container_lifecycle_test.go#L5918-L6054

If you’re able to run the Node E2E tests locally, you can use the following command:

```sh
make test-e2e-node FOCUS="should restart the containers in right order with the proper phase after the node reboot" SKIP="\[Flaky\]|\[Slow\]"
```

title: CEL CIDR parser does not behave as documented
body:
The docs for the CIDR-related CEL extensions say:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8e6d788887034b799f6c2a86991a68a080bb0576/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library/cidr.go#L47

but this is incorrect; the parser actually accepts that kind of string.

This seems to be a mistake: [we seem to have agreed in the original PR that we were going to add that restriction](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121912#discussion_r1395710965), but it accidentally only got added to the docs, not the actual implementation.

So now we need to decide between:
1. This is a bug, the function is not behaving as documented, so we should fix it.
2. People may be depending on the shipped behavior so it would be an API break to change it, so we need to just update the docs to reflect the actual behavior.

This was noticed while RH QE was testing the new UserDefinedNetwork types in ovn-kubernetes; some fields are validated with `isCIDR()` but were allowing non-subnet-like values that then didn't work. (Bug is https://issues.redhat.com/browse/CORENET-6423 but it's currently private.)

AdminNetworkPolicy is also using `isCIDR` for validation and expecting the "subnets/masks-only" semantics, not the "subnets/masks or ifaddr-style IP addresses" semantics...

/sig network
/priority important-soon
/cc @JoelSpeed @tssurya
author: danwinship

comments.body: /sig api-machinery

As a workaround, I believe the following would work for those who expect the documented behaviour
```
isCIDR(self) && cidr(self) == cidr(self).masked()
```

Thinking about it, if we allowed `masked` to exist, then we expected non-canonical representations. I guess we wouldn't have needed `masked` if we errored for a non-canonical CIDR right?

> `isCIDR(self) && cidr(self) == cidr(self).masked()`

Yeah, that's what I told ovn-k to do for now

> if we allowed `masked` to exist, then we expected non-canonical representations

Ah, it looks like `masked` didn't exist in the original proposal, and you suggested it in response to my suggestion that we reject these values, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121912#discussion_r1397156977

Except then you also added the doc string saying that we would reject those values. 😬  

I think if we really don't want to change the behavior of `cidr()`/`isCIDR()`, we should at least add an `isCIDRMask()` or something like that to simplify checking in that case.

But this would mean that `isCIDR` and `utilvalidation.IsValidCIDR` would not do the same thing. (`isCIDR` would actually correspond to `utilvalidate.IsValidInterfaceAddress`, while `utilvalidation.IsValidCIDR` would correspond to `isCIDRMask`...)
cc @alexzielenski @thockin for "declarative validation" tie-ins...

@cici37 @jpbetz Since you both have good experience around the CEL libraries stuff here, wanted to check your opinion. Do we have a choice to fix this behaviour and say it was a bug, or must we keep the behaviour the same now?

> we should at least add an `isCIDRMask()` or something

(FTR, if we go with this, I already implemented it before deciding I should file this bug instead, https://github.com/danwinship/kubernetes/commit/2376a4d5c4b91a15fdca3ccdc010556d9763101b)

/triage accepted
/assign @jpbetz @cici37

We should be *really* careful changing ungated behavior users could reasonably depend on, even if it was not our intention.

Mistakes that are clearly bugged, in the sense that the mistake is wrong and/or harmful, we should clearly fix.

In this case, if someone got broken by us changing the behavior to what we'd documented, could we reasonably claim it is a bug?  I'm not sure I could make the argument, but I'm not a networking expert, so I'm willing to defer of someone with deeper networking expertise says they can.

> in the sense that the mistake is wrong and/or harmful

The thing that the function currently does is a plausible thing that a function called `isCIDR` might do. But the thing that the documentation _claims_ it does is also plausible, and if you assume that the function behaves as documented, you might not ever notice that it also accepts additional strings that you hadn't wanted it to accept, which then potentially gets into "harmful".

In particular, note that we are in the process of making breaking change to core API validation of IP/CIDR-valued fields ([KEP-4858](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/4858-ip-cidr-validation)), part of which exactly corresponds to the suggestion here, because having the validation code accept ambiguously-interpretable values is potentially a security problem. (As of 1.33, using an ifaddr-like CIDR value in a field like NetworkPolicy `ipBlock` will cause an apiserver warning, and as of 1.36 it will be rejected.)

> if someone got broken by us changing the behavior

I'm having a hard time figuring out how to limit GitHub search to "useful results only", but the only existing users of `isCIDR` that I'm finding are:
- the [AdminNetworkPolicy CRDs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/network-policy-api/blob/main/apis/v1alpha1/shared_types.go), which [don't want the current semantics](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/network-policy-api/pull/324).
- the OpenShift [infrastructure config](https://github.com/openshift/api/blob/master/config/v1/types_infrastructure.go) and [network operator config](https://github.com/openshift/api/blob/master/operator/v1/types_network.go) CRDs, which don't want the current semantics.
- the [ovn-kubernetes UDN CRDs](https://github.com/ovn-kubernetes/ovn-kubernetes/blob/master/go-controller/pkg/crd/userdefinednetwork/v1/shared.go), which [don't want the current semantics](https://github.com/ovn-kubernetes/ovn-kubernetes/pull/5588).

Can also see usages in:
* https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/gke-networking-api
* https://github.com/metallb/metallb-operator

Though looking at the use cases, I suspect they wouldn't want the current semantics either

(metallb is just shipping one of the openshift/api CRDs.)

The gke-networking-api one is... interesting... the documentation text claims it accepts CIDRs, the validation accepts `isIP(self) || isCIDR(self)`, and the example in the documentation is `"192.168.1.1/24" or "2001:db9::/64"`. The upstream documentation (assuming I'm looking at the right page) says it takes "IP addresses in CIDR format". So... yeah

This issue is labeled with `priority/important-soon` but has not been updated in over 90 days, and should be re-triaged.
Important-soon issues must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

You can:
- Confirm that this issue is still relevant with `/triage accepted` (org members only)
- Deprioritize it with `/priority important-longterm` or `/priority backlog`
- Close this issue with `/close`

For more details on the triage process, see https://www.kubernetes.dev/docs/guide/issue-triage/

/remove-triage accepted

To avoid breaking backward incompatibility, I suspect the best thing to do here would be to add a `isCIDRStrict` function that internally does `isCIDR(self) && cidr(self) == cidr(self).masked()` and returns the result. That leaves anyone already using this un-broken with an opt-in for the "better" behaviour
what about adding two new functions (names TBD) and deprecating the original `isCIDR` (so we don't have the "obvious" name with the "non-obvious" semantics)?
I don't know what deprecating looks like in a CEL library, @jpbetz @cici37 have we done that before?

So, summarizing (for SIG Arch call discussion March 5)
- `isCIDR` is documented as having the same behavior as `utilvalidation.IsValidCIDR`, but actually has behavior closer to `utilvalidation.IsValidCIDRForLegacyField` with `StrictIPCIDRValidation=false` (boo!).
- This theoretically could cause security problems (which was our argument for doing an API-breaking fix with core validation).
- Presumably since we changed the validation behavior of core fields after several releases worth of warnings, we could do the same with CRD fields. Except that we can't attach warnings to CEL validation...
- If we can't fix the behavior of `isCIDR`, then we could deprecate and replace it. Except that we can't deprecate CEL functions...
- The longer we do nothing, the more chance there is that there will be users accidentally depending on the undocumented behavior of the function making it harder for us to fix later...

@TristonianJones 

These libraries have been upstreamed to the CEL community, and ported to Java, C, C++ as well?

> I don't know what deprecating looks like in a CEL library, @jpbetz @cici37 have we done that before?

No, we've never deprecated an CEL function. If we go that way (not saying we should), I believe we could try to start to warn if a deprecated function is used...

In this case. It's unclear to me how widespread this is.  If we believe use cases are very small to non-existent and we believe it's dangerous to use, treating it as a breaking security fix might be appropriate.

> The longer we do nothing, the more chance there is that there will be users accidentally depending on the undocumented behavior of the function making it harder for us to fix later...

100%

> If we believe use cases are very small to non-existent and we believe it's dangerous to use, treating it as a breaking security fix might be appropriate.

Yeah, it's not like that.

There is a single use case for accepting the more-loosely-validated form (working directly with Linux network interfaces), and everybody else wants the more-strictly-validated form. Up until recently, every CIDR-valued field in `k8s.io/api` wanted the stricter validation, but with the addition of the DRA networking stuff, there is now _1_ CIDR-valued field in `k8s.io/api` that wants the looser validation. Of course there are more APIs working directly with Linux network interfaces outside k/k than inside k/k (CNI/Multus, kubevirt, kubernetes-nmstate, etc), so there'd probably be more people who want the looser validation with CRDs than in core APIs. Though all of the people we could find currently using `isCIDR` in CRDs want the stricter validation (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134224#issuecomment-3352402808). (Of course, it is possible that the people who actually _want_ the looser validation are avoiding `isCIDR` because they read the documentation and so they believe it doesn't do what they want...)

As for "dangerous", it's _theoretically_ dangerous, but it's definitely more annoying than dangerous (in that it may allow users to accidentally enter values that won't actually work).

OK, I think I'm caught up.

I'm supportive of adding `isStrictCIDR()` and `isInterfaceAddress()` (or whatever the replacements should be named) and deprecating `isCIDR()` by emitting a warning for creation of resources that contain uses of `isCIDR()`.  We can detect this statically.

So if you were to do a CRD create (or VAP or whatever), and the resource contains a CEL expression with `isCIDR()` the API response would contain a warning that would be displayed in kubectl output.

We even add a strict mode to CRD creation that fails CRD creation if warnings (CEL compilation or otherwise) are encountered to allow CRD writers to say "I'd rather have the resource creation fail than tolerate warnings".  But that would be future work, I think.

Thoughts?

Sounds good to me.

> deprecating `isCIDR()` by emitting a warning for creation of resources that contain uses of `isCIDR()`. We can detect this statically.

There's nothing existing that does that, right? This would need to be implemented?

> Sounds good to me.
> 
> > deprecating `isCIDR()` by emitting a warning for creation of resources that contain uses of `isCIDR()`. We can detect this statically.
> 
> There's nothing existing that does that, right? This would need to be implemented?

Yes.. and unfortunately this could be quite a lot of work.
ok... well, for now I can create new functions and just note in the documentation that we consider `isCIDR` to be deprecated, and that there might be warnings about it in the future.

> ok... well, for now I can create new functions and just note in the documentation that we consider `isCIDR` to be deprecated, and that there might be warnings about it in the future.

SG. That puts is a strictly better situation than now.

/triage accepted
/assign

title: Clean up features for SIG Node e2e tests
body:
We use features to indicate the environment that is "not standard" for e2e tests - i.e. requires extra configuration beyond feature gates.

This is uber issue to review sig-node features and clean them up:

1. If the Feature is used to indicate just a "category" of tests - remove it
2. If the Feature is used when FeatureGate must be used - replace with the FeatureGate

Once we clear things up we may decide to pass the `Feature` as an argument for the test lane (similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/35531 idea) and have more automated validation that the test requiring the Feature are only run in the test lane implementing this special environment

title: DRA API: driver names may have upper-case characters but is not caseless
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Originally discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134094#issuecomment-3304401401

The API validation allows driver names with upper ("FOO.COM") or even mixed case ("Foo.com"). However, conceptually "FOO.COM" and "Foo.com" are different drivers because all string comparisons compare the strings literally.

We should:
- Document the driver name fields as "this allows upper-case names but is not caseless - it treats upper-case and lower-case as different values". This applies to the fields and the CEL expression documentation.
- Warn about driver names with upper characters. We can do this for fields, but not for CEL expressions (or not easily there).

/wg device-management
/priority backlog


### Why is this needed?

Less surprises for users. Driver names should always be lower case.

Hi, I’m interested in contributing to this issue.
I see that the original discussion suggests:
Documenting that driver names may include uppercase but are not caseless.
Warning users if driver names contain uppercase letters.
I have already updated the documentation in a PR, but I’d like guidance on the warning for uppercase driver names:
What’s the preferred way to surface such a warning in Kubernetes validation functions?
Should it be a field.Error, a log, or something else?
I want to implement this correctly and would appreciate advice on the best approach.

Let's do one PR for all of the changes.

For warnings, [`WarningsOnUpdate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fce5a08b9247b608c73cdeacde939c7e4951bce3/pkg/registry/resource/resourceslice/strategy.go#L90-L92) and [`WarningsOnCreate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fce5a08b9247b608c73cdeacde939c7e4951bce3/pkg/registry/resource/resourceslice/strategy.go#L63-L65) need to be implemented. You can probably find some other implementations to see what such warnings should look like.

I think it's sufficient to warn for ResourceSlices. If a driver ignores the guidance and publishes a its slices with mixed or upper case driver name, then all downstream components like the scheduler have no choice and have to use that name. Sending a warning to them on e.g. a ResourceClaim status update with the driver name makes no sense.

/close

title: remove old conntrack setup workaround once we stop supporting containerd 1.7
body:
Kube-proxy has a very old workaround for the inability to set one of the conntrack parameters at startup, #28697. (If we detect the bug happening, we just fail to set the conntrack parameter, and log an Event.)

It seems that the underlying problem is in the kernel, and is that if you try to start a hostNetwork container with sysfs mounted read-write while there is already a hostNetwork container with sysfs mounted read-only, then the kernel will silently ignore the "read-write" and just give you a read-only sysfs. (eg, https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/24000#issuecomment-906367168)

It was originally believed that the bug only happens at scale, because it was only seen in 1000-node tests, but it might just be that those are the only jobs that are trying to override the relevant conntrack parameter. (At least on Fedora, the default value of `/sys/module/nf_conntrack/parameters/hashsize` is larger than it needs to be to support the default value of `--conntrack-max-per-core`, so kube-proxy wouldn't even try to set it unless you were overriding `--conntrack-max-per-core`.)

Anyway, the problem is believed to be fixed in containerd 2.0.3+ and 2.1+ (https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/11271), and in cri-o since forever ago (https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/pull/2627).

I think we don't require containerd 2.x, so we can't remove the workaround yet. Assuming that the problem even still exists, which I don't think we have any information about... it was allegedly fixed in dockershim in 1.21 (#96877) but it's not clear if any corresponding fix was made/needed/possible in the CRI codepaths.

So:
1. If someone could figure out if the bug ever still exists anywhere (5000Node job logs?) that would be cool.
2. If it doesn't still exist anywhere, we should remove the workaround now.
3. If it does still exist, we should update the [comments in the code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0-alpha.0/cmd/kube-proxy/app/conntrack.go#L76-L82) to reference this issue and the fact that we're waiting until we require a newer containerd.

title: DRA consumable capacity failed to allocate the same device once device consumes counterSet
body:
### What happened?

The device that consumed counterSet is skipped if the counter is not left enough even it was selected and allowMultipleAllocations is set.

The reason is that the checkAvailableCounters is called and return false as it is selected once before the capacity will be checked.

title: Incorrect PodMemory usage after container termination
body:
### What happened? PodMemory metric continued to be available for few minutes after pod was removed from the node. ### What did you expect to happen? PodMemory metric should have been removed from the old pod instance as soon as new pod was destroyed or new pod was created. From initial understanding, kubelet/cAdvisor housekeepingInterval seems to be the static interval at which housekeeping should occur. If allowDynamicHousekeeping is enabled, cAdvisor determines the actual housekeeping interval based on houseKeepingInterval and maxHousekeepingInterval as shown in [manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2) with some jitter. Need to understand the behaviour of [statsCacheDuration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.4/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L55-L58) and maxHousekeepingInterval when kubelet is restarted. Does kubelet dump the cache data to disk before the package upgrade? Moreover, since these maintenance are happening for kubelet upgrades, does time to upgrade and bootstrap kubelet could lead to additional delay in housekeeping. One more weird observation I could find is, node uuid has changed twice, once while upgrading at 11 AM(which is relevant for this issue) and then again at 2 PM(which is unrelated). ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? This was observed during kubernetes upgrade. Node was drained and kubelet was upgraded. ### Anything else we need to know? **Context** In case of Kubernetes Upgrade related maintenances, pods are rescheduled or temporarily evicted from the node. It has been observed that the newly formed pod consumes approximately double the memory of the original pod at startup. Multiple alerts are raised due to this as it can violate set alerting thresholds. Below is the original query raising PodMemory alert for workload. We can notice the query is granular at pod level. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` From the graph view, we can see a sudden spike in memory usage before 11 AM when the pod got rescheduled. However, since the above query doesn't show the pod reschedule, we can fix it by adding pod uid into the query. ``` max_over_time( max by (workload, pod, uid) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, uid) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="",container!="",image!="",namespace=~"scorpius.*"} * on (namespace, pod) group_left (uid) kube_pod_info{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery-2.*"} ) )[15m:] ) ``` Now, the below graph clearly shows data for earlier instance of pod grocery-2-0 is available till 11:10, well into the startup of new instances of pod grocery-2-0. This contributes to the overall memory usage since we are doing a join query with granularity of pod labels. You can also see that once the metrics for older instance stop relaying, the overall memory usage for pod grocery-2-0 drops down. While we have fixed the query to segregate container instances, we can see the cached metrics still getting emitted post 10:55 and before 11:10, after container is terminated. ``` max_over_time( max by (namespace, workload, name, pod) ( sum by (namespace, workload, pod, name) ( container_memory_working_set_bytes{cluster="", namespace=~"scorpius.*", container!="", image!="", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"} * on(namespace, pod, name) group_left(uid) label_replace( kube_pod_container_info{namespace=~"scorpius.*", container="aerospike-server", pod=~"uar-mapi-everest-grocery.*"}, "name", "$1", "container_id", ".*://(.+)" ) * on (namespace, pod) group_left (workload, workload_type) namespace_workload_pod:kube_pod_owner:relabel{cluster="",namespace=~"scorpius.*",workload_type="statefulset"} ) ) [15m:]) ``` ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.33.2 Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 Server Version: v1.31.4 ```
### Cloud provider

title: Add Verbose Logging to net/http for Egress Auditing and Rename probe/http/http.go
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:

Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.

A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.

A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.

Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.

### Why is this needed?

Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.

To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.

The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam. The klog output strips the full file path, so both staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go (our target) and pkg/probe/http/http.go (an unrelated file) show up in logs simply as http.go.

As a result, setting --vmodule=http*=5 to enable our new logs also enables verbose logging in the probe helpers, flooding the logs with messages from liveness and readiness probes. This makes it extremely difficult to isolate the critical egress traffic data needed for validation. Renaming the probe helper file to http_prober.go cleanly resolves this name collision and allows for precise, targeted logging for this important security use case.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should not crash, regardless of compiler optimization settings.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a windows node with `m7i.large` instanceType and `WindowsServer2022FullContainer` amiFamily
2. Create a Windows storage class
3. Create a PVC
4. Deploy a Windows pod with persistent volume:


### Anything else we need to know?

Currently I am suspecting that the crash is related to this specific line which appears in the crash dump:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go#L255

```
klog.V(4).Info(log("attacher.GetDeviceMountPath(%v)", spec))
```
***
1. `log()` function calls `fmt.Sprintf()` to format the `spec` parameter
2. `spec` is a `*volume.Spec` containing a PersistentVolume object
3. `PersistentVolume.String()` method is called (generated protobuf code)
4. This calls `PersistentVolumeStatus.String()` which includes:
   go
  LastPhaseTransitionTime: + strings.Replace(fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime), "Time", "v1.Time", 1) + ,,

5. LastPhaseTransitionTime is a *metav1.Time (pointer to metav1.Time)
6. When fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime)
 is called on a nil pointer, Go attempts to call the String() method
7. metav1.Time embeds time.Time, and time.Time.String() has a value receiver: func (t Time) String()

8. To call this method, Go tries to dereference the nil *metav1.Time pointer, causing a panic

**Windows-specific behavior:**
- fmt.Sprintf normally recovers from panics during string formatting
- However, on Windows with compiler optimizations enabled, sometimes this panic recovery fails
- The panic escalates to runtime.sigpanic and eventually runtime.throw
- **Workaround:** Changing the log statement to print spec.Name instead of the full spec
 object avoids the crash

**Evidence supporting this theory:**
1. Crash disappears with compiler optimizations disabled (-gcflags="-N -l"
)
2. Crash disappears when avoiding the problematic `klog.V(4).Info` call on `spec` and switching to `spec.Name()`
3. Stack trace shows runtime.sigpanic failing to recover properly on Windows
4. Issue is reproducible and consistently tied to CSI volume reconstruction logging

This suggests a bug in Go's Windows runtime where panic recovery during string formatting fails, causing what should be a recoverable panic to become a fatal crash.

I am not sure if this is a known issue in Windows. However, I think a way to fix this is to implement a `String()` method of v1.Time that does an explicit null check, so that we do not have to rely on golangs default sigpanic recovery (which seems to not work well in Windows environments). Is there any concern with this approach?

title: Kubelet rejects pod with "NodeAffinity failed" due to stale informer data
body:
#### What happened

This issue is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100467 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/92067.

We have a controller that adds labels to a node after it starts up. It looks like there are cases where the scheduler is able to see the new node labels and schedule a pod, but the kubelet somehow doesn't see the new labels - it has stale data in its informer cache. Whatever the reason for the stale data, the result is that the kubelet rejects the pod with "NodeAffinity failed".

#### What did you expect to happen

Kubelet to be able to detect the new node labels and not reject the pod. 

The only reason that we need to keep the node affinity / node selector check in the kubelet is in case someone sets `nodeName` directly on the pod, so that it does not go through the scheduler, so we can't just remove enforcement on the node level.

The short-term fix would be for the kubelet to synchronously fetch the node object when (and only when) it sees these "NodeAffinity failed" errors and try again. To ensure we do not introduce additional heavy traffic when there many pods being scheduled at once, we will have to keep a new cache, separate from the informer cache. The logic would be like:
- Read the node object from the informer
- If we get a NodeAffinity failed error, read the node object from our new cache
- If we still get a NodeAffinity failed error, fetch the node object synchronously from the api server
The cache should be updated whenever we see a node object that is newer than the one we are currently storing - this can come from either the informer or from the synchronous fetch. 

Long term, maybe we can re-consider the flow for `nodeName`, or leverage something like [kubelet synchronous admission](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O9rDeYhGWMbtg-DQmhqKvNsQSHWJSwvSEeNpXTKMvZg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6ggs708p6vvu) to keep the scheduler and kubelet coordinated. There are also some more general discussions about what to do when informer data is stale, maybe the outcomes there can help here.

#### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

You'd probably have to restart kubelet a whole bunch of times, and have a controller that modifies the node labels whenever it restarts.

#### Environment
- Kubernetes version: The issue is reported as persistent from versions v1.18-v1.28+, and it is unlikely that it has been fixed in a more recent version.
- Cloud provider: GKE

/sig node
/assign
/cc @tallclair
author: natasha41575

comments.body: /kind bug

/cc @serathius @liggitt 
For discussions on syncing informers.

> The logic would be like:
> 
> * Read the node object from the informer
> * If we get a NodeAffinity failed error, read the node object from our new cache
> * If we still get a NodeAffinity failed error, fetch the node object synchronously from the api server
>   The cache should be updated whenever we see a node object that is newer than the one we are currently storing - this can come from either the informer or from the synchronous fetch.

I think the first & second bullet can be combined. I'm picturing a cache object that looks something like this:

```go
type nodeCache struct {
	nodeName string
	nodeLister corelisters.NodeLister
	cachedNode *v1.Node
	client clientset.Interface
}

func (c *nodeCache) GetCache() *v1.Node {
	informerNode, _ := c.nodeLister.Get(c.nodeName)
	if c.cachedNode == nil || isNewer(informerNode, c.cachedNode) {
		return informerNode
	}
	return c.cachedNode
}

func (c *nodeCache) GetSync (*v1.Node, error) {
	node, err := c.client.CoreV1().Nodes().Get(context.Background(), c.nodeName, metav1.GetOptions{})
	if err != nil { return nil, err }
	c.cachedNode = node
	return node, nil
}
```

I'm just not sure how to do the `isNewer` check. I thought we weren't supposed to parse resourceVersion, but it looks like the [scheduler does it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbd859808d0cef566fbfc89639926b7cc50d9bd5/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L236), so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Then the steps look like:
1. Run the admission check using the node from `GetCache`
2. If there is a node affinity error, rerun the admission check using the node from `GetSync`

My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that. IMO the affinity check should just be a scheduling policy. Once the pod is scheduled to the node, the Kubelet shouldn't need to enforce it.

> My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that.

Yeah I'm not sure I understand what the affinity check in the kubelet is for. If someone is setting `nodeName` explicitly to bypass the scheduler, I could see the desired behavior as being to ignore node affinity (what is the purpose of setting `nodeName` to a node that's just going to reject the pod?). But I agree that it is too late to change this now.

> I'm just not sure how to do the `isNewer` check. I thought we weren't supposed to parse resourceVersion, but it looks like the [scheduler does it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbd859808d0cef566fbfc89639926b7cc50d9bd5/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L236), so ¯_(ツ)_/¯

There's agreement on relaxing to let clients start comparing... specifics proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5505

> My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that.

Yeah, historically labels/selectors and taints/tolerations have been used not only as scheduling directives but also as protection boundaries in combination with admission forcing / forbidding pods from selecting / tolerating specific nodes, so Kubelet also doing a check to refuse to run pods assigned to it but not matching its labels / tolerating its taints is something we can't drop.

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

/remove-priority longterm
/priority important-soon

title: The allocatable and capacity values ​​for "ephemeral-storage" under node.status are not displayed in the same format.
body:
### What happened? I'm checking the status of a node and noticed that the base of the **"ephemeral-storage"** field in the allocatable and capacity fields is inconsistent. The "ephemeral-storage" field under allocatable is in **binary format**, while the "ephemeral-storage" field under capacity is in **decimal format**. title: The crictl test fails on kOps
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build

### Which tests are failing?

[sig-node] crictl should be able to run crictl on the node

### Since when has it been failing?

26.08.2025

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-presubmits#pull-kops-kubernetes-e2e-ubuntu-gce-build

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Related to changes added by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476:
```
exitCode=127 stdout="" stderr="sh: 1: /home/kubernetes/bin/crictl: not found\n", might retry
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The  path for the `crictl` binary has been hardcoded to `/home/kubernetes/bin/crictl`. This is something specific to ContainerOS.
Additionally, `crictl` is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like `[Feature:crictl]`.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig-node
author: hakman

comments.body: /cc @SergeyKanzhelev @mauriciopoppe @ameukam
/sig node
@dims That won't help as the path is hardcoded in the test. Already tried in https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/pull/17605.
In a kOps cluster, is `critctl`'s location added to the `PATH`?

@mauriciopoppe depends on the distro, in most cases the path is `/usr/local/bin/crictl`, but would prefer to not have `crictl` as a fixed dependency for running the test suite. Is there any documentation that marks this a requirement?

The filename is called `crictl.go` so I think it's a dependency. The objective of the test is to verify that running `crictl` remotely through `kubectl exec` is successful across all the nodes in the cluster. 

> Additionally, crictl is not a requirement for a node to run, so maybe this should be a feature-specific test like [Feature:crictl].

I agree, I'll add the feature tag.

Thanks @mauriciopoppe.
Could you also add a few more retries for different paths, or try to run from `PATH`?

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon
/assign @mauriciopoppe
For the short term I'll revert https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133476. Later, I'll do the refactor once again with a feature tag added.

https://testgrid.k8s.io/kops-gce#kops-gce-latest is green!
