title: kubelet_volume_stats_* metrics not available in 1.34
body:
### What happened?

When using Kubernetes version 1.34 `kubelet_volume_stats_*` metrics such as `kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes` are no longer present in `kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$NODE/proxy/metrics"`.

I know that they are in Alpha state and Alpha metrics do not come with any guarantees, but since they are still [documented](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/#list-of-alpha-kubernetes-metrics) I expect them to be visible. If this change was intended, it doesn't seem to be documented.

I was not able to correlate this with anything mentioned in [CHANGELOG-1.34.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.34.md).

title: Pods rejected by kubelet admission control enter 'ContainerStatusUnknown' state after kubelet restart
body:
### What happened?

In scenarios where kubelet [rejects](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8a28b17c3adab3f0c9ffb8107554b2ed5021fd14/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2273-L2279) a pod via its own admission control (`canAdmitPod`), for instance-

- When the NodeResourcesFit filter is disabled in kube-scheduler, or when a pod is directly created with a spec.nodeName (ensuring the scheduler does not validate pod resource requests against a node's capacity) AND the pod's requests exceed the node's available capacity. In this case, kubelet will reject the pod, eg. with the reason 'OutOfCpu'.

- When pods are stuck pending due to taints on a node, and the taint is removed, there appears to be a race between kube-scheduler placing the pod on the node and kubelet detecting the updated taints on the node (which makes sense, they are both presumably backed by independent watches). In this case, kubelet will reject the pod with the 'TaintToleration' reason. This is a lot harder to reproduce though, because it's racey.

This leaves the pod with a status that has an overall failed phase but no containerStatuses.
```yaml
...
status:
  message: 'Pod was rejected: Node didn''t have enough resource: cpu, requested: 8000,
    used: 950, capacity: 4000'
  phase: Failed
  qosClass: Guaranteed
  reason: OutOfcpu
  startTime: "2025-08-27T15:47:53Z"

```

After a kubelet restart (Which can be done for a few reasons, eg. handling in-place node resize, or a node reboot.), these pods transition into a ContainerStatusUnknown state.

```bash
$ kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS     RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     OutOfcpu   0          2s

$ docker exec -it $(docker ps | grep kindest | awk '{print $1}') systemctl restart kubelet

$ kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS                   RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     ContainerStatusUnknown   0          17s

```

where the overall status now has additional conditions for last probe time, container statuses showing container status unknown, etc.
```
status:
  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "False"
    type: PodReadyToStartContainers
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "True"
    type: Initialized
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    reason: PodFailed
    status: "False"
    type: Ready
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    reason: PodFailed
    status: "False"
    type: ContainersReady
  - lastProbeTime: null
    lastTransitionTime: "2025-08-27T15:48:34Z"
    status: "True"
    type: PodScheduled
  containerStatuses:
  - image: busybox:1.37.0-glibc
    imageID: ""
    lastState: {}
    name: busybox
    ready: false
    restartCount: 0
    started: false
    state:
      terminated:
        exitCode: 137
        finishedAt: null
        message: The container could not be located when the pod was terminated
        reason: ContainerStatusUnknown
        startedAt: null
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
      name: kube-api-access-79svn
      readOnly: true
      recursiveReadOnly: Disabled
  hostIP: 172.18.0.2
  hostIPs:
  - ip: 172.18.0.2
  message: 'Pod was rejected: Node didn''t have enough resource: cpu, requested: 8000,
    used: 950, capacity: 4000'
  phase: Failed
  qosClass: Guaranteed
  reason: OutOfcpu
  startTime: "2025-08-27T15:47:53Z"
```

A similar issue can also be reproduced when using init containers
```bash
kubectl get po -A
NAMESPACE            NAME                                         READY   STATUS                        RESTARTS   AGE
default              busybox                                      0/1     Init:ContainerStatusUnknown   0          11s
```



### What did you expect to happen?

I'm not sure if this is by design, but I would expect such rejected pods to remain in an OutOfCpu/TaintsToleration failure state. No containers were ever started as the pod was rejected in admission control. The error _sounds_ like something went missing from the container runtime, but that did not happen, of course.

We could work around this by GCing such pods, but I wonder if this could be handled more gracefully at the Kubernetes layer (and I would also hate to mask genuine container runtime issues by clubbing multiple such ContainerStatusUnknown issues together)


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using 'kind' for ease of cluster LCM, but this can happen in any vanilla K8s cluster.

- Ensure you have kind installed.
```bash
go install sigs.k8s.io/kind@v0.29.0
```

- Create a massive pod (in terms of container requests) that cannot fit on the node based on node selector. eg. pod.yaml

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  ...
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "64000Mi"
        cpu: "8000m"
      limits:
        memory: "64000Mi"
        cpu: "8000m"
```

- Apply the YAML
```bash
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
```
- Verify pod state

```bash
➜  ContainerStatusUnknown-repro kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS     RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     OutOfcpu   0          2s
```

- Docker exec into the kind node and restart kubelet
```bash
docker exec -it $(docker ps | grep kindest | awk '{print $1}') systemctl restart kubelet
```

- Verify pod state

```bash
➜  ContainerStatusUnknown-repro kubectl get po
NAME      READY   STATUS                   RESTARTS   AGE
busybox   0/1     ContainerStatusUnknown   0          17s
```


### Anything else we need to know?

Sifting through the kubelet code, I saw a few sites where we seem to iterate over the containers for a pod and if any are missing statuses (eg. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/850bc09e9b78e49ec2459515379ae042a142e5c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L441-L470) - my guess is post restart there's a full sync being run and kubelet has lost track of the fact that no containers were ever started for that pod. I imagine it's possible to instrument kubelet with targeted logging to see the specific site where this is happening.


### Kubernetes version

Reproduced in multiple k8s versions-

1.31.14 (VMware)
1.33.0 (kind)


### Cloud provider

N/A, reproduced on VMware and kind.

### OS version

N/A, does not seem OS specific. reproduced on Photon OS and kind.

title: Device Plugins: "Unexpected: unhealthyDevices and endpoints became out of sync"
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet puts this error in the log 5 minutes (`endpointStopGracePeriod` I guess) after running DRA e2e "supports extended resources together with ResourceClaim" test: `I0822 10:03:19.580504 2854861 devicemanager.go:471] "Unexpected: unhealthyDevices and endpoints became out of sync"`

title: kubelet: Refactor ComputePodQOS by extracting resource-collection logic (no behavior change)
body:
@ndixita Hi! I know you’re very busy. if you have a moment, I’d really appreciate your quick thoughts on this small refactor 🙏 

While reading the kubelet code, I came across the TODO comment you left in ComputePodQOS, which prompted me to think about this. If this looks reasonable, I can open a PR with the extraction and tests

### Summary
`ComputePodQOS` currently does two things:
1. collect resources from the Pod/containers, and
2. decide the QoS class.
Per the existing TODO, I propose extracting the resource-collection into a helper to improve readability and testability (behavior remains the same).


### Proposal
Introduce a helper like:
```go
func collectPodResources(pod *v1.Pod) (v1.ResourceList, v1.ResourceList, bool)
```

and simplify `ComputePodQOS`:
```go
func ComputePodQOS(pod *v1.Pod) v1.PodQOSClass {
    reqs, lims, isGuaranteed := collectPodResources(pod)

    if len(reqs) == 0 && len(lims) == 0 {
        return v1.PodQOSBestEffort
    }
    if isGuaranteed && resourceListsEqual(reqs, lims) {
        return v1.PodQOSGuaranteed
    }
    return v1.PodQOSBurstable
}
```

### Why
- Clear separation of concerns (“collect inputs” vs “decide QoS”)
- Easier unit testing for edge cases (pod-level vs container-level, initContainers, missing cpu/memory)
- Pure refactor, no semantic changes


### Tests
- Add focused unit tests for the helper covering

title: ServiceCIDR is known to not work in some clusters, but blocking it via VAP violates conformance
body:
The ServiceCIDR API requires support from non-core-k8s components in some clusters, and thus is not guaranteed to work in all clusters. The [ServiceCIDR documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/network/extend-service-ip-ranges/#preventing-unauthorized-servicecidr-creation-update-using-validating-admission-policy) explains how you can use VAP to block usage of the API in this case. (Though there are some problems and https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/51748 updates those docs.)

However, it turns out that doing this violates conformance, because the test `[sig-network] ServiceCIDR and IPAddress API should support ServiceCIDR API operations [Conformance]` requires that `e2e.test` is able to modify the default ServiceCIDR.

The test case just adds an annotation, so we could hack up the VAP to allow the specific change that the conformance test makes, but this seems like cheating, and would also be fragile.

Does it make sense for conformance to require ServiceCIDR to be available as an API, given that it doesn't work in some clusters and we explicitly document how to disable it? (FWIW I guess the same question could be asked about NetworkPolicy, except that everyone has gotten used to the fact that the NP API exists even in clusters where it doesn't work so no one tries to disable it...)

/sig network
/area conformance
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon
cc @aojea
author: danwinship

comments.body:
> Does it make sense for conformance to require ServiceCIDR to be available as an API, given that it doesn't work in some clusters and we explicitly document how to disable it? (FWIW I guess the same question could be asked about NetworkPolicy, except that everyone has gotten used to the fact that the NP API exists even in clusters where it doesn't work so no one tries to disable it...)

I think we can add it as ineligible for conformance

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4e8b192b66cc2a6952b8f1a5067e563c4019c276/test/conformance/testdata/ineligible_endpoints.yaml#L277-L297

> The ServiceCIDR API requires support from non-core-k8s components in some clusters

Which non-core components? Service is implemented by kube-proxy ...? I would expect clusters to be compatible with the APIs implemented by core components.

> The [ServiceCIDR documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/network/extend-service-ip-ranges/#preventing-unauthorized-servicecidr-creation-update-using-validating-admission-policy) explains how you can use VAP to block usage of the API in this case.

... We also test privileged pods which we advertise options to restrict. (And some clusters like GKE autopilot do not permit them)

Some components need to know the set of all active servicecidrs. Network plugins / service proxy implementations often need to create routes related to service IPs. (e.g., in ovn-kubernetes, service proxying happens on the OVN bridge, so there needs to be a route for each service CIDR from the host network namespace to the OVN bridge, or else hostnetwork-to-service traffic would hit the default route and get sent out eth0).

In theory, all such components should eventually be updated to deal with ServiceCIDR, but we can't assume that will be true in the first release where the API was enabled by default. (And we _still_ don't assume all clusters will implement NetworkPolicy...)

> I would expect clusters to be compatible with the APIs implemented by core components.

There's no way this feature could have been added as a k8s API that would have made it automatically work with all existing software, due to things like the fact that there is no such thing as global configuration in k8s.
(I don't love the fact that the API is available by default and you have to disable it if you know it wouldn't work, rather than the other way around, but 🤷‍♂️ )
AFAIK is only ovnkube the one with issues, cilium, calico, kindnet, antrea, flannel ... all of them work just fine without any changes

It's not just ovnkube; OpenShift wouldn't work right without changes even if it was using a different network plugin, because, eg, we have an admission plugin that needs to know the service CIDRs, and it doesn't currently know to watch ServiceCIDR. At any rate, I assume you aren't arguing that ovnkube is implementing service proxying in an "illegal" way, so even if it was just ovnkube that was affected, it's not ovnkube's fault.

The ServiceCIDR feature implicitly assumes that it's fine for kube-apiserver to change the set of service CIDRs at any time, under the theory that nothing except kube-apiserver needs to care what the service CIDR was. Except we knew that wasn't true even within k/k; kcm and kube-proxy both care sometimes. But anyway, _there was no way this feature could have been added as a k8s API that would have made it automatically work with all existing software_, so the options were to add it in a way that didn't automatically work everywhere, or to just continue not adding it even though we knew lots of people wanted the feature.

(Though for future reference, the rollout may have been a little less bumpy if we hadn't gone from "beta but disabled" to "GA and enabled" without passing through "beta and enabled"...)

> It's not just ovnkube; OpenShift wouldn't work right without changes even if it was using a different network plugin [...]

> Though for future reference, the rollout may have been a little less bumpy if we hadn't gone from "beta but disabled" to "GA and enabled" without passing through "beta and enabled"..

This still seems ... less than convincing. We have one set of additional packages that needs updating to new changes in Kubernetes.

We often have other action required changes that affect external software, that doesn't preclude it from being in conformance

That software combination does not need to certify on the day of 1.34 release, it can even continue to advertise the certified conformance logo for quite some time, the CNCF won't even be ready to process submissions for some weeks and doesn't require submitting more than ~annually.
cc @dims @johnbelamaric

> one set of additional packages

It's one set of additional packages that _I_ know about. And, contrary to what Antonio said, Antrea did need to be changed to support this; it's just that they did it already. (They need the change for the same reason ovn-kubernetes does; because they need to create routes for each service CIDR.) I did not bother to check every other package.

And this isn't some sort of surprise; we _knew_ it was going to break third-party components when it landed, and we agreed, as part of promoting it to GA, that we would fully support allowing clusters to disable the feature. We just learned from [KEP-2593](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2593)'s failure and made sure the feature was designed in a way so that all third-party components could _eventually_ be updated to handle `ServiceCIDR` (which wasn't possible with KEP-2593's `ClusterCIDR`, which is why it got reverted).

_And_ it turns out, Antonio already even added the correct API endpoints to [the `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` file](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133613#issuecomment-3202670338), he just accidentally also made the conformance test test the endpoints that weren't supposed to be part of conformance. So the bug here is really just "we have a conformance test which is testing something we already documented as not being part of conformance". (I hadn't realized that when I filed the bug.)

ACK -- it's just important that we're clear about why we're dropping something from conformance. "Some optional third party packages don't support it [yet]" is not a good reason, and we don't want this being cited for the next conformance change.

"We already agreed these endpoints are out of scope" is a good reason :-)

>  I assume you aren't arguing that ovnkube is implementing service proxying in an "illegal" way,

absolutely never tried to imply that specially because this is not about the implementation of Services ... we discussed this heavily and I agreed with you there and now, ...  so forget about this comment and treat it as a "before going to sleep inappropriate comment in github" , on my mind was reading as "this was promoted lightly" and I wanted to justify myself that I spent time in evaluating the impact, I added jobs in kops to run with cilium and other plugins, asked other communities, but obviously I didn;t do it for openshift since I always rely on you :)

> (Though for future reference, the rollout may have been a little less bumpy if we hadn't gone from "beta but disabled" to "GA and enabled" without passing through "beta and enabled"...)

This is not possible since https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/20c9001ee24191c64add9d2ffcb6da3ed56fc9f4/keps/sig-architecture/3136-beta-apis-off-by-default , features that depend on API groups to graduate have this deadlock, you can not enable the beta feature without enabling the API , ...  I spent a lot of time trying to find a solution to this and I could not find a better way, DRA went through the same .... it is an area that require someone to put a considerable time to try to solve it

> And it turns out, Antonio already even added the correct API endpoints to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133613#issuecomment-3202670338, he just accidentally also made the conformance test test the endpoints that weren't supposed to be part of conformance. So the bug here is really just "we have a conformance test which is testing something we already documented as not being part of conformance". (I hadn't realized that when I filed the bug.)

That is my fault, Ben point is about the impact of changing a conformance test, do we relax the VAP or do we make the endpoint ineligible for conformance? I do not have an opinion, but seems your argument is strong and convincing

title: will kublet re-execute the startup probes of the pods on the node when restarts?
body:
When I modified the kubelet configuration and restarted it, the startup probes of pods on the node seemed to be re-executed. However, since the logic of the startup probe is once logic in starting, re-execution caused the pods to enter a ContainerNotReady state.
This led to an online incident. So I'd like to know if this behavior of kubelet is as expected? If so, any best practice or suggestions? Thanks very much.

hi @debuggy this is clearly a bug and it's related to https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4781 in a sense
/triage accepted

Here is a repro example. You can create a pod like this and restart the kubelet on the node where this pod is scheduled to.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ubuntu-startup-probe-random
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ubuntu-container
    image: ubuntu:latest
    command: ["bash", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
    startupProbe:
      exec:
        command:
        - bash
        - -c
        - |
          fname=$(mktemp /root/startup-XXXXXXXX.tmp)
          echo "Created random file: $fname"
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
```

You can check the `/root` to see if it is re-executed.
```
[root@paco ~]kubectl exec -it ubuntu-startup-probe-random -- bash
root@paco:/# ls /root
startup-98IjnaJG.tmp  startup-O2FxZmDi.tmp

comments.body:
In step h, `1 timed out trying to allocate devices` indicates that the filter operation for one node did not complete within 10 seconds (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132033). **Why** it takes that long is unclear. Perhaps the scheduler really was CPU starved?

Is it always this one test which fails?

> The test restored the deviceclass at 02:17:56 (from e), and it seems the scheduler did not pick up DeviceClass update, I did not see any "DeviceClassUpdate" event, is this not expected?

Are other events logged? I don't think events get logged in sufficient detail to draw the conclusion that the update was missed. If it was, there would be no scheduling attempt.

I just checked a successful run https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-k8sbeta-default/1955102875705151488

I do see the `DeviceClassUpdate` event.
```
I0812 03:24:14.360703      11 scheduling_queue.go:1216] "Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue" pod="dra-1603/tester-1" event="resource.k8s.io/DeviceClassUpdate" queue="Active" hint=1
```

That log message is printed because the pod was moved, not because of receiving the event. If the pod wasn't in the unschedulable queue when the event was received, there's no output about receiving the event because it had no effect and there are many such events. Logging all of them would be too much.

I still think the main problem of at least this one run is the `1 timed out trying to allocate devices` - that shouldn't have happened. It doesn't seem to occur often. https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?test=retries%20pod%20scheduling%20after%20updating%20device%20class has some failures, but none related to it.

Searching for other occurrences (https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=timed%20out%20trying%20to%20allocate%20devices) leads to exactly one other failure in another test (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-k8sbeta-default/1954404589973278720).

I'm tentatively leaning towards "control plane overloaded" as the explanation for this issue.

> I'm tentatively leaning towards "control plane overloaded" as the explanation for this issue. I did not see any metrics dump in the e2e artifacts, so I used the audit entries from the kube-apiserver to plot a latency distribution: - use only the `GET` requests: jq filter `select(.stage == "ResponseComplete" and .verb == "get" and .objectRef != null and .objectRef.subresource == null)` - latency of a request in milliseconds is `event.StageTimestamp.Time.Sub(event.RequestReceivedTimestamp.Time).Milliseconds()` failed run: - we can see an elevation in the latency distribution (highlighted in the rectangle) that lasts for about 3m , this can potentially be the control plane overload - if we look at the test run, it overlaps with the degradation window. successful run: - the elevation in the latency distribution is pretty similar to the failed run - on the contrary, the test run does not overlap with the degradation, it runs about 8m later where the latency distribution seems normal.

/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

title: Debian now deprecates public key file used for K8s APT repo
body:
Hi, the K8s repo at https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/ uses a public key file having a hashing algorithm which Debian APT no longer considers safe.  The message emitted by APT (in response to command `apt update`) is:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
```
The command `apt update --audit` outputs:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
Audit: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Sub-process /usr/bin/sqv returned an error code (1), error message is:
   Error: Policy rejected packet type
   Caused by:
       Signature Packet v3 is not considered secure since 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
```
As I understand it, this would be because the public key is hashed using SHA1, rather than SHA256 or SHA512.  

I can suppress this warning (presumably until 1 February 2026) by copying file `/usr/share/apt/default-sequoia.config` to new file (in new parent directories) `/etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/apt-sequoia.config`, and changing the date in the last line from `2026-02-01` to `2027-02-01`.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Emit events when resize is marked as pending
body:
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127172, we decided to emit an event only when a resize is completed. We now want to also emit an event when a resize is marked as pending (deferred or infeasible).

When a deferred resize is retried, we will emit a new event if the message changes (i.e. the node's allocated resources have changed). 

/assign
/sig node
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

comments.body:
/triage accepted
/priority important-longterm

This is running into the "master is technically 1.35 but really still 1.34" issue with the fast forward approach to releasing.

It should resolve itself when 1.34 releases, or the script can be updated to handle this edge case.

cc @pohly 

@michaelasp has done some similar work recently for compat-version skew testing

I was thinking about using https://dl.k8s.io/release/latest-n.n.txt when https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable-n.n.txt is not available. Does this make sense to do?

@michaelasp which approach did you use?

For version skew, we checked whether or not the tag contained alpha.0 and just moved a version back if needed. I'm not sure if using latest-n-n will work since no matter what it is still considered to be 1.34 even if the tag has 1.35 in it. In this case we just made the skew n-2 instead of n-1 if it contains alpha.0 (e.g https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/experiment/compatibility-versions/e2e-skip-version-testing.sh#L87-L94)

> This is running into the "master is technically 1.35 but really still 1.34" issue with the fast forward approach to releasing.

I think it's the opposite: "master is 1.35 before there is a stable 1.34". As you said, this would resolve itself eventually, but handling this more gracefully in the meantime is worthwhile.

> For version skew, we checked whether or not the tag contained alpha.0 and just moved a version back if needed.

This sounds like a hack to me. Why should v1.35.0-alpha.0 be excluded from skew testing against v1.34.0 (assuming of course that there is one)? This seems to make the assumption that "if we are alpha, then there's no previous stable release yet" - that assumption may or may not be correct.

I like the fallback to pre-releases as suggested by @bart0sh better.
Or is the rationale that "alphas are so similar to the previous release, it's not worth testing against that previous release"?

> Or is the rationale that "alphas are so similar to the previous release, it's not worth testing against that previous release"?

I believe that the k8s binary still "thinks" of itself as 1.34 when it is in the 1.35-alpha.0 stage iirc. @BenTheElder can keep me honest here.

> > This is running into the "master is technically 1.35 but really still 1.34" issue with the fast forward approach to releasing.
>
> I think it's the opposite: "master is 1.35 before there is a stable 1.34". As you said, this would resolve itself eventually, but handling this more gracefully in the meantime is worthwhile.

What I mean is:

During code freeze while we have created the release-1.N branch, any changes landing in master must still be valid for v1.N, even through master is now tagged as an early v1.(N+1) version as far as build/test/CI are concerned.

Since we are still fast-forwarding, the code at that state must tolerate both 1.35 alpha and v1.34.

> Or is the rationale that "alphas are so similar to the previous release, it's not worth testing against that previous release"?

Specifically during the fast-forward time window we are still really developing 1.34 for the most part. We won't be merging 1.35 only changes yet.

In a related way, some of the code will only start to change on `-alpha.1` and greater, (API deprecations/removals) because that currently means we stop serving them ~3 weeks into the next release cycle instead of during the code freeze window where we're still fast forwarding.

So ... while in a pure sense I'd prefer to have everything working as if v1.(N+1), it's not the most pragmatic, and we already make that trade-off elsewhere.

---


We could also consider switching from stable builds on the previous release branch to just the *latest* build on that branch, but I assume there was an intentional decision to use stable tagged releases, in which case that would be a bigger trade-off than the one we just made.

Personally I prefer that approach, I think for testing Kubernetes it makes more sense to float at the latest commits in all branches.
... and we _should_ not be regressing within stable release branches. So the distinction between tagged or not is small.

> During code freeze while we have created the release-1.N branch, any changes landing in master must still be valid for v1.N

Agreed, therefore the tests against N-1 must continue to work.

> So ... while in a pure sense I'd prefer to have everything working as if v1.(N+1), it's not the most pragmatic, and we already make that trade-off elsewhere.

So treating v1.(N+1).0-alpha.0 like v1.N is basically just ensuring that this minor tag doesn't suddenly change what is being tested. The proper, less pragmatic way would be to ensure that together with starting the N+1 development cycle we also have all jobs ready for it. I can see why that is not feasible.

 In the case of DRA that means that in addition to the n-1 and n-2 jobs that we had leading up to v1.34, we also need n-3 (v1.35 with v1.32). The testing against v1.32 is what we lost when v1.35.0-alpha.0 was tagged because "n-1" became v1.34 and n-2 became v1.33.

There's a chicken-and-egg problem: if the jobs treat v1.35.0-alpha.0 like v1.34, then the new "n-3" job cannot be added yet because it would try to test against v1.31, which would fail in the case of DRA. The "n-3" would have to be introduced without the "ignore alpha" special case and then later that special case needs to be added, to be prepared for v1.36.0-alpha.0.

title: Race condition in kubelet's PodCertsManager might lead to memory leaks
body:
### What happened?

Introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4624cb9bb92186358e001be392e50e5d23b5cdd9, and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2825 gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2826 is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a unit test that runs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2822, expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

### Anything else we need to know?

Discussed at https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C05MW3382US/p1754992465556979

### Kubernetes version

1.34.0
</details>

</details>

/priority important-soon
We really expect the tests to leave the cluster in a clean state and be safe to run repeatedly for development.

A test in the default suite should not be doing that, it makes me think we might need to mark even the remaining test as [Disruptive].

End-users also sometimes run these tests to validate their clusters. At least _most_ of them focus on `[Conformance]` thankfully.

I think it is a known issue that extended resources remain forever in a node status, even after uninstalling the corresponding Device Plugin. cc @klueska for conformation.

However, they should be reported with zero capacity. The production code needs to handle that situation gracefully. Does it currently assume `example.com/foo is set == resources provided by device plugin`? I think that assumption is false, it needs to check for `example.com/foo > 0`.

Node status after removing the example device plugin:
```
    allocatable:
      cpu: "36"
      ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
      example.com/resource: "0"
      hugepages-1Gi: "0"
      hugepages-2Mi: "0"
      memory: 65531360Ki
      pods: "110"
    capacity:
      cpu: "36"
      ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
      example.com/resource: "2"
      hugepages-1Gi: "0"
      hugepages-2Mi: "0"
      memory: 65531360Ki
      pods: "110"
```

> [deployDevicePlugin](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/test/e2e/dra/deploy_device_plugin.go#L34) leaks the extended resource example.com/resource in node's status.Allocatable/Capacity. This causes conflicts for multiple tests using the extended resource in the same cluster.

This goes beyond test conflicts. Suppose a node was using a Device Plugin for some hardware. The admin uninstalls the Device Plugin and installs the DRA driver instead. Now the extended resources must be allocated via the DRA driver, no matter what the node status says. This is a blocker for beta.

/priority important-soon
/milestone v1.35

if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it. It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.

> Node status after removing the example device plugin:
> 
> ```
>     allocatable:
>       cpu: "36"
>       ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
>       example.com/resource: "0"
>       hugepages-1Gi: "0"
>       hugepages-2Mi: "0"
>       memory: 65531360Ki
>       pods: "110"
>     capacity:
>       cpu: "36"
>       ephemeral-storage: 1055762868Ki
>       example.com/resource: "2"
>       hugepages-1Gi: "0"
>       hugepages-2Mi: "0"
>       memory: 65531360Ki
>       pods: "110"
> ```

@swatisehgal @ffromani Just wondering why this is done this way? Would it help if we  stop counting unhealthy devices for capacity [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L473)?

> if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.

Is that known to clear it?

> It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.

Have you seen that happening? It seems that the scheduler doesn't schedule pods onto such nodes.

> I suspect it's implemented this way in purpose to distinguish between local node resources and cluster-level resources.

I'm not sure about that. That node status isn't about cluster-level resources. I suspect it is more because the kubelet cannot distinguish between "device plugin temporarily down" and "permanently removed".

> I'm not sure about that. That node status isn't about cluster-level resources. 

This is what I've read [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/nodestatus/setters.go#L278-L280). 

> I suspect it is more because the kubelet cannot distinguish between "device plugin temporarily down" and "permanently removed".

It's not that sophisticated, at least to my knowledge. When plugin deregistered or disconnected, Kubelet sets all its devices as `Unhealthy`, but includes them into the node status' `Capacity`. This is what you've quoted above: `Capacity: 2` in your example are those `Unhealthy` devices. This is why [I've asked maintainers about it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3213349044).

Good news is that the API server doesn't seem to be involved in updating `Capacity` and `Allocatable` fields. They're maintained by Kubelet. At least this is what I see in my experiments.

> > if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.
> 
> Is that known to clear it?
> 
node.status.Allocatable/Capacity is owned by kubelet, hence i think so, though i have not verified it. @bart0sh did you have a chance to verify it?

> > It is confusing to see an extended resource is scheduled to a node with node.status.Allocatable: 0.
> 
> Have you seen that happening? It seems that the scheduler doesn't schedule pods onto such nodes.
> 
scheduler could potentially schedule pods onto such nodes if those nodes happen to have DRA extended resources, and we change the DRA extended resources logic to allow that.

@yliaog 
> node.status.Allocatable/Capacity is owned by kubelet, hence i think so, though i have not verified it. @bart0sh did you have a chance to verify it?

So far I've changed Kubelet code to set both fields to 0 when plugin is unregistered and they stay unchanged for a long time. After that I went further - changed the code to stop publishing those fields if they're set to 0 and they've disappeared from the node status. That worked well.

However, I suspect that it was a design decision to publish them and also count Unhealthy devices as capacity to make them visible. For example if Allocatable is set to 0 and Capacity to 2, educated user/admin would understand that there are 2 unhealthy devices on the node and most probably it means that device plugin is disconnected. 
But all of this is just an educated guess. @klueska @ffromani and @swatisehgal can explain how it was designed and how it works.

@yliaog No, it was not a design decision. [Device Plugin KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3573-device-plugin) explicitly states that 
```
In general we expect Kubelet to remove any devices that are owned by
the failed device plugin from the node capacity.
We also expect node allocatable to be equal to node capacity.
```
which is good for us as we can consider current Kubelet behaviour as a bug and fix it.

> [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly) [@yliaog](https://github.com/yliaog)
> 
> > [@pohly](https://github.com/pohly) commented [4 days ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3197978535)
> > I think it is a known issue that extended resources remain forever in a node status, even after uninstalling the corresponding Device Plugin. cc [@klueska](https://github.com/klueska) for conformation.
> 
> I tried to modify Kubelet not to report local node extended resources with Allocatable/Capacity 0 and it worked just fine. However, I suspect it's implemented this way in purpose to distinguish between local node resources and cluster-level resources. [@ffromani](https://github.com/ffromani) [@swatisehgal](https://github.com/swatisehgal) [@SergeyKanzhelev](https://github.com/SergeyKanzhelev) Is it correct assumption?

I can only quickly comment before I'm going OOO for the full next week (till Sep 1).
This is likely correct, and there is no clear decisive record of why it is implemented like that. To be reasonnably sure, we need to reconstruct history from comments (both design docs at time) and reviews. Is not unheard that a [very early implementation bug survived till today,](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423#issuecomment-2934790530) and I won't be surprised if we find more instances along the way.

Another main problem is this behavior has been with us since many years. It's very likely someone depends on it in a way we can't imagine (Hyrum's law in full swing). So, albeit I stress that the suggested behavior looks better from every angle we can think of, we need to be super careful about the fix.

I think we need to carefully address these 2 items before we can move on.
And, to be redundant: I agree and I like much more if kubelet clears the extended resources as proposed.

@ffromani Thank you for the detailed answer! To trigger the discussion I've submitted https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133727, so we can discuss it further. The change is simple, but I agree that we need to be careful with it due to the reasons you've explained.
@yliaog While we're discussing the fix (which can take long, I suspect), can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

> if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.

@klueska said that restarting the kubelet does *not* clear the status.

> can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

I [believe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168) updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I agree that fixing kubelet is going to take time. Even if gets fixed, due to version skew clusters might use an older kubelet without the change. We should also look into fixing this in the scheduler. I think it should be safe to try with DRA when `allocatable` is zero: if the scheduler was trying to schedule without DRA, it would simply fail. With DRA there is at least a chance that it works.
/retitle DRA Extended Resource: support nodes where device plugin was uninstalled

> I think it should be safe to try with DRA when allocatable is zero

zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer. It means that plugin either unregistered or disconnected **at least** [5 minutes ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/types.go#L116-L120).

> I https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168 updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I'm guessing here, but stopping Kubelet, removing its checkpoint file and starting it again should do the trick as well.

> zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer.

Safer in which sense? What problem does waiting for 5 minutes avoid?

If `allocatable` dropped to zero only because the device driver temporarily got stopped (e.g. for an update), then it's still safe to try scheduling with DRA because there won't be DRA devices for the node, because those are still owned by the device driver.

> Safer in which sense?

In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node. We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

> In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node.

I think it's the other way around. If `allocatable` is zero, scheduling is guaranteed to fail unless we try to use DRA. Trying with DRA immediately *increases* the chances that scheduling will succeed. Waiting for `capacity` to become zero is *reducing* the chances.

> We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

Not for the same hardware.

> i see is it may cause application operators confusion, they see their pods are scheduled to a node with allocatable == 0.

But only if the DRA driver has been installed, right? Why would this be confusing? The admin clearly wants to manage the hardware with DRA, so scheduling the pod is what they want.
/assign @bart0sh

title: Pod crashloop backoff isn't entered until after the first restart
body:
While working on a crashloop backoff fix, I noticed that containers are often restarted immediately when they first crash, rather than being delayed by the appropriate backoff time. Essentially, containers have to crash twice before a backoff is applied.

When a pod first runs, [doBackOff](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b4b973c23757b28d1753c0803f85dfb655d905f1/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1607) is called but exits early because the container status is not “exited”. The container then starts and crashes, with the restart count at 0.

In the next sync loop, `doBackOff` is called again and returns false because no entry exists from the previous crash (because of the early exit). The backoff tracker adds an entry due to the call to `backOff.Next()` before returning. The container is restarted with a restart count of 1 and crashes a second time.

In the third loop, `doBackOff` properly reports the backoff duration and the pod is enqueued.

/sig node
/kind bug
author: hankfreund

comments.body:
> I noticed that containers are often restarted immediately when they first crash, rather than being delayed by the appropriate backoff time. Essentially, containers have to crash twice before a backoff is applied.

The current implementation works like this, and I think it’s tolerable. What problem did you run into?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/flowcontrol/backoff.go#L96-L108

/triage accepted

upstream/consistency contract: Kubelet should restart immediately after the first failure, and apply exponential backoff starting from the second. Following the approach suggested in the issue would violate this contract, affecting timing assumptions and state checks in end-to-end/consistency tests.

title: Segfault on e2e tests after 1.34 RC
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

All kind tests are failing due to a segfault in the apiserver with the 1.34 rc

### Which tests are failing?

Many e2e tests running on the newest RC

### Since when has it been failing?

Since the release was cut and we bump the tag to 1.34

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#kind-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Not fully sure but it seems due to these two commits conflicting with each other.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131902/files

and 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132965/files

One uses a metric that is deprecated in 1.34 and is causing a nil pointer exception, seems like that causes that metric to be set to nil but seems likely to be the case from the logs.

An easy fix might be to use the new metric defined by @serathius in the second PR. 

CC @liuxu623 who made the first change.

Seems likely to be a release blocker.

title: An object created through SSA with a non-nil deletion timestamp will not get deleted
body:
### What happened?

```
$ cat cm.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:42:06Z"
  deletionTimestamp: 2025-08-05T16:42:06Z
  name: test
  namespace: kubevirt-vm

$ k apply --server-side -f cm.yaml
Warning: Detected changes to resource test which is currently being deleted.
configmap/test serverside-applied

$ k get cm test  -oyaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:45:59Z"
  deletionTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:42:06Z"
  name: test
  namespace: kubevirt-vm
  resourceVersion: "257079249"
  uid: caa288c7-9b51-4365-a062-a4020d4bef93
```

Then deleting it causes it to go, so I am guessing this is rooted in insufficient event handling in the GC controller, since only SSA allows to create objects with a non-nil deletion timestamp:
```
$ k delete    -f cm.yaml
configmap "test" deleted

$ k get cm test  -oyaml
Error from server (NotFound): configmaps "test" not found
```

The CM to immediately be gone

title: The pod is in the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
body:
### What happened?

We found that after the kubelet process restarts, some pods dependent on device plugins may enter the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
The reason is that when the kubelet restarts, it retrieves the pod list from the apiserver and begins processing the pods. At this point, the device plugin has not yet had the chance to register, which can cause the pods to enter an UnexpectedAdmissionError state. As a result, the containers are killed, and the workload then pulls up a new replica.
Assuming the service has only two replicas, the aforementioned reasons may lead to the pod being rebuilt, during which the service will be interrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Containers should not exit due to kubelet restarts.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure the pod to depend on the device plugin and restart kubelet.

This should be handled by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118635 done in 1.28 . @Black-max12138 could you please add more details to understand the case on which you hit this issue?

When the kubelet restarts, if the device plugin does not register in time, the canAdmitPod method returns false, and the rejectPod method sets the pod to a failed state. In the next loop, the container will be stopped. @ffromani 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/948afe5ca072329a73c8e79ed5938717a5cb3d21/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2593-L2597

> [@Black-max12138](https://github.com/Black-max12138) thanks for the update! In 1.28 we added code in device manager to handle the kubelet restart case, which is meant to prevent this very issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.0/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L585 because it was reported already back in time: [#118559](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118559) > > We also have some e2e tests to ensure this behavior: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.31.0/test/e2e_node/device_plugin_test.go#L315 > > so, in order to understand this issue, it's helpful to understand what is different in your flow. It would help to have more precise reproduction steps, or even better a new e2e test, because from what I can infer from the original description, you seem to restart just and only the kubelet, thus you should fall in the fixed flow above. Thank you for your reply. I just took a look at the code and have a few questions. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/948afe5ca072329a73c8e79ed5938717a5cb3d21/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L598-L601 The `sourcesReady.AllReady()` method returning true indicates that the kubelet is already able to communicate with the apiserver. The `isContainerAlreadyRunning(podUID, contName)` returning true indicates that the container is still running. Therefore, when the kubelet restarts and the SyncLoop ADD logs are already visible, `sourcesReady.AllReady()` should be true, and at this point, the if condition should be false. So, is there still a bug here?

I think I see the problem. The assumption here was that `AllReady()` stays `false` up till all the pods have been processed. We may still have a race here if indeed `AllReady()` gets true as soon as the kubelet can communicate with the apiserver. We need to revisit this flow
/priority backlog
Bumping. This issue is affecting us too, relatively frequently.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137919 should fix this issue

title: Enabling the EventedPLEG feature gate causes pods with sidecar containers to get stuck in the pending state
body:
### What happened?

Enabling the `EventedPLEG` feature gate causes pods with sidecar containers to get stuck in the pending state

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod can enter the running state.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enabling the EventedPLEG feature gate and create a pod with sidecar container.

```
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
  labels:
    app: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: alpine:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'while true; do echo "logging" >> /opt/logs.txt; sleep 1; done']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /opt
      initContainers:
        - name: logshipper
          image: alpine:latest
          restartPolicy: Always
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /opt/logs.txt']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /opt
      volumes:
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}
EOF
